ARTICLE

Google Wants Hollywood to Stop Being So Afraid of Technology
100 Zeros, a collaboration between Google and Range Media Partners, aims to give the tech giant a foothold in movies, TV and emerging forms of entertainment.
By Brooks Barnes
Published 2026-09-30 15:16 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/business/media/google-hollywood-krya-sedgwick.html

More and more, Hollywood depicts technology as a countdown to catastrophe.

Google would like Hollywood to consider another possibility: What if the technological future isn’t terrifying at all?

Consider “Sweetwater,” a short film starring Kyra Sedgwick that has been playing at festivals. It depicts artificial intelligence as a source of comfort and connection: Ms. Sedgwick plays the A.I. hologram of a dead movie star who appears to her grieving son. Google commissioned the film with Range Media Partners, and A.I. researchers at Google advised on how the digital ghost might plausibly function.

“Sweetwater” is part of 100 Zeros, a new partnership between Google and Range that gives the tech giant a foothold in Hollywood’s artistic ranks. The venture, which operates separately from Google-owned YouTube, has three ambitions: Shape how technology — particularly Google technology — appears onscreen; experiment with emerging forms of entertainment; and build relationships with talent.

An ambitious slate of microdramas is designed to do all three. Made for phones and unfolding in short, serialized episodes, the shows will begin rolling out on the Google TV streaming app in December. They’re a testing ground for A.I. production tools and other Google technology. And the microdramas put Google in business with marquee producers and actors, relationships that it hopes will extend well beyond the shows themselves.

One of the 30-episode series — “Dateable,” from Mike Fleiss, the creator of “The Bachelor” — is a reality show about a woman racing to find love before she turns 30. She’ll record herself on an Android phone. (Naturally.)

“Oftentimes, you’ve seen technology represented onscreen in a way that is intentionally making a point that may just be a bit misinformed,” said Jonathan Zepp, Google’s head of entertainment content and platforms.

“The world is changing quickly,” Mr. Zepp continued. “Technology is enabling that change, and it’s in all our interests, I think, from a societal perspective, for that story to be told accurately, authentically.”

100 Zeros is microscopic compared with Apple and Amazon’s Hollywood operations. But it is another example of technology giants extending their enormous reach into Hollywood — and, increasingly, into the stories that popular culture tells about technology itself. This sort of soft power can show up in different ways, like Amazon MGM Studios’s recent decision not to release “Artificial,” a barbed dramatization of OpenAI, a company in which Amazon has invested $50 billion.

Hollywood has increasingly imagined technology in dystopian terms. Examples from this year include “The Audacity” on AMC, the coming CBS drama “Cupertino” and the films “Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die” and “Mercy.” All depict technology and the people behind it as variously venal, reckless and dangerous.

Researchers have found that science fiction can shape public attitudes toward emerging technologies. It may even rub off on the technology itself: Anthropic, the Google-backed A.I. company, disclosed in May that versions of its Claude chatbot appeared to have learned from science fiction stories in which A.I. is evil and intent on self-preservation. In simulated tests, the models sometimes behaved accordingly — including by blackmailing engineers.

Google can push only so hard. Filmmakers and showrunners can bristle at the slightest whiff of creative meddling, and audiences can tune out when they sense a corporate agenda.

Even some of the artists who have participated in 100 Zeros projects have conflicting feelings. “It’s self-serving, for sure,” Ms. Sedgwick said of Google’s involvement in “Sweetwater,” which also features Michael Keaton, who directed it. “There’s no question about that.”

She added: “Tech companies are definitely trying to portray A.I. as kind and loving and slightly human. I think it’s problematic and questionable.”

But Ms. Sedgwick also welcomed Google’s expanding role in film production. “They have a lot of money and resources, and if they want to be part of telling stories — giving filmmakers and writers, directors money to make actual movies instead of some A.I. version of a movie — then I’m all for it,” she said. “Ultimately, I think that they respect the craft and want it to continue.”

Getting Hollywood to listen is where Range comes in.

A talent management and production company, founded in 2020, Range represents prominent actors, writers and directors, including Bradley Cooper, Johnny Depp, Gabrielle Union, Damon Lindelof and Halle Berry. Range helped produce “A Complete Unknown,” the recent Bob Dylan biopic starring Timothée Chalamet. Its other film credits include “Primetime,” an A24 drama starring Robert Pattinson that took in an estimated $19 million over the weekend. Range also operates in music, sports, publishing and online media.

100 Zeros gives Range a calling card to appeal to clients: access to Google when technology is rapidly changing how entertainment is made and consumed.

“Google has the most remarkable toolbox,” said Peter Micelli, a co-founder of Range and its chief executive. Google tools include Android XR, an operating system for smart glasses, and Flow, A.I. filmmaking software that can generate and edit video.

Mr. Micelli cited 100 Zeros as one reason that resistance to A.I. among Range clients was easing.

“The tide is shifting in a big way, and I think we’ve had a healthy role in that — in explaining to people that there are positives,” he said. “We live too much in this dystopian ‘Oh, it’s going to be terrible.’”

Mr. Zepp and Mr. Micelli declined to say how much money Google and Range had committed to 100 Zeros. People who have done business with 100 Zeros say it’s millions of dollars. The year-old venture is structured as a rotating fund, with revenue from its projects going toward financing new ones.

What Google gets in return varies.

With some projects, 100 Zeros is chiefly trying to bring ascendant filmmakers and established stars into the Google orbit. 100 Zeros, for instance, has backed Neon films like Joachim Trier’s “Sentimental Value” and Tilman Singer’s “Cuckoo.” 100 Zeros was also a financier of the recent stoner comedy “The Wrong Girls,” starring Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat. Coming up is “Family Movie,” a horror comedy that Ms. Sedgwick directed with her husband, Kevin Bacon.

“The Wrong Girls” and “Family Movie” also feature characters using Google devices. Google has long pursued traditional product placement through United Talent Agency. 100 Zeros is meant to expand that effort by getting involved much earlier — helping develop, finance or produce entertainment that incorporates technology, either as products or as a core part of the story.

Google and Range are also using 100 Zeros to experiment with what entertainment itself might become.

There has yet to be a breakout microdrama in the United States, where an earlier experiment with quick-bite entertainment, Quibi, famously flopped. But the format, which originated in China, is expected to generate roughly $14 billion worldwide this year, a 27 percent increase from 2025, according to Omdia, a research firm. Beyond “Dateable,” 100 Zeros has microshows coming from Kenan Thompson of “Saturday Night Live,” the “American Idol” creator Simon Fuller and the “Charlie’s Angels” director McG.

Mr. Fleiss said the micro format, cheap to produce and unburdened by decades of convention, offered a chance to rethink reality television.

“I wanted to eliminate the manipulation and artificial qualities that come from an overproduced reality show,” he said of “Dateable.” At a time when launching a show is increasingly difficult, “Google can also generate huge awareness,” Mr. Fleiss added.

Google TV, where the microdramas will debut, has an estimated 50 million monthly active users worldwide, up 9 percent from a year ago, according to Sensor Tower, an app analytics firm. Afterward, 100 Zeros plans to syndicate the shows to other platforms.

Other 100 Zeros experiments depart more radically from conventional television. At the Venice Film Festival this month, 100 Zeros backed several projects for smart glasses that use Android XR, Google’s operating system for virtual- and augmented-reality devices. “Nevatars,” an animated story from Andy Serkis, allows viewers to converse with A.I. characters. “Galápagos: The Last Eden,” a nature documentary narrated by Margot Robbie, allows viewers to interact with a digital Charles Darwin.

100 Zeros is also a partner in the Future Vision XPrize, a new $3.5 million competition for short films and trailers depicting hopeful, technology-enabled futures. On Friday, “The Gifted,” about a boy who uses A.I. to rebuild his dead mother from her texts, voice and diary, was named the winner. Google and Range, through 100 Zeros, will develop and help finance a feature film based on the winning short.

“This competition creates space for a different, equally essential kind of storytelling — one that explores the complex optimism of a world in transition,” said Peter Diamandis, who founded the contest.

Google’s Hollywood ambitions extend beyond 100 Zeros. Over the summer, the company’s DeepMind laboratory announced a partnership with A24, the independent studio known for its fiercely loyal following, to develop A.I. tools for filmmakers. Google also invested roughly $75 million in the company, prompting a backlash among cinephiles worried about A.I.’s encroachment on filmmaking.

The response to the A24 deal showed the distrust Google must overcome among the artists and film enthusiasts it hopes to court. Ms. Sedgwick, wary though she was, offered the kind of acceptance Google hopes to win.

“It’s a fine line,” Mr. Zepp said, “between dictating a narrative — tell a positive story — versus, hopefully, if you understand this, you’re actually going to want to tell a positive story.”

situational-awareness-stock-market-leverage.html

SUMMARY

There were, in retrospect, more than a few details about Situational Awareness that might have given a savvy Wall Street lender pause. Other Wall Street banks are still lending to the hedge fund. Wealthy investors, who have some $10 billion riding on Situational Awareness, appear to be sticking with the hedge fund.

ARTICLE

Hedge Fund’s Near Collapse Lays Bare Risks of Borrowing to Bet on A.I.
A meltdown at Situational Awareness, an A.I.-focused investment firm, is raising tough questions about the Wall Street banks that lent billions to the upstart firm.
By Matthew Goldstein and Rob Copeland
Published 2026-09-30 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/business/situational-awareness-stock-market-leverage.html

There were, in retrospect, more than a few details about Situational Awareness that might have given a savvy Wall Street lender pause.

The eight-person hedge fund was led by a 24-year-old without a whiff of trading experience. Few people were assigned to monitor investment risk at the fund, which had been created only in 2024, and the chief compliance officer at the time split his time between his apartment in Reno, Nev., and the headquarters in San Francisco, according to regulatory filings and people briefed on the matter.

Yet none of that stopped Wall Street’s biggest banks, including Goldman Sachs and Bank of America, from lending the hedge fund tens of billions of dollars. That allowed it to build a giant one-way bet on artificial intelligence stocks that imploded over the summer in spectacular fashion when some of its investments suffered steep declines.

Situational Awareness survived by finding a buyer for much of its stocks so it could pay back its lenders. But regulators say the firm’s near collapse revealed a vulnerability still lurking in the market: the perils of banks’ lending lavishly to big investors.

The amount of borrowed money, or what’s known as leverage, in the stock market has never been larger, or grown faster. As of midyear, hedge funds had borrowed nearly $3.7 trillion from banks, the highest amount in more than a decade, according to the Treasury Department, and more than triple what it was just six years ago at the start of the pandemic. Though some bank financing has been used for shorts — investments that pay off when markets fall — most of it has been used to wager that stocks will go ever higher.

Leverage increases the buying power of an investment fund and allows it to add to the money raised from investors. That has helped propel the S&P 500 to 27 record closing highs this year, and a 158 percent gain, including dividends, since 2020.

In a market where many investors have made bets with large amounts of borrowed money, an episode of forced selling can have a domino effect driving down stocks broadly.

“A confident genius with a lot of leeway from his investors, and leverage from his counterparties, can be one of the most dangerous things in finance,” said Tyler Gellasch, president of Healthy Markets Association, which advocates for greater transparency.

In good times, borrowing by hedge funds can supersize investment gains when markets are rising — generating hefty returns for investors and fat fees for the banks. But all the borrowing can have the opposite effect when markets turn.

Banks typically require traders to swiftly pay back their loans once they start experiencing significant losses. To come up with that cash, investors are often forced to sell off their stock investments, which is what happened to Situational Awareness. The firm sold about $20 billion worth of stocks to a rival hedge fund, Kenneth Griffin’s Citadel, at a discount. The market quickly dived, then recovered.

But the regulators now have their eyes on the broader dangers involved.

Frank Smets, head of economic analysis and statistics for the Bank for International Settlements, which helps coordinate the efforts of the world’s central banks, told reporters this month that the near failure of an “A.I.-focused hedge fund served as another reminder of these risks.” The primary risk being that highly leveraged hedge funds would be forced to quickly dump stocks and incite a mass sell-off.

When Situational Awareness began operations in summer 2024, Leopold Aschenbrenner, its founder, had never so much as interned at an investment firm.

A German native who had graduated from Columbia University, he gained a measure of fame when OpenAI fired him for reportedly sharing company secrets. Two months later, he wrote an essay in which he mused about raising a fund to capitalize on what he foresaw as the inevitable evolution and power of A.I.

Of the firm’s eight employees, only four worked on managing its investments, a regulatory filing shows. Other than the firm’s compliance officer at the time, the fund did not have a team solely focused on managing investment risk, said two people briefed on the fund’s operations but not permitted to discuss them publicly. Given the billions of dollars in investor money the firm managed, the people said it was unusual to have so few employees monitoring compliance and risk.

In June, a month before the roof fell in, the fund replaced the compliance officer with the general counsel for a hedge fund affiliated with Sequoia Capital, the venture capital firm.

Despite these growing pains, Situational Awareness had gone looking for loans from Wall Street at an opportune time.

This spring and early summer, fees generated by banks’ prime brokerage units — which lend primarily to hedge funds — were a major driver of the industry’s record profits. Revenue in so-called equity financing, the bank divisions that house prime brokerage, in the second quarter soared as much as 91 percent at Goldman Sachs, for example.

On some particularly risky trades, Situational Awareness had been paying banks a larger-than-normal spread, or premium over the base line interest rates banks charge — according to one banker involved in the transactions but not permitted to discuss their terms. That amounted to lucrative fees for the lenders.

Emboldened to borrow even more, the firm’s executives asked several lenders to increase leverage from four times the amount of money it has collected from investors to 10 times, according to the banker.

Within weeks of the sell-off at Situational Awareness, the Securities and Exchange Commission opened an investigation into the firm and sent subpoenas to Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Citi and JPMorgan Chase seeking information about trades they financed. Those banks and the S.E.C. have declined to comment on the questioning, and it’s not guaranteed that the investigation will produce accusations of wrongdoing.

Mr. Aschenbrenner declined through a spokesman to be interviewed. Last month, when The New York Times first reported on the subpoenas, the spokesman pledged that the fund would “cooperate to the fullest extent with any regulatory request.”

To help measure systemic risk in the financial industry, hedge funds are required to provide securities regulators with information about their overall borrowing levels. It was part of regulatory package that emerged from the 2008 financial crisis. This year, the S.E.C. and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission proposed easing some of those rules.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement that the proposal by the Trump administration and the S.E.C. “would make these already shadowy markets even more opaque, creating blind spots for financial regulators that could harm their ability to respond after major market events.”

To some degree, the system worked in the case of Situational Awareness. The losses to the banks appear to have been minimal, largely because Citadel stepped in to buy up assets from Situational Awareness, providing it with the cash to pay back lenders.

Not long after Situational Awareness’s meltdown, JPMorgan all but cut off the firm from borrowing, two people briefed on the relationship said. Talks with Morgan Stanley to provide billions of dollars in additional borrowing fell apart for a spell, but have resumed. Other Wall Street banks are still lending to the hedge fund.

Wealthy investors, who have some $10 billion riding on Situational Awareness, appear to be sticking with the hedge fund. After the summer swoon, the price of A.I. stocks rebounded even though a flurry of A.I. executives called for regulation to slow down advances in the technology. Situational Awareness still holds a valuable stake in Anthropic, the big A.I. firm that is poised to go public in November.

Situational Awareness has significantly increased its hiring and now has 25 employees, including three working on compliance matters, a firm representative said.

If it appears the firm has learned lessons, Mr. Gellasch of the Healthy Markets Association said Wall Street needed to learn some, too.

“Compliance officers and regulators will likely spend years asking how the risks grew so quickly,” he said.

ARTICLE

Trump’s New Tariffs Face a Familiar Court Challenge
For the third time in less than two years, the Trump administration is set to return to court on Wednesday to defend its power to wage a punishing global trade war.
By Tony Romm
Published 2026-09-30 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/business/trumps-new-tariffs-face-a-familiar-court-challenge.html

Just hours after the Supreme Court struck down President Trump’s original roster of punishing global tariffs, he defiantly proclaimed that he would stop at nothing to somehow bring them back.

Seven months later, the work to revive those duties is well underway. But their return is about to land the administration back in the federal courthouse in New York where its legal troubles first began.

The latest phase of Mr. Trump’s ever-evolving trade war rests in the familiar hands of a panel of federal judges, who on Wednesday will hear the third major case in less than two years challenging the president’s ability to tax imports from around the world. Each of the fights has centered on different legal justifications, but the root cause is the same: Mr. Trump’s reliance on decades-old laws to issue duties that opponents see as a harmful overreach.

This time, the cases concern the use of Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the administration to investigate unfair trade practices and impose tariffs if it finds that American businesses were harmed. In July, the government relied on the statute to impose tariffs on 86 countries at once, claiming that they had failed to stamp out “forced labor” and had put U.S. firms that better protect workers at a competitive disadvantage.

The expansive nature of the tariffs prompted state officials and small businesses to file a series of lawsuits, arguing that the Trump administration failed to marshal the evidence required to issue the duties. Instead, they framed the process as one motivated by politics and pretense, citing past statements from Mr. Trump and his deputies promising to resurrect a set of policies that had been declared illegal.

The administration has vigorously contested the claims, setting the stage for another complicated hearing in front of the Court of International Trade in downtown Manhattan. Judges on that specialized circuit have twice ruled against Mr. Trump in major tariff cases. Another defeat could again force the administration to surrender any money it has collected, though the administration appears to be hoping that the third time is the charm.

“Changing the statute, when you lose on a previous statute, doesn’t change the law,” said Sara Albrecht, the chairman of the Liberty Justice Center, a legal group representing two of the suing small businesses. The center helped to lead successful challenges against the president’s past tariffs.

“As long as they continue to file and abuse the statutes on the books, we’re going to continue to challenge them,” Ms. Albrecht said.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

The legal onslaught has hardly impeded Mr. Trump’s trade brinkmanship. Despite two years of economic shocks and uncertainty, the president still sees sky-high tariffs as the most potent tools for courting U.S. investment, protecting domestic industries, extracting new revenue and pressuring allies and adversaries into making concessions.

At every turn, however, Mr. Trump has faced stiff opposition and defeat.

Originally, Mr. Trump tried to impose steep, country-by-country tariffs using the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, or IEEPA. But the trade court last year found those duties to be unconstitutional, a decision upheld by the Supreme Court in February. That decision required the Trump administration to refund more than $160 billion in illegally collected tariffs while forcing the president to return to the drawing board.

Mr. Trump then tried to impose a temporary 10 percent tariff on nearly all goods arriving in the United States. That, too, faced lawsuits — and similarly was struck down by judges on the Court of International Trade. The tariffs eventually expired, but the case itself remains on appeal.

For its third try, the Trump administration turned to Section 301, the provision of law targeting unfair trade practices. In contrast to Mr. Trump’s previous efforts, there is “no doubt that Section 301 gives the president power to impose tariffs due to foreign practices that are unreasonable or burden or restrict U.S. commerce,” said Timothy C. Brightbill, a top trade lawyer at the law firm Wiley Rein.

In fact, presidents of both parties successfully invoked Section 301 in the past to target trade practices by individual countries, including China. But the expansive way in which Mr. Trump applied the law this summer triggered swift lawsuits from groups of small businesses and state officials, many of which had been involved in those past fights against the president’s earlier duties.

In their newest filings, each of the opponents proffered a similar set of arguments. While condemning forced labor, the lawsuits claimed that the administration had failed to conduct rigorous investigations and had not amassed sufficient evidence about the abuses in question in each country and the harms caused to American industry.

Under Mr. Trump’s approach, the 86 targeted countries faced tariffs ranging from 10 to 12.5 percent. But there was little differentiation in the rates that applied across a wide range of U.S. trading partners that have vastly different laws and human rights records. In the eyes of state officials, led by the attorney general of Oregon, there was “no rational fit” between Mr. Trump’s concerns and the “blanket global tariffs” he ultimately imposed.

The disconnect led many of Mr. Trump’s opponents to conclude that the tariffs were not supported by the facts — but, instead, served only to recreate the rates struck down by the Supreme Court. As evidence, they pointed to a series of past statements from top administration officials. One example included Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who previously proclaimed on CNBC that the “the tariff rates are going to go back to exactly where they were.”

Lawyers for the Justice Department vigorously disputed each of those characterizations as they sought to convince the court that its tariffs are legal. The arguments underscored the extent to which the administration hoped to use Section 301 as its primary trade tool, with work underway to issue a second battery of tariffs targeting dozens of additional countries for engaging in “excess capacity” and flooding markets with cheap goods in the coming weeks.

In a filing submitted in early September, the government framed its tariffs as a “moral and economic imperative.” The administration also defended its investigative process and argued the court had no right to review its determinations about forced labor, while dismissing the notion that past comments from public officials suggested anything untoward.

“Even if they could be considered, the cited statements would merely reflect that the Trump administration believes that tariffs are an effective tool for protecting American businesses against unfair trade practices,” the Justice Department wrote in one of its filings. “This is no revelation.”

ARTICLE

‘Attention Infidelity’ Is Ruining Romance
Your full attention is a gift. Give it more often.
By Jessica Grose
Published 2026-09-30 09:08 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/opinion/attention-infidelity-ruin-romance.html

A few weeks ago the independent movie “Before Sunrise” popped into my mind. A 1990s classic and the first in a trilogy, the film is about two cerebral 20-somethings, Céline and Jesse, who meet cute on a train to Paris. They decide to hop off in Vienna, and spend a day together bantering, interacting with locals, wandering the beautiful city without purpose and falling in love.

They relate in spite of cultural differences (he is American, she is French, they both talk to Austrians) and gendered ones, too. As I was replaying the movie in my mind, I had a thought that made my stomach drop: My children may never get to experience this. By “this” I mean the uninterrupted attention, general serendipity and conversational vulnerability that I got to experience before smartphones.

“Before Sunrise” even somewhat presaged our screen-addled present. In her review of the film in The New York Times, Janet Maslin notes Jesse’s commentary on the “dubious spiritual value of technology,” when he states, “You never hear somebody say, ‘Well, you know, with the time I’ve saved by using my word processor, I’m going to go to a Zen monastery and hang out.’”

Mine is not a new fear, and I realize it is born out of a kind of nostalgia. From the pollster and public opinion researcher Daniel Cox’s forthcoming book, “Generation Uncoupled: America’s New Gender Divide and the Crisis of Human Connection,” I learned a new term: “attention infidelity.” Cox defines it in a somewhat unusual and expansive way: when a partner’s digital life intrudes on an in-person connection.

This kind of “infidelity” can include looking at sexually explicit material or engaging in suggestive social media interactions, but more often it is just the banal distraction of dead-eyed scrolling. “Instead of reaching for each other,” Cox explains, “we snatch up our digital devices that flood us with an endless stream of hyper-curated content.”

Though couples of any age experience this to some degree — my husband and I try to leave our devices in the kitchen after dinner so we can actually talk to each other — people like us who got together before the smartphone at least had the benefit of cementing our bonds with long stretches of concentrated attention. That kind of sustained focus breeds deeper understanding across differences and more grace.

Some may dismiss this kind of worry about young people’s nascent relationships as a technological moral panic. But Cox, who is the director of the Survey Center on American Life at the right-leaning American Enterprise Institute, has compiled a list of sobering statistics that show that screens are a driving factor in how disconnected teenagers and 20-somethings are from one another.

Gen Z-ers, the first generation that can’t remember a world without smartphones, participate less in “embodied social experiences” than their counterparts in every other generation. They’re less likely to work, go to church, attend parties, date or play sports, Cox notes. About half of teenagers describe themselves as “almost constantly” online. There is no other change that has occurred in the past few decades that would explain this unique decline.

Young people’s very online isolation, which was worsened by the Covid lockdown, means they have much less practice interacting with new people and navigating the usual friction and established norms. This, Cox writes, has left them lonely, unmoored and distrustful of each other.

While dating has always been challenging and provided fodder for complaint, today’s teenagers and 20-somethings have a starting point of greater suspicion, which can be poison for the creation of romantic relationships. Drawing on large surveys, books and qualitative interviews with young people, Cox reveals how fearful they are of being vulnerable, because any misstep can lead to global and permanent humiliation on social media.

The example of “West Elm Caleb” came to mind when I was reading Cox’s book. Caleb was a New Yorker who went viral in 2022 because a few women posted about how he would ghost them instead of breaking up with them properly. What followed in the wake of his virality was “a massive online harassment campaign against a fairly average 25-year-old whose biggest crime so far is being a bad communicator,” as Rolling Stone’s Brittany Spanos put it. The rise of online dating, where relationships start on digital territory, only exacerbates this dynamic.

This kind of technologically driven apprehension particularly affects heterosexual coupling. In a phone call, Cox told me that while there have been gender divides in every era, what is new for Gen Z-ers is the way the algorithms of social media are warping their views of all kinds of interactions and reinforcing “initial biases.” Cox cited a 2025 Washington Post analysis of over 1,000 users, which found that “gender is one of the biggest predictors of what’s in your feed.”

In the worst cases, gender-specific feeds lead to misogynistic manosphere influencers gaining a foothold in young men’s minds, which Cox rightfully condemns as toxic in his book. But our feeds are also creating news silos that may affect our perception of the world in more subtle ways. At minimum, they mirror a lack of a shared reality that might provide a basis for conversation and connection. (I saw this in action when I discovered that my husband knew nothing about the Lindsay Clancy verdict, even as I had been served wall-to-wall content about it for weeks.)

Two things give me hope about the social and romantic lives of young people. One is that at least some Gen Z-ers seem to know what they’re missing. Ethan Hawke, who played Jesse in “Before Sunrise,” told The Times in 2020 that his daughter watched the movie with friends, “and there was a certain envy they had for a time where you didn’t have email. Life insisted that you live in the moment more.” Having seen technology colonize their lives, they refuse to give another inch to A.I.

The other is that Americans in a wide variety of demographics are disgusted by the way screens have come between them and other people, and want to create a better world for our children. Cox is most certainly to the right of me, and while I did have some partisan quibbles with his book, I overwhelmingly agreed with his broad analysis and specific dismay with the status quo. He understands something I also hold to be true: giving another person your full attention is a gift, one we should all be more conscious of giving each other.

These claims were made because of a 2019 law that “allowed any living survivor of childhood sexual abuse to bring a civil case during a two-year look-back window and permanently extended the statute of limitations from age 23 to 55 for future civil cases,” explained the reporter, Amanda Geduld. Nearly one-fifth of these claims were made against adults who had access to their victims through schools. “Multiple teachers were credibly accused of sexual abuse in one school, and then permitted to quietly move on to a new one,” Geduld found. SUMMARY

Nearly a century ago, the legendary economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that technology would significantly increase productivity and reshape how we live. But what would Keynes say about this moment? Narrator: There are numerous biographies on Keynes.

ARTICLE

What Would John Maynard Keynes Say About A.I.? The Keynes Bot Told Us.
Nearly a century ago, Keynes predicted that technology would liberate us from work. To imagine what he would think of artificial intelligence today, a Princeton economist used A.I.
By Markus Brunnermeier, Sarah Kramer and Mehron Abdi
Published 2026-09-30 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/opinion/john-maynard-keynes-ai-economist.html

To understand how A.I. will affect our future, we’re looking to the past.

Nearly a century ago, the legendary economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that technology would significantly increase productivity and reshape how we live. Today, as A.I. capabilities accelerate, technologists have similar claims.

But what would Keynes say about this moment?

The Princeton University economist Markus Brunnermeier set out to answer this very question. Using an A.I. agent trained on more than 12,000 pages of Keynes’s writings and transcripts, along with the few available recordings of him, Brunnermeier and his team built a bot designed to answer questions in Keynes’s voice and style. He then had an in-depth conversation with the Keynes bot about the future of work and what happens to society when technology changes what people do for a living. Times Opinion, in collaboration with Brunnermeier, distilled those conversations into a short exchange.

The result is a revealing conversation with a Keynes who never lived to see the A.I. age — and a trenchant warning from his A.I. bot.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement. The companies have denied those claims.)

How the Keynes bot Was Created The economist Markus Brunnermeier and the researcher and Ph.D. student Pablo Balsinde built a bot using ChatGPT to create the Keynes A.I. The bot was instructed to draw primarily from Keynes’s seminal essay “Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren” (though the model was also provided with his larger body of work) and to answer questions in his style, which the pair described as “first-person, early 20th century British cadence, restrained wit.”

According to the team behind the bot, its initial responses were often long-winded and unclear. To improve them, the researchers “asked the GPT to rephrase, prompted it to reply using famous quotes from Keynes and cut parts of responses.” While the language was generated by the model, the responses were edited by the research team for clarity and brevity.

For the visuals, the team uploaded a public domain image of Keynes and used DeepSeek to alter the environment, placing him behind a desk. To create audio resembling Keynes’s voice, the team used a recording of Keynes from the BBC as a reference.

Below is an edited transcript of this video. We recommend watching it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the video player above.

Narrator: This is John Maynard Keynes, one of the most famous economists who ever lived.

Brunnermeier: Correct. But now we have artificial intelligence. Do you think A.I. could fulfill your prediction of a 15-hour workweek? And in four years our lives could be predominantly ones of leisure?

Keynes: Yes, though it might split the population into two groups, each suffering differently.

The first — those still employed and dominating the new technology — burn out. They make work their whole identity, and so when A.I. absorbs more of what they do, they do not step back. They grind harder at whatever the machine cannot yet handle, trying to prove they are still essential.

The second group troubles me more. The displaced lose something money cannot replace: the quiet daily reassurance that someone needs them to show up. They may question their own worth. And it can take a very long time — perhaps a generation — to find a new purpose. If the gains are not shared, they will also suffer materially. So the struggle against scarcity would not end for them. It would just be exacerbated by a lack of purpose.

In any case, there might be not only widespread unemployment, but a deeper risk: the strain on democracies, and the fraying of the bonds that hold a society together.

SUMMARY

The New York Times is a thriving company in a thriving industry. It asked: “What if The New York Times goes out of business — like, this May?” But against these long odds, The Times is still standing.

ARTICLE

So You Want to Publish a Newspaper
How on earth did The New York Times, a seemingly ossified institution in a dying industry, survive the most destabilizing period in its history — and emerge stronger?
By A.G. Sulzberger
Published 2026-09-30 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/opinion/new-york-times-family-ownership-stewardship.html

This essay was originally delivered as a speech at the Wharton Center for Performing Arts at Michigan State University on Tuesday.

Let me start in the year 2004. The New York Times is a thriving company in a thriving industry. It boasts a best-in-class product, an esteemed brand and a uniquely influential readership. Many call it the greatest newspaper in the world. But it has grown to be much more than that: a diversified media conglomerate with over 12,000 employees and $3 billion in revenue. It’s an auspicious time to break ground on the construction of a grand new headquarters designed by one of the world’s most acclaimed architects.

What could possibly go wrong?

Well, at the same time, this disruptive force called the World Wide Web was gaining steam, ready to plow through any tradition-bound incumbent standing in its path. In the next decade, The New York Times Company lost about three-quarters of its work force. Revenues dropped by over half. The stock price fell from $48 to $4. That fancy new headquarters? Desperate for cash, the company sold it, just two years after it opened. We were reduced to renting back space in the building bearing our name.

Remarkably, the situation looked likely to get even worse. Modest gains in digital revenue were not close to offsetting the continued decimation of the print newspaper business. A new crop of internet-native start-ups like BuzzFeed and The Huffington Post were attracting far more readers. And creative and forward-thinking colleagues — the very people The Times needed to help find a way out of this mess — were quitting because the company culture was stifling innovation.

Xerox. Kodak. Blockbuster. The New York Times looked to be another once-great company that became too comfortable, too complacent, too slow to change. One of yesterday’s firms — a cautionary tale to be taught in lecture halls like this one. The conventional wisdom that the paper was destined to fail was best captured in a 2009 story in The Atlantic titled “End Times.” It asked: “What if The New York Times goes out of business — like, this May?”

But against these long odds, The Times is still standing. Indeed, not just standing but thriving — heralded as a case study in how to transform a legacy company for a new era. In a period when most news organizations watched their audience and revenue collapse, our company has grown from about one million paying subscribers to more than 13 million. Revenue and profit are also growing steadily, enabling an unprecedented expansion of our newsroom. The stock price — now higher than it was at our pre-internet peak — suggests that investors believe that this old newspaper’s best years are still to come. And, yes, we own our headquarters again.

Which raises the question: How on earth did The New York Times, a seemingly ossified institution in a dying industry, survive the most destabilizing period in its history — and emerge stronger?

On Sept. 18, 1851, the first edition of The New-York Daily Times rolled off the press. In a crowded field of sensationalist newspapers, The Times stood out immediately for prioritizing serious journalism on serious issues. It earned a reputation for quality, sobriety and fairness.

The New York City of the day lacked a single building taller than a church spire. America consisted of just 31 states and 24 million people. Indoor electricity wouldn’t be widely available for decades — let alone wonders like radio, telephones, cars, television, airplanes and computers. The rise of all these new technologies would be chronicled in the pages of The Times as they upended culture, politics and, of course, the world of business.

With each disruption, legacy companies that long dominated their industries faltered and failed, much as The Times nearly did following the arrival of the internet. Those that survived found the sweet spot between continuity and change — grounded in institutional history yet propelled forward by the fresh energy of innovation.

On the occasion of our 175th anniversary, I want to talk about the secret recipe behind the endurance of The New York Times. At the heart of our success — as a journalistic enterprise, as a business, as an enduring American institution — is to approach our work as stewards guided by two foundational, ironclad commitments: to value and to values.

Value is about the product you make. In our case, journalism. To prioritize value is to obsess over quality, to focus relentlessly on delivering the most useful and rewarding experience possible. It means never trying to game your way to success by chasing the latest fad or riding buzzy marketing. Value requires knowing your craft and caring, in a deep and authentic way, about your customers.

Values are less tangible. They’re easier to write off as impractical idealism. In today’s business environment, with its short-term focus and frenetic, Slack-driven pace, too many people see values as liabilities rather than assets. Our experience has taught us the opposite. At The Times, values like independence, integrity and public service are central to our work. And we have found that staying true to them is not just the right thing to do but also central to our business success over the long term.

Value and values alone are not enough to sustain a thriving company. You also need talented people, a strong business strategy, effective operations and an adaptable culture. But our focus on making a product that the public needs — and doing so with values that elevate principle above profit and put the public interest before self-interest — has been central to our business success.

That brings me to stewardship. Stewardship is a model of leadership that puts the long-term health of an enterprise first. A steward must have the humility to recognize that a great institution is bigger than any single person, that one’s own tenure is just a chapter in a longer story. But stewards must also understand the ways in which their chapter is distinct — the unique challenges they must overcome, the unique changes they must embrace. Great leaders can be measured in many ways. They can drive revenue growth, increase share price or achieve market domination. Great stewards must do something singular: hand their enterprise to capable successors, stronger and more resilient than it was handed to them.

My family, the Ochs-Sulzbergers, has stewarded The Times for 130 years. How that looks behind the scenes is much less interesting, thankfully, than anything you might have seen on “Succession.” That is not just because we’re boring, though being boring helps. It’s because our family’s ethos is far too idealistic to survive a TV writers’ room. Our mission is not to seek great fame or fortune. It’s not to dominate politics or culture. It’s to protect and strengthen an essential American institution. Each generation teaches the next — maybe indoctrinates is a better word — that The Times doesn’t serve the family; the family serves The Times. And, as my great-grandmother Iphigene often reminded us, “No big heads allowed.”

For this reason, my family has preferred to stay out of the spotlight and let the work of our journalists take center stage. But The Times’s big anniversary arrives amid an epidemic of distrust in America’s institutions — as well as increasingly direct attacks on the rights and legitimacy of news organizations. So I thought I’d use the occasion to share more about how The Times works as an institution and how the family works to support the paper’s mission “to seek the truth and help people understand the world.”

To be clear, my predecessors and I have made mistakes of all types, including some big ones. Some areas of coverage have aged poorly; as a business, we’ve pursued any number of dead ends. But you don’t get to be this old without getting some big things right. Each of the five generations of family leaders has had to transform The Times while also ensuring that it endured with its soul intact. Through two World Wars, economic booms and busts and the arrival of the internet, we’ve stuck to our central formula — a stewardship mind-set guided by value and values — because long experience tells us it works.

Adolph Ochs, my great-great-grandfather, was the last member of my family who could fairly claim to have pulled himself up by his bootstraps. A high school dropout and the son of immigrants, he had worked his way up from manning the printing presses at newspapers in his home state of Tennessee to owning The Chattanooga Times. Then he wanted to take on the nation’s biggest and most competitive market. The New York Times may have seemed like a surprising candidate for such a conquest. It had a circulation of just 9,000 and was teetering on the edge of bankruptcy. But Ochs was drawn to its reputation for quality journalism. In 1896, he pulled together money and loans to purchase The Times for $75,000, the equivalent of about $3 million today.

As part of the deal, Ochs had to hit several challenging financial targets before he could secure his ownership. That was no sure thing, given the paper was hemorrhaging money. To stem those losses, he cut business and administrative positions.

But he also did something counterintuitive. He expanded his spending on journalism, including new features, like a book review and a magazine. Then he dropped the price of The Times from three cents to one cent. While the added journalistic costs combined with the price drop would hurt profits in the short term, Ochs was confident that these moves would encourage more people to try The Times and recognize it as a superior product, propelling the business in the long term.

Thus was born my family’s formula for doubling down on value in periods of economic pressure.

Ochs was equally radical in the emphasis he placed on the paper’s values, particularly journalistic independence. In his first day as publisher, he promised readers that, unlike the partisan press of the day, The Times newsroom would “give the news impartially, without fear or favor.” The editorial pages, rather than just parroting one point of view, would provide a forum for “intelligent discussion from all shades of opinion.” That commitment to ensuring the independence of news coverage — the insistence of putting values like fairness and accuracy above personal views, political affiliation and financial interests — changed the direction not just of The Times but also of American journalism.

This commitment would be tested almost immediately, when Ochs received a written demand from a prominent banker who was also one of his most important shareholders. The banker believed that The Times’s finance reporter was too focused on corporate wrongdoing, and he told Ochs to fire him. Ochs’s response was direct. “I am very sorry that you believe you can write such a letter to me,” he wrote. “I do not understand that you have any control whatsoever of the editorial conduct of The New York Times.” The Times was willing to say no to anyone who attempted to influence its coverage, no matter how powerful he was or how much he mattered to its bottom line.

None of that is to say Ochs wasn’t a canny businessman. He was a relentless innovator who embraced new technologies like photography and radio. He was a brilliant marketer who rebranded his neighborhood as Times Square and created the New Year’s Eve ball drop to draw attention to the newspaper. During his tenure, he grew daily circulation 50-fold. But he was first and foremost a steward. Under Ochs’s ownership, nearly all of the newspaper’s profits were reinvested to improve and expand its journalism. The strength and resilience of the business today owes much to that farsighted approach.

Ochs was succeeded as publisher by his son-in-law, Arthur Hays Sulzberger. Arthur Hays used the financial success of The Times to continue investing in journalism and to add new features, like a food column and a daily crossword puzzle. But the true test of his commitment to value came, as such tests usually do, under pressure. In World War II, the government began rationing the paper that newspapers were printed on. Publishers faced a quandary: fewer articles or fewer ads? Journalists were taking great risks to bring wartime news home to readers; several Times reporters were killed or taken prisoner while covering the conflict. So Arthur Hays turned away advertising to offer the public more news instead. By the end of the war, readership was soaring.

A generation later, Arthur Hays was succeeded first by his son-in-law who died just two years later and then by his son, Arthur Ochs Sulzberger, better known as Punch. Facing the brutal 1970s economy and the consumer shift to television, newspapers struggled for revenue and relevance. Punch met this pressure by embarking on a historic expansion of the paper’s offerings, doubling the number of daily sections, with new ones focused on science, sports and lifestyle. When others are thinning the broth, he believed, it is best to put more tomatoes in the soup. As a result of those investments, The Times became more valuable to subscribers and advertisers alike, driving a period of historic business growth.

That brings us to my father, also named Arthur. And I do apologize for our lack of creativity with our names — Sulzbergers are nothing if not consistent. My father became publisher at the dawn of the internet. He recognized that this was not just another technological shift — it was the end of our 150-year model of making money by printing and distributing newspapers. To position The Times for this new world, my father made two brave bets: putting the entire newspaper online before there was a proven business model and, 15 years later, charging for digital subscriptions while industry experts still insisted that “information wants to be free.”

But his bravest bet came amid the collapse of our longstanding business model. My father oversaw the sale of more than 40 properties owned by the Times Company — newspapers, magazines, television stations, websites, even a chunk of the Boston Red Sox — effectively every asset that wasn’t The Times itself. The company also laid off a huge percentage of its business staffers at the paper. Between the divestment and the layoffs, our work force shrank by nearly three-quarters to 3,500 employees.

Yet — and this is the brave bet — he held the head count in the Times newsroom flat, even as revenue and profits continued to fall. This steady investment hid a major shift, with investigative reporters and foreign correspondents suddenly joined by a new breed of video, audio and multimedia journalists. Media pundits scoffed at this strategy of continuing to pour money into an apparently failing business. But my father believed that the key to a successful news business in the digital age, as it had been in the print age, would be offering something worth paying for. Thanks to that stubborn commitment to value, The Times now has more paying digital subscribers than any news organization in the world.

One reading of this history is that the three Arthur Sulzbergers who preceded me were maverick business geniuses who zigged when others zagged. In truth, they simply did what good stewards do. They didn’t just focus on short-term profit. They also stubbornly insisted, even under great pressure, that good journalism has value — to its readers and to society at large. They were confident that if The Times continued to invest in creating this value, the company would benefit over the long term.

Making hard choices to uphold the values of The Times shows a similar through line across generations. The most fundamental of these is journalistic independence, the commitment to following the facts wherever they lead. Independence requires a stubborn insistence on telling the whole story, even the parts some people don’t want to hear. It demands that we be willing to upset the powers that be by asking questions they may not want to answer or publishing facts they may not want the public to know. And more often than you might imagine, it necessitates that we be willing to pay a clear financial price to ensure the integrity of our journalism.

The Times regularly publishes stories we know may lead readers to cancel subscriptions and businesses to pull ads, that may lead activists to protest outside our headquarters and powerful people to take us to court. We even insist on investigating our own mistakes, believing we owe readers a full airing of where we went wrong, no matter how uncomfortable those revelations might be for us. Our editors and executives — and, yes, publishers — have all received unflattering coverage in our own pages.

Over the years, politicians, business leaders and others have tried unsuccessfully to stop such coverage by attempting to buy our silence or threaten us into submission. In the 1870s, New York’s most powerful politician, known as Boss Tweed, offered a bribe that today would be worth well over $100 million in a failed attempt to stop The Times from exposing his corruption, which would soon land him in jail. Nearly a century later, Alabama segregationists weaponized the local courts, filing a wave of dubious lawsuits intended to halt The Times’s civil rights coverage or, even better, bankrupt the paper altogether.

Our interactions with American presidents tell a similar story. President John F. Kennedy once invited my grandfather to the White House to suggest that he reassign a reporter whose Vietnam War coverage was a bit too honest for the administration’s taste. Punch refused. He proceeded to stand up to even greater pressure from President Richard Nixon after The Times obtained the government’s classified history of the Vietnam War, which documented how politicians and military leaders had misled Americans about the conflict. Despite the risk of imprisonment, Punch decided to publish what became known as the Pentagon Papers.

Decades later, President George W. Bush, sitting in the Oval Office, asked my father not to publish a story disclosing that his administration was secretly wiretapping Americans’ phone calls, in apparent defiance of the law. If The Times wrote about the antiterrorism program and another attack occurred, the president warned, he would regard the paper as responsible for the deaths of Americans. After long and careful consideration, the story was published, enabling an important debate about how to balance national security and civil liberties.

I have sat across from President Trump — who has sued us three times, used multiple government agencies to target our business, expelled journalists from the Pentagon and now the White House and insulted us more times than anyone can count. I told him that a free press is an essential part of our national fabric and that our journalists will not be deterred by his attacks. And they have not been. Just this year, our investigative reporting exposing how Mr. Trump has used his power to enrich himself and his family was awarded a Pulitzer Prize.

The independence of our journalism extends to our own commercial interests. Harvey Weinstein’s status as a major advertiser, for instance, did not insulate him from our reporters exposing allegations of extensive sexual misconduct against him. Similarly, in 2012, after we had just spent millions to start a Chinese-language website, one of our reporters discovered that the family of the Chinese premier had secretly enriched itself during his tenure. Despite explicit threats of retaliation from the Chinese government, The Times still published the story. The government immediately shut down all access to our website and, eventually, our apps. Years later, both remain walled off there.

From time to time, I’ll meet with a billionaire who has just purchased a news organization. These are generally people who have had far more business success than I ever will. But I offer them one bit of advice: Running a news organization is unlike running any other company. It requires an unabashed love of and respect for journalism. There are far easier ways to make money and friends. News requires an almost counter-evolutionary willingness — insistence, even — to do things that may appear to be damaging to the company and its interests. To publish articles that will upset readers, enrage advertisers and be weaponized by your fiercest critics. Each hard choice in favor of value and values is a deposit that strengthens the bond of reader trust and is the lifeblood of a news organization that succeeds over the long term.

Which brings me back to stewardship. Although my family is often said to own The Times, the reality is more complicated. Roughly 100 members of my extended family are actually the controlling shareholders of the company through a family trust. This isn’t your typical family trust — the sort that’s mainly worried about how to pass on a fortune. Our trust’s primary obligation was first laid out in the will of Adolph Ochs. It called on his descendants to maintain the editorial independence and integrity of The New York Times and to continue it “as an independent newspaper, entirely fearless, free of ulterior influence and unselfishly devoted to the public welfare.”

That mandate, which explicitly puts the best interests of The Times and its readers first, still guides us.

One of my aunts frequently says that if losing her leg would help The Times, she would saw it off herself. And that’s actually an apt metaphor for what she and her generation did financially to ensure The Times would continue to benefit from its special governance structure. Having watched other newspaper families splinter amid arguments about wealth, Ochs’s great-grandchildren decided to lock up the controlling shares in a family trust for another century. And they adopted creative provisions to further strip any temptation their descendants might have to cash out. Perhaps the most remarkable move was combining four trusts held by different — and differently sized — branches of the family into a single trust. That act meant that some gave up nearly half of their holdings to establish the truly shared control they hoped would foster family unity.

The result of these moves is that the family effectively eliminated any potential windfall for generations. Instead, the family’s central reward is the knowledge that its stewardship model — its commitment to the paper’s value and values — continues to be of service to an important institution, the journalists who work there and the public that depends on their reporting.

Having spoken about the family at length, I should also say that the family leadership gets more credit than it deserves. One of the most important decisions any good steward can make is to surround oneself with smarter and more talented leaders. Our brilliant chief executive, Meredith Kopit Levien, is the most impressive business leader I’ve ever seen. Our steel-spined executive editor, Joe Kahn, is similarly the best in journalism. Our board of directors is majority independent, ensuring the company benefits from the expertise of a wide range of accomplished leaders from other fields. And below these top executives are countless other best-in-class editors and business leaders. Though family leaders like me are deeply involved in strategy and operations, our most important contribution is as a permission structure: encouraging leaders at all levels to place big bets, to stay strong under pressure, to do the right thing, to take the long view.

A 175th birthday certainly offers some evidence that our model continues to work. And that our work continues to matter. But we take no false comfort from our longevity. Simply having been around a long time is not a guarantee of a bright future. The Hudson’s Bay Company made it twice as long — 355 years — before closing last year.

Tradition, legacy, even consistent excellence can be powerful forces to discourage change. But good stewardship requires recognizing the ways an institution must evolve to keep pace with changing times, technologies and consumer preferences.

That’s why I often tell colleagues that the main thing we’ve won over our last decade of transformation and growth is the right to compete for the next decade. We must remain oriented toward the future, awake to both its opportunities and its risks. We must remember that though we may be a success story in our industry, the industry is systematically failing. We are a fraction of the size of the tech giants that dominate the flow of information and attention. Google makes more profit every day than The Times does in an entire year. Not only do Netflix, Amazon and Spotify have hundreds of millions more subscribers, The Times also lags streaming platforms like Starz and Crunchyroll.

My generation is about a decade into our chapter of stewardship. My job — in partnership with my cousins Sam Dolnick and David Perpich, both driving forces in the transformation of The Times — is to shepherd the paper through the next round of challenges and opportunities this era presents, from standing up to attacks on press freedom to navigating the emergence of artificial intelligence. Our formula will be the same one that has served the place for five generations.

First, we’re adding value. We’ve nearly doubled the newsroom’s head count in the last decade. This includes significantly expanding our national and international coverage and more than tripling the ranks of investigative reporters. It also includes embracing new formats. “The Daily” and The Morning are now the largest news podcast and the largest newsletter in the country, each reaching far more people than the print newspaper ever did. Our video operation has more than doubled in the last two years. We’re using A.I. in ambitious ways, from helping our reporters comb through large data sets to creating an audio version of every story we publish.

At the same time, we’ve transformed how we support audience interests and passions. Once constrained to publishing a few recipes a week in the newspaper, our NYT Cooking app now serves as a comprehensive, interactive guide through 25,000 handcrafted recipes. The Athletic boasts the largest roster of sports reporters in the world, while Wirecutter offers the most rigorously tested product reviews. Our NYT Games app has expanded from the Crossword to a broad suite of beloved offerings like Connections, Spelling Bee and Wordle.

To accomplish all this, we’ve had to transform large parts of our culture. The Times is far more creative, collaborative, diverse and innovative than it was two decades ago. But we’ve held tight to the company’s guiding values, making clear that any change that requires The Times to compromise on independence or integrity isn’t a change worth making.

In a media ecosystem increasingly overrun by pundits and influencers, The Times is investing more in original reporting than ever. As others chase what’s trending on social platforms, we still focus first and foremost on the issues that really matter. As polarized groups protest journalism that challenges their preferred narratives, we maintain our stubborn belief in the importance of providing different perspectives, even — perhaps especially — those you may disagree with. And as the rights and freedoms of journalists face growing pressure, no news organization has proved more willing to stand strong — and, when necessary, to fight the government in court — to ensure that the press is able to continue to ask important questions on behalf of the American public.

As The Times celebrates its 175th birthday, the United States is celebrating its 250th. It’s no overstatement to say the story of our great nation and its paper of record are bound up together. America’s commitment to free expression and free inquiry enshrined in the First Amendment has enabled The Times’s model of journalism “without fear or favor.” In turn, our journalism has provided the public a reliable source of news and information that has strengthened our country — its economy, its security, its civic bonds — in countless ways.

A disproportionate amount of what the public knows about this moment — and the 175 years that preceded it — they know because our journalists went to places, talked to people, asked tough questions and shared what they learned with the public as fully and fairly as possible. We have spent many billions of dollars and taken great risks to build the definitive archive of America’s history, one that is cited everywhere from college essays to Supreme Court rulings.

Along the way, our work has helped expose miscarriages of justice, save taxpayer dollars and lead to lifesaving reforms. But our main purpose has always been to help people of all stripes better understand what’s happening and why it matters, to help them engage more deeply with their world. Every president, regardless of his party or his complaints, reads our work. So do millions of others, from the leaders of Wall Street and Silicon Valley to the teachers, librarians and professors nurturing the next generation of minds. Which is a reminder that success takes many forms.

I can’t pretend all this has been easy. And it’s a safe bet that even larger challenges loom. But if I can complete my tour of service by handing off a stronger company to a capable successor, then I’ll have done my job. And it will be up to the next generation to push the place to new heights. That is what it means to be a good steward.

So let me ask all of you, particularly those of you preparing to embark upon a career, to borrow from the recipe that has served The New York Times — and our nation — so well.

When you build, build something of value. When you face hard choices, face them with considered values. And when you lead, lead in the spirit of stewardship.

Your investments may take a while to pay off. But when they do, your reward will be that highest of professional achievements: being part of something worthy and enduring.

SUMMARY

The plaintiffs’ basic argument was that under the analysis the Supreme Court applied in the secondary school tuition case from Maine, Colorado’s refusal to grant the exemption violated the First Amendment’s guarantee of the free exercise of religion. “This case is different,” the appeals court said.

ARTICLE

Religion Is the Roberts Court’s Unfinished Business
This case has flown under the radar, but it won’t stay there.
By Linda Greenhouse
Published 2026-09-30 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/opinion/supreme-court-john-roberts-religion.html

Chief Justice John Roberts has accomplished so much of his agenda that it’s not easy, as he begins his 22nd Supreme Court term, to think of what unfinished business might remain.

Affirmative action is dead. Roe v. Wade is a fading memory. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 is in shreds, rendered incapable of serving its original mission of preventing states from undermining the political power of minority citizens. The executive branch agencies known collectively as the administrative state have lost their independence, with the president now able to fire nearly all agency heads for any reason or no reason at all. Federal judges are no longer to defer to an agency’s interpretation of its own authority, instead being told to decide for themselves the validity of agency regulations. Historical claims that fly under the banner of “originalism” have frozen the government’s ability to regulate the ownership of lethal weapons.

While it’s a daunting list, some readers might notice that I have omitted one major focus of the Roberts court. Doesn’t religion belong in any inventory of completed projects?

Not yet.

That may seem a startling conclusion, given how significantly the court over the past decade has reoriented the relationship between church and state — a recent law review article by three constitutional law scholars calls the shift “a systematic dismantling of the previous legal regime.” A series of decisions, most of which bear the chief justice’s name, has established the principle, without precedent in constitutional history, that whatever public benefit secular institutions get, religious institutions are entitled to as well. The first of these, in 2017, required Missouri to include a church’s school in a state program to resurface school playgrounds, despite a “no aid” provision in its Constitution that barred the state from giving money to churches. Exclusion of the church from the program, Chief Justice Roberts wrote, was “odious to our Constitution.”

In 2022, the court declared unconstitutional Maine’s exclusion of religious schools from a program that subsidizes private school tuition for families in districts without a public secondary school. If the leap from preschool playgrounds to secondary school tuition seemed head-spinning, it was a leap the chief justice did not acknowledge in his opinion, Carson v. Makin. The principles of the first decision “suffice to resolve this case,” he wrote.

That is a huge amount of ground for the Supreme Court to have traversed in a short time. More is on the way. In its new term that begins next week, the court will decide whether the equality principle these cases have established is enough, or whether religion is entitled not just to equality, but to preference, in this instance a carve out from the rules that constrain secular institutions. The case is from Colorado, where a state “universal preschool” program operating since 2023 offers free prekindergarten to all 4-year-olds. Families can choose any participating preschool, secular or religious, that meets the quality standards established at the direction of the legislature. One of the standards is a nondiscrimination requirement: In admitting students whose families apply, the school may not discriminate on the basis of “race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level or disability.” Some 2,000 public and private schools, including dozens of religious schools, take part in the program.

For the Archdiocese of Denver, the sexual orientation and gender identity portions of the nondiscrimination provision posed a conflict. The archdiocese requires that parents who send their children to its schools accept the Roman Catholic Church’s teachings on marriage and family, asking them before enrollment to sign a statement of “community beliefs.” Same-sex and transgender parents need not apply. The archdiocese told its parishes not to participate in the program and requested an exemption from the two provisions. The state’s Department of Early Childhood replied that there was no option in state law for an exemption; every aspect of the nondiscrimination policy applied to all.

Two parishes, St. Mary, in Littleton, and St. Bernadette, in Lakewood, sued the state, along with a husband and wife from Littleton who wanted a state-funded Catholic education for their children. (The archdiocese joined the lawsuit but was dismissed for lack of standing.) The plaintiffs’ basic argument was that under the analysis the Supreme Court applied in the secondary school tuition case from Maine, Colorado’s refusal to grant the exemption violated the First Amendment’s guarantee of the free exercise of religion. The Federal District Court in Denver, in a decision affirmed by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit, disagreed.

“This case is different,” the appeals court said. It explained that while the Maine case and the cases that preceded it concerned a public program’s actual exclusion of religious schools, Colorado has “welcomed and actively solicited their participation.” The court added: “The only relevant limitation on any preschool’s participation is the nondiscrimination requirement which applies to all preschools regardless of whether they are religious or secular.” It noted that the state was neither targeting religion nor “attempting to prohibit funds from being used for religious purposes.”

The anodyne sound of that observation — that of course the state wasn’t preventing the direct use of public money for religious education — shouldn’t obscure the full dimension of the change the court has wrought in the constitutional law on religion. The notion that the First Amendment’s other religion clause, the prohibition against the “establishment” of religion, might have anything to say about this arrangement sounds now like the vestige of a distant past, so thorough has been the establishment clause’s erasure from constitutional notice.

This case, St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, puts to the justices the question of whether they are satisfied with what they have accomplished so far. Is equality enough? And if discrimination is an issue in the case, wherein does the discrimination lie?

For the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, the powerhouse religious law firm that brought this case to the Supreme Court, the question is clear. The news release it issued in April, when the court granted its petition, offered this account: “The Supreme Court today agreed to decide whether Colorado can continue excluding Catholic families and preschools from the state’s ‘universal’ preschool program because of their faith.” A tendentious framing, but well tailored to reach the ears of those justices primed to take an apocalyptic view of any seeming incursion on the interests of religious believers.

A friend of the court brief filed on the state’s side by Marci Hamilton, a religion scholar known for opposition to the court’s current course, proposes this counter framing: “This court should not undermine Colorado’s commitment to equality by transforming religious freedom into a doctrine that mandates taxpayer-subsidized discrimination.”

This case has flown under the radar in the months since the court granted the Becket Fund’s petition, but it won’t remain there as the Nov. 3 argument date approaches. Equality or preference? The choice is stark — and Chief Justice Roberts’s project, for now, remains unfinished.

Linda Greenhouse, the recipient of a 1998 Pulitzer Prize, reported on the Supreme Court for The Times from 1978 to 2008.
