SUMMARY

When I served in President Joe Biden’s White House, we had good economic news to report: robust job creation, rising wages, low unemployment and a manufacturing jobs revival. The economic indicator that hurt Mr. Biden the most, inflation, is higher today than it was when Mr. Trump returned to office. While I was the press secretary, the Biden White House often operated as if we still had a media ecosystem built for accuracy and process, rather than one built for immediacy and vibes.

ARTICLE

This Mistake Doomed Biden. Trump Is Falling Into the Same Trap.
When leaders ignore people’s lived experience, their political messaging collapses.
By Karine Jean-Pierre
Published 2026-10-02 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/opinion/trump-biden-economic-message.html

When I served in President Joe Biden’s White House, we had good economic news to report: robust job creation, rising wages, low unemployment and a manufacturing jobs revival. Yes, inflation spiked early in his term, but by the time he left office, it had come down considerably.

Mr. Biden wanted his team to highlight his domestic agenda. His policies were working, and he wanted the country to understand what he was doing and why. But the polling was clear: Our economic message didn’t land.

Senior White House advisers, myself included, would meet for hours, day after day, trying to get a handle on the mismatch between the strength of the data and the flagging public confidence. There were differences of opinion and long discussions about the best way to move forward. We pored over the numbers, worked through different messaging options and kept looking for a way to break through.

But Americans weren’t feeling it. Too many people were struggling with the prices of groceries, rent, child care and gas. Their lived experience did not match the encouraging economic news, and that disconnect shaped the entire public conversation.

We believed that if we laid out the evidence clearly enough, people would see what we saw. They didn’t, and we didn’t adjust to meet them where they were.

Some of Mr. Biden’s advisers worried that too much emphasis on the very real challenges people were facing would undermine the case we were making. Others argued that failing to acknowledge those challenges upfront made us sound out of touch. Every day that we failed to reach consensus, the public mood hardened.

The truth is, we had a stale message and outdated models for delivering it. It cost Mr. Biden and, eventually, Vice President Kamala Harris dearly. President Trump is now making a mistake even more damaging.

The economic indicator that hurt Mr. Biden the most, inflation, is higher today than it was when Mr. Trump returned to office. The bond market has been roiled. The Federal Reserve just raised interest rates. Mr. Trump’s trade wars and his war with Iran are hurting the overall economic picture. All of which helps explain his sinking poll numbers.

Mr. Biden repeatedly talked of growing the economy “from the middle out and the bottom up,” but that mantra ultimately didn’t resonate. Mr. Trump’s refrain that we’re the “hottest country anywhere in the world” is a no-sale, both because the facts really aren’t on his side and because he’s barely acknowledging Americans’ legitimate economic worries. By and large, people aren’t buying his assertions that “affordability” is a “fake word” or his insistence that higher gas prices are “a very inexpensive price to pay” for his war aims.

When leaders neglect lived experience, the message collapses.

Why? To start, facts and figures alone no longer carry the weight they once did. There was a time when people would absorb accurate information presented clearly through official channels, like the White House press briefing. They might disagree on what it meant, they might challenge certain points, but it wasn’t automatically treated as spin.

Today, anyone can be a content creator, producing videos, podcasts and memes with subjective, sometimes bogus interpretations of the news. Many Americans now get their news only from outlets that confirm their political leanings. Social media algorithms clearly favor outrage and certainty, not accuracy.

In that environment, official charts and summaries rarely break through. While I was the press secretary, the Biden White House often operated as if we still had a media ecosystem built for accuracy and process, rather than one built for immediacy and vibes.

A TikTok about high prices, filmed with a phone in a grocery store aisle or in front of a gas pump, could garner more attention than anything I said at the daily White House briefings or any interview given by a cabinet secretary on the Sunday morning talk shows. And once a narrative rooted in daily life takes hold, it is almost impossible to dislodge.

We learned that lesson with the economy and again with the debate around Mr. Biden’s age. Looking back, we misread the public mood, thinking the age conversation would fade. At best, my responses from the podium about Mr. Biden’s age failed to put out the fire; at worst, they fueled it.

The Trump White House should realize that over the next two years, there will be only more, not less, scrutiny when the president appears to drift off during meetings, is cagey about the results of his medical exams or goes on one of his erratic, late-night social media screeds. His communications team should know by now that the prices at the pump and the self-checkout line are undefeated.

When people don’t believe what their government says, institutions lose legitimacy. Conspiracy theories flourish. Urgently needed legislation stalls. Elections are lost.

Part of the challenge is that Americans no longer share a single information space: Media fragmentation has created separate realities. And when a government cannot establish shared facts, democratic decision-making becomes harder.

In some ways, Mr. Trump’s style — direct, emotional, repetitive and unmediated — fits the incentives of the current environment. But it has limits. A decade ago, his bluster, so unlike traditional politicians, grabbed ears and eyeballs. Now even many of his fans can see that he’s frequently just seeking attention. Look at just about any poll and you get the sense that voters increasingly don’t trust him.

That tension, the ability to dominate the conversation while struggling to earn trust, defines this moment.

Once people believe their government is not speaking to their reality, it becomes incredibly difficult to earn that trust back. I felt that tension every day in the White House briefing room. I see it happening again now.

Karine Jean-Pierre is the author of “Independent: A Look Inside a Broken White House, Outside the Party Lines.”

SUMMARY

When the deputy attorney general personally announces an indictment from Justice Department headquarters, it signals a matter of national importance. So when Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter announced that he would hold his first news conference, observers rightly expected a major case. But that did not stop the Justice Department from offering him up to the public as an election saboteur.

ARTICLE

The Trump Administration Has Gone After a Mailman and a Cyclist. Who’s Next?
The Justice Department is trawling to find perpetrators on whom to pin conspiracies. Ordinary citizens are being ensnared.
By Liz Oyer
Published 2026-10-02 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/opinion/trump-target-ordinary-citizens.html

When the deputy attorney general personally announces an indictment from Justice Department headquarters, it signals a matter of national importance. So when Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter announced that he would hold his first news conference, observers rightly expected a major case.

Instead, Mr. McCotter announced an indictment of a rogue postal worker for improperly disposing of mail. The Utah mail carrier, Damon Matai Seei, was apparently covering a colleague’s delivery route at the time. By his own admission, he was feeling “overwhelmed,” and sought to “lighten his workload” by discarding a batch of undelivered mail in a church dumpster. In an interview with federal law enforcement, he admitted this was a “poor decision” made out of “frustration” and “laziness.”

Mr. Seei claimed that he believed the discarded mail was advertising material. But according to prosecutors, it also included 300 mail-in ballots for a primary election. He was charged with a single felony count of delay or destruction of mail, which is one of several commonly prosecuted postal crimes.

Mr. Seei had no apparent intent to interfere with an election. But that did not stop the Justice Department from offering him up to the public as an election saboteur. The deputy attorney general called Mr. Seei — a 34-year-old with no prior criminal history — “a danger to the public and to the integrity of the electoral system.” Mr. McCotter and his boss, Attorney General Todd Blanche, each appeared on Fox News to shore up the story.

Their chest-thumping highlights how desperate Justice Department leaders are to substantiate the president’s claims of election interference, and how miserably they are failing. At the news conference, Mr. McCotter admonished reporters: “Remember, folks. Voting fraud is real.” In other words: We may not have much proof, but trust us.

Recent polling shows that President Trump’s baseless claims about mail-in voting fraud are persuading few people outside his base. Still, the officials who surround him remain doggedly committed to proving otherwise — much like the ministers who refused to tell the emperor he was wearing no clothes. After Mr. McCotter’s news conference, a top Justice Department spokeswoman lashed out at a correspondent who characterized Mr. Seei’s prosecution as “a case about a tired mailman.” On its official X account, the department posted a highly produced video in which Mr. McCotter insists weakly, and without evidence, that the case is “just the tip of the iceberg.”

These actions are reminiscent of the aftermath of the 2020 election, when a rogue Justice Department official sent a letter to Georgia election officials falsely claiming that the department had evidence of “significant” irregularities in the state’s election. His plan was stymied only because the rest of the Justice Department’s senior leadership threatened to resign if it went forward. The acting attorney general, Jeffrey Rosen, reportedly told Mr. Trump he could not “change the facts” of the election.

What’s different and scarier now is that the Justice Department’s leadership is working together to validate the president’s election lies from the top down. Turning fiction into fact is now part of the job description. A refusal to concede that Mr. Trump lost the 2020 election has become a litmus test for all his political appointees.

Initially, Mr. Trump’s justice system targeted specific individuals who had angered him — such as Senator Mark Kelly or the former F.B.I. director, James Comey. Now, it has adopted a dragnet approach, trawling to find perpetrators on whom to pin conspiracies cooked up by the president. Ordinary citizens are being ensnared.

David Hearn, a man from Maryland, was one of them. In June, U.S. Park Police officers and National Guardsmen were deployed to patrol the reflecting pool, under pressure to prove the president’s claim that “SICK, DERANGED PEOPLE” intentionally destroyed its lining. Mr. Hearn, passing through the National Mall on his bike, stopped to put his hand in the water. He was arrested on the spot and later charged with felony destruction of property.

The case against Mr. Hearn crumbled when prosecutors were forced to substantiate it with evidence. Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, had to dismiss the indictment — earning the ire of the president — but only after Mr. Hearn was thrust into the national spotlight and painted as an enemy of America. In a news release, Ms. Pirro had said Mr. Hearn’s “deliberate acts of destruction” were “an affront to our shared history and the dignity of our national heritage.”

Most Americans didn’t fear for our personal safety when the Justice Department came for James Comey, Mark Kelly and Letitia James, the New York attorney general. These were professional political actors who chose to be in the national spotlight. Of course, no one should be subjected to a frivolous or vindictive criminal investigation. But they were people the president viewed as enemies. Now, he’s getting desperate and targeting civilians.

So far, the courts have consistently rejected Mr. Trump’s politically motivated prosecutions. Most Americans can see these cases for what they are: flimsy and pathetic — a sign of Mr. Trump’s weakness. As Mr. Hearn and Mr. Seei experienced firsthand, the president’s control of the levers of justice has the potential to do great damage, even if the charges ultimately don’t stick.

The solution is for those in Mr. Trump’s orbit to stop enabling him. That’s unlikely to happen. Mr. Trump is now relying, to an unusual degree, on a revolving cast of opportunistic political appointees. The flagging career work force has been increasingly marginalized, as leadership is demanding total loyalty and is aggressively squashing dissent.

Mr. McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general, warned that “the actions of even one malicious actor” can undercut the security of our democratic elections. He’s not wrong — but what his news conference illustrated is that the malicious actors are the ones inside our government.

Liz Oyer writes about the rule of law in her newsletter, Lawyer Oyer.

SUMMARY

Because bravery has turned into a cliché masking the profound social and economic injustices of this war. Men went to war, he says, because it was more embarrassing not to. Of course, I don’t equate the two sides of this war.

ARTICLE

Please Spare Me Your Talk of Bravery
In the Ukraine war, bravery has turned into a cliché masking profound social and economic injustices.
By Alyona Synenko
Published 2026-10-02 05:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/opinion/ukraine-russia-war-draft.html

A friend of mine is a draft dodger. Everything he does is governed by the unspoken rules of the nationwide hide-and-seek that is playing out between recruitment squads roaming the streets of Ukrainian cities and some two million men wanted for draft evasion.

Buying groceries can be a life-or-death decision. He never steps outside without checking messaging apps where men share information about checkpoints and recruitment raids in our home city, Odesa. These channels count their subscribers in the tens of thousands.

In Odesa, we clock the disappearances — a barista in my favorite coffee shop, an artist who painted cityscapes in the nearby square, a friend’s brother. Coming across a gaping void where a familiar face used to be has become routine.

More of us are taking action. Almost every week, videos appear online of bystanders trying to wrestle men out of conscription vans to rescue them. Last year, 341 clashes between military recruiters and civilians were registered — nearly triple the number in 2024. I used to pause at these videos, dismayed by the brutality of the violence that permeated everyday life. Now I scroll past them, disturbed by my lack of reaction. I’ve grown used to living in this male version of “The Handmaid’s Tale.”

Last autumn, my friend got caught next to his apartment building. It rained that day, and he slipped in the mud running from recruiters. A recovering drug addict who vomited all night and an older man who was picking up his prescription medication were among his fellow captives. “It felt like we were mere bodies there for sale,” my friend said about the day and night he spent at the Territorial Center of Recruitment and Social Support, before he managed to raise the necessary sum and bribe his way out.

Would you accuse him of being a coward? I didn’t. Because bravery has turned into a cliché masking the profound social and economic injustices of this war.

“In fact, this is our brand,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said in the spring of 2022. “To be brave.” He added, “We will spread our courage. We will start a special global campaign.” Billboards in Times Square, a Vogue photo shoot featuring the president’s wife as a “portrait of bravery” and enthusiastic media headlines promoted Ukrainian courage at home and abroad.

Earlier this year, NATO’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, echoed the same theme, describing his interaction with a Ukrainian mine detection dog: “I even looked the dog in the eye, and he told me that he will never give in.”

Even though self-preservation is a basic human instinct, we have been conditioned to despise and mock running from war by millenniums of literature and art. Throughout history, the fear of being labeled a coward has kept soldiers in the fight and sometimes kept wars going against the tide of dissenting public opinion. “If I left that war and let the Communists take over South Vietnam,” President Lyndon B. Johnson said, “then I would be seen as a coward.”

During the Vietnam War, the largest antiwar movement in U.S. history appropriated the insult, rebranding war as moral cowardice. In “The Things They Carried,” by Tim O’Brien, the character of the same name says, “I was a coward. I went to the war.” Men went to war, he says, because it was more embarrassing not to.

Estimates of the number of young Americans who left the country during the Vietnam War to avoid fighting range from 40,000 to 100,000, with Nixon’s speechwriter Pat Buchanan dismissing them as “malingerers, opportunists, criminals and cowards.” When Ukraine loosened exit restrictions for men aged 18 to 22 in August last year, the number of men those ages crossing the border into Poland soared to 1,600 per day over the following two months.

At the same time, hundreds of thousands of young Russians have chosen to leave their country since 2022.

Of course, I don’t equate the two sides of this war. Ukraine was, after all, invaded, and in the days afterward hundreds of thousands of ordinary Ukrainians, men and women, volunteered to join the armed forces. With long lines snaking around enlistment centers, the number of volunteers was so overwhelming, some were sent home. But in the nearly five years of the brutal war, a new kind fear has taken over. We have grown used to drones and explosions in our cities. Now, what scares me and most people I know is the glaring absence of any realistic prospects for peace. We are scared to watch our country bleed its best people and its future.

Many men who refuse to fight are protesting the unequal burden of the war — while some sacrifice their lives, others amass wealth. When Andriy Yermak, Mr. Zelensky’s former chief of staff and, until last year, the second most powerful man in the country, resigned his post mired in a corruption scandal, he told The New York Post that he would go to the front lines. The promise remains unfulfilled, and as a friend of mine said with a chuckle, “All of us will end up at the front before he does.”

So many bright and kind people have been killed. And, every day, Ukrainian soldiers show superhuman levels of selflessness and courage. But their bravery must not be cheapened and paraded as a cardboard cutout to divert attention from growing inequality and corruption. And from the lack of any honest and serious conversation about how we can achieve peace.

Samuel Johnson once said that “mutual cowardice keeps us in peace. Were one-half of mankind brave, and one-half cowards, the brave would be always beating the cowards. Were all brave, they would lead a very uneasy life; all would be continually fighting: but being all cowards, we go on very well.”

I would be happy to live in Johnson’s utopia, populated with cowards who value their lives and the lives of others. And I would take it over this world, where leaders who are supposed to keep us safe though diplomacy and dialogue instead engage in self-important and shallow militaristic discourse.

My grandfather served as a Soviet Navy officer during the Cuban missile crisis, and I have always been disturbed and fascinated by this period in history. Adlai Stevenson, the U.S. ambassador to the U.N. at the time, who advocated diplomacy over military action to avoid escalation, said: “I know that most of those fellows will probably consider me a coward for the rest of my life for what I said today, but perhaps we need a coward in the room when we are talking about nuclear war.”

When I read the news or jump out of bed in the middle of the night during an air raid, I wish there were more diplomats like him in the world today.

Alyona Synenko is a writer from Odesa, Ukraine.

Not because I wanted to die — I knew even a small amount of bleach could be fatal, and I would never actually choose to drink it — but because I felt so repulsed by our actions.

ARTICLE

Nothing Could Purify Me After What I’d Done
Not showering, not praying, not even drinking bleach.
By Gabrielle Shiozawa
Published 2026-10-02 04:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/style/modern-love-i-wanted-to-be-a-good-mormon-but-i-was-gay.html

My first love convinced me to drink bleach.

I was 20, a junior at Brigham Young University in Utah, and already behind by Mormon standards when it came to love and dating. I wasn’t old enough to rent a car or order a drink, yet most of my classmates were dating, engaged or married. We had a children’s playroom in our university library. Classmates brought babies to lectures. It was not a question of if, but when, I would be wed.

Mormon doctrine teaches its followers to marry young, stay sexually abstinent before marriage and have as many children as possible. This is already a tightrope to walk, but I took it even more literally with my then-untreated scrupulosity, a form of obsessive-compulsive disorder characterized by a relentless thought cycle of fear and doubt surrounding morality and religion.

I was consumed by anxiety around everything church related, constantly fearing I had committed a sin I couldn’t remember and that I was unworthy of the blessings my high-demand religion promised. Yet I had never been in any rush to get married before I was inundated with church culture at BYU and felt pressured to check all the boxes.

As a freshman, I had met with my bishop to confess my failures. “All five of my roommates have already gone on dates,” I said. “Also, I haven’t told anyone this, but I’m worried I might be into women.”

“Well, you haven’t acted on those impulses, have you?” he said. “It’s fine to be a lesbian as long as you don’t act on it. You know, I think I understand lesbians, because I, too, am attracted to women.”

His spiritually sanctioned advice was: “Go flirt with boys!”

For two years, I tried. A recently returned missionary took me swing dancing. A too-forward man held my hand, without asking! And a former cop bought me a $50 steak and showed me his gun collection.

I had just about given up on dating when my neighbor, a fellow student, asked me out. I tallied his qualifications as we walked to a bowling alley. He was exactly my height, but his fluffy blond hair made him seem a few inches taller. He laughed endearingly.

I wanted to be a good Mormon girl, to date and marry the way I was supposed to. This man felt safe, so we kept going out. We were each other’s first kiss, at 20 (me) and 22 (him).

“I’ve been waiting to have my first kiss with someone really special,” he said. “I think it’s you.”

Which sounded sweet, but also just seems like something any sexually repressed Mormon would say. And we were two sexually repressed Mormons.

We spent most of our 11 months of dating cooking together in my half-lit apartment kitchen, doing homework on his dingy couch and ignoring how bad we were at kissing. He got me into rock climbing, having no idea he was introducing me to the gayest hobby possible that I would later take up with my future girlfriend.

There were sweet family dinners at his childhood home, a weekend road trip to my Southern Nevada hometown for hiking and camping, and game nights with his high school friends.

I made the mistake of asking my mother what she thought of him after bringing him home like a fish I’d caught, as if to say, “Look! Aren’t you proud?” But she said he was nerdy, and I then made the mistake of telling him that, which went as well as you might expect.

Every time I found myself attracted to a woman, I went to my boyfriend’s apartment to confess. To his credit, he always laughed and said, “You’re probably bisexual,” which felt incredibly progressive. But being a good Mormon meant ignoring that part of me.

I loved that neither of us had any clue what we were doing.

Sure, he convinced me he knew more. He was two years older, and the church’s patriarchal structure convinced me he was the decision maker. He told me not to be clingy, scolded me when I was too prideful. He reminded me that his future wife wouldn’t be someone who struggled with self-harm or lost her temper the way I did.

I felt ashamed. I didn’t trust myself enough to argue. I cried and said I would do better. I grew up being taught that “enduring to the end” was part of being a good Mormon. I believed this meant not only staying true to my religion but also to my first boyfriend. After all, if I could endure dating him, I would never have to kiss another man.

A few months in, he admitted he had never meant to ask me out, but I’d gotten the wrong idea when he asked me to go bowling, and then we just kept hanging out.

Somehow, this revelation didn’t convince either of us to end the relationship.

It wasn’t hard to stay pure. I wanted to cuddle on the couch and go car-camping in the canyons and hike holding hands in the soft morning fog. In the Mormon Church, sexual sin is taught as being almost as bad as murder. My only relief was convincing myself I was more righteous for having no desire to be intimate with a man. I didn’t want his rough hands on my body. I wanted to say no.

But as we lay in the back of my car, he asked for more than I wanted to give. I said, “No, I’m not ready,” and then my voice shook, and I said, “It’s OK.”

His hands on my body. My hands on his.

I remembered what they said at church about women being responsible for maintaining their virtue, for keeping men from temptation, and a sick feeling grew in my stomach.

I drove us home. He said nothing while I hunched over the wheel and sobbed. In a few months, I sold that car, even though I loved it, because every time I looked in the back seat I remembered that I was no longer clean.

As a child, my O.C.D. convinced me the only way to be morally clean was to be physically clean. I drank drops of hand sanitizer in elementary school whenever I didn’t pray the right amount and then wondered why I got stomachaches. As a teenager, I was so ashamed of my first crush on a girl that I washed my hands until they cracked and bled. With no good bacteria left to fight against disease, warts broke out across the backs of my hands. I lived in shame, warts all over my knuckles, and I still couldn’t stop scrubbing them, convinced I would never be clean.

Then I was 20, and I no longer drank drops of hand sanitizer, and I washed my hands a normal amount. But because of what happened in that back seat, I was now dirty again and needed a new salve. I could scrub myself raw in the shower, take medication for the urinary tract infection I got from his hands on my body and pray until my voice grew hoarse, but nothing could fix what I’d done.

So I started obsessing about drinking bleach. Not because I wanted to die — I knew even a small amount of bleach could be fatal, and I would never actually choose to drink it — but because I felt so repulsed by our actions.

I joked about it with my boyfriend. I couldn’t talk about what happened between us, so I joked about drinking bleach.

Then one day he took me to his kitchen and said, “Maybe this will get you to stop talking about it.”

We stood barefoot, afternoon sun streaming in. He held a bottle of bleach in one hand and poured me a capful. Probably a tablespoon. I smelled it before he lifted it to my mouth, sharp and bright.

I didn’t question it. He was just helping me face my fears. Right?

I looked in his eyes and nodded because I thought I loved him. I loved someone who brought poison to my lips and called it a cure. I tipped the liquid back like a shot. Like salty, rancid almond milk. Cold and quick. I wanted to gasp. I swallowed instead. I waited for it to burn, but I felt nothing but nausea.

I wouldn’t tell anyone about this for years, not because I thought he was wrong but because I thought he was right. After all, I did stop talking about bleach after that.

A few weeks later, he came to my apartment to tell me God told him it was time for us to break up. “Your family will never come around to liking me,” he said. “I don’t want to live like that.”

“Anyway,” he said with a laugh, “at least now you know you like men.”

Gabrielle Shiozawa is a writer in Walnut Creek, Calif.

ARTICLE

Tom Ford and the Problem of ‘Sexy’
In an age of naked dressing, what does titillation look like?
By Vanessa Friedman
Published 2026-10-02 07:59 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/style/tom-ford-haider-ackermann-naked-dressing.html

No one in fashion did sexy with quite the same gusto and lasciviousness as Tom Ford in his heyday: carving logos in pubic hair for his Gucci advertisements; introducing the high-fashion G-string.

So it’s not really a surprise that Haider Ackermann, Ford’s successor at his namesake brand, has embraced the ethos — though Ackermann’s take on titillation leans more toward seduction and away from smut. In a world where naked dressing is now taken for granted on both red carpets and in real life, however — during a season where lingerie and bralets have become so commonplace, they have the frisson of a T-shirt — figuring out what qualifies as “sexy” is increasingly hard.

It’s not simply bare skin any more, or a glimpse of something once shocking. It’s not getting your cleavage out, or flashing a crotch shot in a teeny-tiny metallic cocktail dress, like those offered by Antonin Tron of Balmain in a show that traded heavily in 1980s look-at-me glitz. It’s not the micro minis and underboob-flashing bandeaus of Stella McCartney’s dancing-on-the-tables environmental activists. It’s not even the gilt nipple covers under sheer black knits featured in Daniel Roseberry’s Schiaparelli show, an otherwise soignée paean to the glamour of Champagne hour.

Even the Row, a brand practically monastic in its commitment to the Zen of the monochrome trouser suit, featured a crocheted bra beneath a sheer T-shirt in a show that was essentially an argument for the solution of great pants and an artisanal top: tiny lace tablecloth tops, heavily fringed piano shawl halter tops, little beaded tops made from antique scraps. So what’s a house that trades on libido to do?

Since arriving at Ford, Ackermann has found his answer in focusing less on exposure and more on the allure of exposure to come; by teasing the possibility of what’s next, rather than baring it all. By channeling what the designer called in this collection’s show text, “the feeling that something has happened, or is about to,” through clothes so perfectly tailored and sensuously worn they seem like a sartorial caress.

And by putting them on grown-ups, including a number of models of a certain age, in the rare recognition that the older generation are still sexual beings (an idea almost never addressed elsewhere in fashion, which is still obsessed with chasing the youth vote).

That was certainly the case this season, although — perhaps in response to all the nakedness around him — Ackermann also took the undercurrent of eroticism and made it even more overt. With mixed results.

It started with the soundtrack: a symphony of unabashed heavy breathing, with the occasional moan. It started with a set made of mirrors, refracting the come-on of a glance. And it started with two perfect navy pinstripe suits — one for her, one for him (part of Ackermann’s signature is a sort of wardrobe mirror-imaging, so a version of what is worn by one gender is also often worn by the other), and a white T-shirt. Made of fishnet.

Button-up shirts were unbuttoned to the navel, generally worn with nothing underneath; tank tops cut in a deep U that dipped well below the breast bone. There was a lot of black leather (jackets, bullet bras, cropped tops) and transparency. Sheer skirts seemed to have been dropped to the level of equally low-riding jeans, revealing the G-strings or boxers beneath. Then the legs came out. And the butt cheeks.

One very buff guy wore a caramel sweater paired with a bubble-gum pink banana hammock. Another, a tuxedo jacket and teeny tiny cutoffs that could barely contain his thighs. Halter-neck crystal bodysuits appeared as monokinis. Rather than a finale of evening dresses, there was a finale of black bathing suits so tiny they were more like abstract squiggles over the body than actual garments.

“There is something deeply sexual in a body that reveals itself without offering itself,” Ackerman wrote in the show text. But amid all said revelation, something more enticing was lost.

Part of the power of Ackermann’s clothes has been in their subtlety; the way they turn a garment into a come-hither glance. Like, in this collection, an olive green trench coat that zipped both up and down (and practically purred “Unzip me”) or a ruby halter-neck dress, cut to reveal a triangle of flesh at the front and a bit of leg at the side.

They were a reminder that when everything is available, what’s really sexy is capturing the imagination, and letting it run wild.

ARTICLE

Judge Blocks Border Wall Construction in Big Bend in Texas
The ruling dealt a setback to the Trump administration’s plans for hundreds of miles of barriers that have drawn local opposition.
By J. David Goodman
Published 2026-10-02 20:32 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/us/border-wall-big-bend-texas.html

A federal judge in El Paso on Friday halted border wall construction across the Big Bend region, dealing a blow to the Trump administration’s effort to erect hundreds of miles of barriers despite fierce local opposition.

The federal government “shall not build border barrier or related infrastructure, or engage in any construction or ground disturbing activities, in the Big Bend sector,” the judge, Kathleen Cardone, wrote in her order, which she read from the bench.

In a two-page order granting an injunction in the case, the judge said the federal government could not rely on waivers of environmental and other laws it had granted itself to speed up the construction, writing that it “must comply with all applicable laws.” Judge Cardone ruled that the government could not use the waivers until the case was resolved.

She wrote that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on the merits of at least one of their claims.

The lawsuit, filed in the Western District of Texas by plaintiffs including a river boat guide and a church preservation group, sought to stop U.S. Customs and Border Protection from building border barriers across a more-than-500-mile stretch of the frontier with Mexico. The plans, which include some barriers in Big Bend National Park, have been the focus of months of protests and stop-and-start construction activity.

In a statement, the border protection agency said that it was working “on next steps” with the Justice Department. “We stand by our assessment and remain confident in our legal authorities to secure the border while preserving the unique landscape of the Big Bend region,” the statement said.

The order came days after federal lawyers told the court in a legal filing that the border protection agency would resume barrier construction in several areas in the Big Bend region, though not the national park, after a voluntary pause on activity. The agency also said in the filing that it was revising its plans for the national park — where bulldozers and heavy machinery had already begun operating in August — and would make them public early this month.

Outside the courthouse, river guides and environmental activists cheered after the order was issued.

“We dodged a bullet today,” said Billy Miller, a river guide who lives in Terlingua, Texas, and was one of the plaintiffs in the suit. “It means that we can continue to introduce people to the wildness. Their plan was going to ruin the experience of anybody going out there.”

The opposition to border construction in the Big Bend region of Texas, a remote area known for its rugged wilderness, included national groups and local residents. Among the arguments made by the plaintiffs was that few illegal crossings take place in the area because of the inherent dangers posed by its remoteness. The Big Bend sector records far fewer crossings than any other portion of the Texas-Mexico border.

Federal officials have argued that barrier construction was necessary, even if crossings were currently low, because the number would increase as barriers were constructed in other parts of the border and migrants looked for new ways to get into the country.

Still, opponents considered the ruling as a significant victory.

“No construction can continue,” said Laiken Jordahl, who was in the courtroom on Friday and is an advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental nonprofit that is one of the plaintiffs. “All the bulldozers have been stopped across the entire border sector.”

SUMMARY

The first loud noise that Earl Caldwell heard on the night Martin Luther King Jr. was murdered was the sound of a soda bottle falling from the second-story balcony of the Lorraine Motel. Thinking it was a gunshot, Caldwell rushed to the door of his room. Caldwell knew it had to be King.

ARTICLE

A Shot Rang Out. M.L.K. Went Down. And a Reporter’s Instincts Kicked In.
Earl Caldwell was staying at the Memphis hotel where the civil rights leader was killed.
By Marc Lacey
Published 2026-10-02 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/us/mlk-shot-caldwell.html

The first loud noise that Earl Caldwell heard on the night Martin Luther King Jr. was murdered was the sound of a soda bottle falling from the second-story balcony of the Lorraine Motel.

Thinking it was a gunshot, Caldwell rushed to the door of his room. It was a false alarm.

Then came a second sound, this one louder. He likened it to an explosion in its ferocity, and it turned out to be what he feared: a rifle shot directed at King, mortally wounding him.

Caldwell was the lone reporter at the motel in Memphis on that spring night in 1968. He was in Room 215. King was upstairs and several rooms over, in 306. Caldwell’s dispatch in the next day’s New York Times captured one of the civil rights movement’s seminal moments. There would be weeks of rage over the murder, which he covered. And decades of dispute over how it all went down, which he participated in as well.

“Reporters believe that if you are there, you can see what happens and then you can tell it, the real story, witnessed firsthand,” Caldwell wrote more than 50 years after the assassination. “That day — April 4, 1968 — was my lesson on what really happens: You are there, yet you don’t see everything. But in the tangle of events, there is a sliver of whatever it is that happened that comes past you, and that’s precious.”

The Times had sent Caldwell to Memphis to keep close to King, who was then under siege. There were death threats against him and challenges to his leadership. A week earlier, a rally he led in Memphis for striking sanitation workers had turned violent, and critics questioned whether he was in control of his movement anymore.

Caldwell, who joined a virtually all-white staff at The Times in 1967 after a decade of reporting on sports and news for smaller papers, had never met King before shaking his hand in Memphis on that trip. And he almost bungled his first big assignment.

He had landed an interview with King the day before the fatal shooting, in which King spoke of the movement’s future. But as a storm swept through Memphis that evening, Caldwell was unaware of King’s last-minute decision to go to Mason Temple, a local church, and deliver what would be his final speech, the one in which he seemed to anticipate his own death.

Caldwell never heard King say he’d been to the mountaintop. That he had “seen the Promised Land.” That he thought he “may not get there with you.”

When Caldwell learned of King’s speech the next morning on the news, he thought he might lose his job. The church had been full of competitors, who captured King’s prophetic words. Caldwell spent the day trying, and failing, to match the story he had missed.

That evening was warm, and Caldwell, back in his motel room, kicked off his shoes, stripped down to his underwear and left his door cracked open.

Then the bottle fell.

And, at just after 6 p.m., history unfolded one floor up.

Caldwell darted into the motel parking lot. He saw King’s driver with his hands on his head screaming, “Oh, no, oh, no, oh, no.”

“What’s the matter?” Caldwell shouted. “What’s the matter? What’s going on?”

Someone responded: “They shot him. They shot him.”

Caldwell knew it had to be King.

“I dashed out into the lot but a few steps outside the door I remembered my trousers,” he said, recounting these events later that month in an internal Times publication called Times Talk. He put on his pants. He slipped into some shoes. He grabbed a jacket, a stack of paper and a pen. Then he rushed out, forgetting his room key and locking himself out.

He had missed King’s prophetic final speech. He had heard but not seen the gunshot that killed him. As he later noted, on-the-scene reporting often comes down to luck. (“You are there, yet you don’t see everything.”) So with respect to the details that he was able to observe, Caldwell tried to be meticulous. Hustling up the motel stairway to the murder scene, he bent over and, as he told a friend later, inspected the wound in King’s neck.

“Earl’s reportorial instincts were as sharp as a tack,” said Jack White, a retired journalist who spoke to Caldwell many times about the events of that night. “Dr. King is lying there on the ground. He’s being cradled by Ralph Abernathy. Earl gets close to King and he told me about the gaping hole in his face and said he put his fist up — and he’d later describe it as fist size. He wasn’t just guessing. He actually put his fist up to Dr. King’s face.”

Joseph Louw, a South African photographer who was working on a documentary about King, was also at the Lorraine that night. He took the famous image of King sprawled on the balcony with his closest aides pointing in the direction from where the fatal shot had come. In another of Louw’s photos, Caldwell is visible next to King’s body.

At some point, Caldwell sprinted to a nearby pay phone and inserted two nickels. Out of breath, he told his editor in New York what had occurred, prompting a wholesale remake of the next day’s front page.

“Blood gushed from the right jaw and neck area. His necktie had been ripped off by the blast,” Caldwell dictated over the phone to a rewrite man in New York, who turned his account into a story that appeared under a banner headline: “Martin Luther King Is Slain in Memphis; A White Is Suspected; Johnson Urges Calm.”

The details Caldwell gathered transported readers to the scene. “Dr. King was shot while he leaned over a second-floor railing outside his room at the Lorraine Motel,” the article reported. “He was chatting with two friends just before starting for dinner.”

There was one detail in his article that would be debated for years. Caldwell quoted King’s driver, Solomon Jones Jr., saying that he had seen a man creep away from a thicket across from the motel. Although Caldwell did not mention it in his Times story, he said later that he, too, saw a man moving through the bushes.

This was at odds with the F.B.I. account. The bureau insisted that James Earl Ray, who pleaded guilty to the killing, had acted alone and had fired from a nearby rooming house. (Ray later recanted.)

Caldwell believed that the shot might have come from someone in the bushes and resented that no one from the government interviewed him until 1998, when President Bill Clinton reopened the investigation into the shooting at the behest of the King family. Ultimately, the Justice Department reaffirmed that Ray had acted alone, writing in its report that Caldwell “understandably misrecollects observing someone in the brush.”

Caldwell was disillusioned, and in his subsequent job as a columnist for The New York Daily News he regularly raised what he considered the unsolved mystery of King’s killing. His friend Jack White said that Caldwell fumed at the suggestion he had misremembered anything.

Today, the Lorraine houses the National Civil Rights Museum, and Caldwell’s former room is now a storage closet. But earlier this year, the museum added an exhibit on alternative theories of the killing. Caldwell’s deep baritone can be heard describing holes in the F.B.I.’s case.

The next chapter in Caldwell’s career proved equally momentous. As the Black Panther Party rose in prominence after King’s death, Caldwell was dispatched by The Times to Northern California to report on the group. He earned the Panthers’ trust, spending long hours inside the group’s hangouts, where he witnessed its stockpile of weapons. In one attention-getting piece, he quoted a Panther leader saying that the group backed the “overthrow of the federal government.”

Under the directorship of J. Edgar Hoover, the F.B.I. was intent on undermining the Panthers and frequently pressed reporters for information on their sources. Once, as Lee Levine recounts in a forthcoming book, “In Bad Faith: Earl Caldwell and the Fight for a Free Press,” an agent showed up at the Times newsroom in New York seeking information from Caldwell about a story, and Caldwell handed over his notes.

But now, aware that any cooperation with the government would end his access to the Panthers, he rebuffed the F.B.I. He then received a subpoena ordering him to testify before a federal grand jury. After an attorney for The Times suggested that he would likely have to turn over some information to federal authorities, Caldwell retained his own lawyer. Reporters, he insisted, should not be used as spies for the government. “It goes against everything you stand for in journalism,” he later told Time magazine. He refused to appear before the grand jury and was held in contempt of court.

He fought the subpoena all the way to the Supreme Court, which, in a case that included two other reporters, ruled that the First Amendment did not protect Caldwell and the other journalists from having to testify. (Earlier this year, the Trump administration invoked the ruling to argue that its subpoenas of five Times reporters was lawful. A federal judge disagreed, and prosecutors withdrew the subpoenas.)

Though he lost his case, the ruling against Caldwell prompted dozens of state legislatures to enact “shield laws” protecting journalists from being forced to turn over their confidential sources to the government. It also solidified his place at the center of much of the drama of the civil rights era.

“You have to show up to be in place where things are happening,” said Alex Caldwell Maynard, Caldwell’s godson, who has stayed close to him even as he has suffered ill health and, now 91, has moved to a nursing home. “He seemed to be everywhere.”

ARTICLE

In Alabama, Trump Relives His Glory Days (This Time With Some Empty Seats)
The Deep South was the birthplace of the mega MAGA rally. How do people on the Gulf feel about President Trump now?
By Shawn McCreesh
Published 2026-10-03 02:29 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/us/politics/alabama-trump-rally-glory-days.html

On Friday night, President Trump turned up in Mobile, Ala., to give a campaign rally five weeks ahead of the midterm elections.

What on earth was he doing all the way down there?

“I’m really here because, sometimes,” he said, “you’ve got to pay respect to the people that loved you right from the beginning.”

The indoor arena at the University of South Alabama purred.

As Republican prospects for November have darkened, Mr. Trump has started to really throw himself into the campaign trail. So far, that trail has led him to some interesting destinations. A Republican president, campaigning in ruby-red Alabama? Texas? Oklahoma? What’s next, Nebraska? Yes, actually, that is where he will be on Monday.

Mobile occupies a mythic place in Trump lore, though. This is, in some sense, the birthplace of the MAGA rally, that traveling roadshow of Mr. Trump’s that would come to define the next decade of national political life in America.

“I don’t know if you know. It sort of all began here,” Mr. Trump reminded his audience as soon as he took the stage Friday.

When he came here in August 2015, his rise had only just begun. It was shortly after the first Republican primary debate. He was still duking it out against Marco Rubio, Jeb Bush and Ted Cruz, and still being treated by much of the news media as little more than a tulip craze.

Mr. Trump’s campaign apparatus at the time was small and scrappy and run out of his tower on Fifth Avenue in Manhattan. His campaign made the potentially embarrassing move of staging his event in Mobile at a massive, open-air football stadium. They were vindicated when some 30,000 people showed up, much to the shock of the establishment and the candidate himself.

“It was a big friggin’ deal,” recalled Michael Glassner, a political operative who was there working for Mr. Trump that day.

“I’ve either been on presidential campaigns, or been around them, since 1988, and there never really had been something on that scale for a primary candidate, in modern American politics, to my knowledge,” Mr. Glassner said.

It was the moment he realized that the Trump phenomenon “was going to break all of the rules” of politics, he added.

One aide who traveled with Mr. Trump to Mobile that day was Corey Lewandowski. “I was in his vehicle,” Mr. Lewandowski recalled. “We passed a number of homes that were in communities that weren’t affluent at all, and there were people outside sitting in their chairs, holding handmade signs, waving, supporting. It was very, very humbling.”

The significance of that moment, he said, was that “at a venue in the Deep South, with a candidate who many chastised or criticized for being married three times, and said didn’t quote unquote uphold traditional Republican values, that clearly was not on the minds of the people of Alabama. They turned out in record numbers.” This was a sign of much to come.

The president relived those glorious days from the stage Friday night.

“We packed the stadium and the rest was history,” he said, “right here in Mobile.”

But that was then.

These days, Mr. Trump is in political trouble, even with members of his famously loyal base. The indoor arena that he spoke at on Friday was a fraction of the size of the football stadium he once spoke in — security concerns are such that he rarely speaks in outdoor venues anymore — and still the place was not full. Some upper sections were almost completely empty.

Mr. Trump’s poll numbers have been falling for months. On Friday, The New York Times reported that he personally instructed his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads praising him and his presidency.

A day before the rally in Mobile, this reporter took a circuitous drive along the Gulf Coast and detected signs along the way that Donald Trump’s decade-long love affair with the Deep South may be wilting.

“I’m very disheartened right now,” a 76-year-old, three-time Trump-voting woman named Kris Rouse said while grocery shopping at a supersized Walmart in the Mississippi town of Pass Christian.

“Most of the things that he said were going to happen have not happened,” she said as she pushed her cart around the produce aisle. “The gas has gone up, the groceries have gone up, and my taxes on my property have gone up. I’m a senior citizen on a fixed income, and it’s hard right now.”

She retired after 33 years of working in a local bank branch, but has since picked up a part-time job as a door hostess at Waffle House because, she said, “it’s necessary.”

She is done with Mr. Trump, she said, and won’t be voting for anyone this November. Some of her friends are sticking with the president, but there are lots of “others who are just like me,” she explained.

But what about the president’s promise that he is going to send everybody a check for $5,000?

“Nope,” she answered. “I don’t think we’re going to get anything else from Trump.”

(On Friday, in Mobile, Mr. Trump said again that he was going to send out checks for $5,000, and reminded his audience that he sent a check for $1,776 to members of the military. The $5,000 giveaway would cost more than $1 trillion and likely require congressional approval, for which there seems to be very little.)

Asked what she made of the big ballroom project the president is hard at work on back in Washington, Ms. Rouse laughed bitterly and gave a one-word reply.

“Ridiculous.”

Over in the bread aisle, there was a little more sympathy and jingoism to be found.

“He has made some mistakes, like they all have,” said Skip King, a 75-year-old retired construction worker. He allowed that gas and groceries had gotten more expensive, but said that was a price worth paying if it meant toppling the Iranian regime. He only wished Mr. Trump would hurry up.

“We need to quit playing handsies,” the old construction worker said as he tossed a box of Jiffy corn muffin mix into his cart. “We are the most powerful nation on this planet, and we need to prove it, and show it, and show no mercy.”

“I’d still vote for him,” he concluded.

A few miles up the coastline, in the town of Ocean Springs, Ala., at the corner of Government Street and Washington Street, a man and a woman wearing red MAGA hats were stopping people at random to talk about “the importance of voting in the midterms,” as the man put it.

His name was Adam Francisco. He was 43 years old. The woman said her name on the internet was “Freedom and Whiskey,” and that she could not give her actual name for “safety” reasons. She was 30 years old. Both were MAGA influencers. Each held a camera and a foam-topped microphone on a grip. They were on a mission, driving around the entirety of “the Gulf of America” to warn about Democratic socialism, to remind people why they loved Mr. Trump in the first place, and to hopefully get some good viral content, of course.

They stopped two elderly women on the corner. A friendly chat ensued. Then the women strolled on. “Pro-choice Democrats,” Mr. Francisco said.

He acknowledged that gas prices are a huge liability for the president. “If he doesn’t get them down by between now and Nov. 3, I’m going to say that I’m a little concerned about the Republicans’ chances,” he said. “I’m not in denial about it.”

The last town in Mississippi before the Louisiana state line is a small and swampy one called Pearlington. It’s the sort of place where alligators swim in the bayou behind the local dive bar — and the bartender swims with them, or so she says.

The road out of town leads to a broken-down bridge that used to be the way to New Orleans. Beside the bridge is a gas station with three pumps. The two women working behind the counter there Wednesday morning shook their heads slowly at the mention of Mr. Trump. One said it had never cost her this much to fill up her truck. Asked how many people around these parts had turned on the president, she estimated half.

ARTICLE

Agency Diverted $1.4 Billion in Science Funds Mandated by Congress
The move, affecting about one-fifth of the National Science Foundation’s primary research budget, is the latest sign of how the White House is asserting more control over grants.
By Adam Sella, Christopher Flavelle and Irena Hwang
Published 2026-10-02 18:41 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/us/politics/national-science-foundation-research-funds.html

The National Science Foundation, one of the biggest sources of federal research funding, withheld $1.4 billion that Congress had intended for research over the course of the past year, according to internal data reviewed by The New York Times.

The extraordinary move — holding back about one-fifth of the N.S.F.’s primary research budget — is the latest sign of how the Trump administration is finding creative ways to work around Congress. Lawmakers from both parties have consistently opposed White House-led proposals to cut funding to major science agencies, including the N.S.F. and the National Institutes of Health.

Since the N.S.F. was founded over 75 years ago, the agency has spent nearly all of its budget on so-called basic research from a wide range of scientific fields, which has led to major advances in technology such as M.R.I.s, semiconductors and the internet.

The White House wants to redirect the money to a limited set of administration priorities, including artificial intelligence and quantum computing, according to two people with knowledge of the administration’s plans.

Congress appropriates money to the N.S.F. on two-year cycles, so the agency could still spend the held-over money in the new fiscal year, which began on Thursday.

But Democratic lawmakers see the strategy as more of a political power grab by the White House.

“The money should be granted as Congress intended, and essentially, they’re ignoring what Congress did,” said Representative Zoe Lofgren of California, the top Democrat on the Science, Space and Technology Committee. “It’s a dramatic attack on the science enterprise that has served us very well since World War II, when this whole system was set up,” Ms. Lofgren added.

The White House and the N.S.F. said that diverting the money was allowed under Congress’s two-year appropriation.

Mike England, a spokesman for the science foundation, said in a statement that the agency had “carried over funds to invest in agency priorities that are aligned with broader administration initiatives.”

Mr. England said the agency “remains committed to investing in meritorious foundational research across the sciences and engineering that advances American scientific leadership.”

The Trump administration’s efforts to gain more power over grants have played out across the government, where funding decisions have historically been led by experts.

Last month, the N.I.H. signed an agreement to collaborate with the Defense Department, drawing criticism from Democrats on Capitol Hill who warned that the plan could allow the Pentagon to go around Congress and gain access to billions of dollars meant for infectious disease research. The administration previously fired the N.S.F.’s independent oversight board. And it has canceled or delayed thousands of grants across both agencies as part of its quest to punish elite universities and eliminate spending President Trump and his aides view as “woke.”

Mr. Trump’s science adviser, Michael Kratsios, has criticized the agency’s system for deciding which grants to fund. In a report released in July, Mr. Kratsios wrote that the science foundation, under the Biden administration, awarded too many grants that focused on diversity and equity. He also argued the N.S.F. should issue more “fast grants,” in ways “that bypass external review panels.”

The plan to divert N.S.F. funding was reported earlier by Nature, a science journal.

Several people with knowledge of the situation described confusion inside the agency as the staff complied with White House guidance to carry over money as funding deadlines neared. Some divisions had to pull back research proposals that were recommended for funding after peer review, these officials said.

Altogether, the $1.4 billion carried over after the last fiscal year ended on Wednesday amounted to 19 percent of the N.S.F.’s primary research budget allocated by Congress. That is a far higher percentage than in either of the two prior fiscal years, when less than $175 million went unspent, according to internal data from the agency.

At an agency town hall this week, leaders stood by the plan to divert money to administration priorities while offering assurances that the N.S.F. would also remain true to its roots, according to a recording reviewed by The Times.

When an employee raised concerns about whether the N.S.F. would continue supporting basic research, an official responded that “we’re transitioning.” Still, the official said, the agency would continue to “focus on our mission of foundational research.”

ARTICLE

Trump Directed Use of Taxpayer Money for Ads Praising His Presidency
The government-funded ads show just how much President Trump has been able to use federal money for his own aims.
By Maggie Haberman, Hamed Aleaziz, Shane Goldmacher and Jonathan Swan
Published 2026-10-02 19:36 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/us/politics/trump-ads.html

President Trump personally instructed his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads praising him and his presidency, setting in motion a $20 million contract that used funds from the Department of Homeland Security, according to people familiar with the matter.

The ads have run across cable and network television — on Fox News, CNN and MS Now, with football games on Fox and with national newscasts on CBS, ABC and NBC, including “Meet the Press,” which Mr. Trump is known to watch.

Mr. Trump was eager to see the laudatory ads on the air and told Russell T. Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, to come up with the money from within the government, the people said. Mark Paoletta, the budget office’s counsel, and Will Scharf, the White House counsel, both said it would be legal to use D.H.S. funds. The president and Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, both spoke with Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, about the ads.

On Sept. 20, U.S. Customs and Border Protection — which falls under D.H.S. — awarded the contract to LMD, a Maryland marketing firm, federal records show.

This article is based on interviews with 12 people familiar with the president’s interest in the ads and how they came to be. They spoke on condition of anonymity to describe the president’s demand.

The taxpayer-funded ads have been criticized by Democrats and even some Republicans as a possible violation of federal laws against using taxpayer dollars for “publicity or propaganda purposes.” And they come as the president is also directing spending from his super PAC — MAGA Inc., which entered the fall with $400 million — for which he has been raising money since he won re-election in 2024.

It was not clear why taxpayer funds, and not money from the super PAC, were used for the spots.

The White House has called the ads public service announcements and said they are appropriate because there is no “call to action” to vote for any candidate. Some of his aides also noted that Mr. Trump is not running for office now, in an attempt to blunt criticism of the ads as violating federal laws about the use of public money.

When pressed by a reporter on Wednesday, Mr. Trump said: “If somebody said that that’s wrong, I’ll gladly pay the money.”

“But these are ads for the country,” he added. “You have to understand. I’m not promoting a candidate. I’m not promoting myself because I’m not running for office. I’m promoting the country.”

At least four spots have run so far, at a cost of about $5.5 million, and that is expected to grow, according to the media tracker AdImpact and people familiar with the spending. One played images of Mr. Trump to the song “Love Me” by Christian Berishaj, who performs as JMSN. (The artist has protested the use of his song.)

Another was identical to a Trump campaign video from 2024 that condemns “villains” whom the president perceives as enemies. The use of material originally made during Mr. Trump’s political campaign has given fuel to critics who reject the White House claim that the ads are simply public service announcements.

A third ad, about the Iran war, features remarks from both Mr. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Such public service spots typically say which agency paid for them. In this case, all of the ads had an unusual tagline: “Paid for by the U.S. government.”

‘Love Me’

On Aug. 7, Mr. Trump was in the Oval Office with a group of Republican strategists working with his team, along with James Blair, his top political adviser, and Ms. Wiles. Natalie Harp, his ever-present assistant and provider of positive news about himself, was there as well.

At the time, Mr. Trump’s advisers were waiting for him to sign off, finally, on spending from his super PAC for midterm candidates, after months of anxiety from Republican candidates about whether he would help them financially in tight races.

But during that meeting, the president was much more interested in looking at videos of himself.

He turned to Ms. Harp and asked her to show the group the type of imagery he favors.

Ms. Harp pulled up a series of videos made by the White House digital team on her tablet: Mr. Trump standing in front of vast crowds; Mr. Trump beside Marine One; Mr. Trump with fighter jets streaking overhead.

One video showed Dana White, the U.F.C. president, at the 2024 Republican convention, calling Mr. Trump “the toughest, most resilient person that I’ve ever met.” Mr. Trump has talked with delight about that quote repeatedly ever since.

Mr. Trump made clear he planned to travel to support candidates in the midterms, but also that his presidency needed to be promoted, front and center, in the commercials his advisers were making.

Later that month, The Atlantic reported that MAGA Inc. was planning a blitz of midterm ads, with Trump as the centerpiece.

Instead, a Trump-linked nonprofit called Securing American Greatness aired a spot featuring the Dana White quote, spending just under $60,000, according to AdImpact. The ad primarily aired over Sept. 2 and Sept. 3 around Washington, where Mr. Trump was sure to see them.

But then, weeks later, several ads glorifying Mr. Trump began appearing across the country — this time paid for by taxpayers, by way of Customs and Border Protection.

The ads included the “Love Me” spot, in which Mr. Trump says in a voice-over that “America will never be a communist country.”

As the taxpayer-funded spots began running, MAGA Inc. has spent directly to help out in one specific race, putting more than $20 million into the Texas Senate campaign. Two other new groups linked to MAGA Inc. — No Going Back PAC and Safety and Affordability PAC — were recently created and have spent and reserved more than $163 million on spots in races across the country.

But those ads feature Mr. Trump only sparingly.

Asked to comment for this story, the White House press office sent an unsigned statement saying, “These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders and abroad.”

The White House has said there is precedent for using taxpayer money for the ads. “Don’t let the Fake News get away with their lies about our epic Public Service Announcements that have been running on tv,” Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, posted on X on Sept. 27.

His office sent out an email stating that “presidential public service announcements are nothing new,” comparing the spots to efforts to promote health care policy in past administrations, or President Woodrow Wilson’s World War I propaganda campaign.

The Government Accountability Office has found likely or confirmed violations of the anti-propaganda rule before, including during the tenures of both President Barack Obama and President George W. Bush. Those cases concerned publicity campaigns related to policies, not ads focused on the presidents themselves.

‘This Is My Money’

The money for the ads was freed up on Sept. 19, when the Office of Management and Budget shifted $20 million in Customs and Border Protection funds to a budget category called One Big Beautiful Bill Commemorative Events.

The next day, C.B.P. awarded a $20 million contract to LMD, a marketing firm based in Columbia, Md., that federal records show had past work as a government contractor. The actual purchase of the airtime was made by a second firm, LMO, according to a person familiar with the events, who wasn’t authorized to discuss them publicly.

A spokeswoman for the Office of Management and Budget declined to comment on the reporting for this story. A spokesperson for the Homeland Security Department would only say, “D.H.S. follows all applicable rules for contracting decisions and keeps all decision makers informed. All contracting decisions are made in accordance with applicable law.” Officials with LMD and LMO did not respond to requests for comment.

The spots started out airing narrowly but soon ran in heavy rotation not just on cable channels, but on broadcast networks as well. They ran heavily on the network morning programs like “Good Morning America” and “CBS Mornings,” according AdImpact, and appeared in entertainment shows including “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” and “The Amazing Race.” One aired repeatedly during weekend football broadcasts on the Fox network.

The ads are not the first costly television campaign under Mr. Trump, nor are they the first controversial ones. In 2025, Kristi Noem, the homeland security secretary at the time, appeared in a $200 million-plus government ad campaign. The ads, which showed Ms. Noem on a horse at Mount Rushmore, ultimately drew the president’s disapproval, and became the justification for replacing Ms. Noem.

The latest ads promoting Mr. Trump come as his standing with the public has dropped. His approval rating sits at around 37 percent, a number that has been low and steady for months, according to a polling tracker by The New York Times. Republicans are increasingly fearful of a Democratic sweep of both House and Senate, and losses in state legislatures.

Mr. Trump has remained a prodigious fund-raiser for his various construction projects around Washington and at the White House, as well as his future presidential library. Last month, he promised to spend “probably” $400 million to $500 million on midterm election races, but he made clear who holds the purse strings to his super PAC.

“This is my money that I control,” Mr. Trump said.

Reporting was contributed by Jim Rutenberg in New York and Luke Broadwater in Washington.

ARTICLE

Truckers Are ‘Just Trying to Hang On’ When a Fill-Up Tops $1,000
Truckers are among the hardest hit by the soaring cost of diesel fuel. High prices are forcing some to stay on the road for months and others to park their rigs.
By Audra D. S. Burch
Published 2026-10-02 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/us/truckers-diesel-costs.html

When Sean Howarth started his independent trucking business last year, he made sure to reserve one week a month for his family — a girlfriend and her two children — at home in Miami between three weeks on the road.

Then came the war in Iran, which sent the price of diesel fuel skyrocketing and turned a fill-up into an $1,000-a-tank ordeal. For now, the only way to make ends meet, Mr. Howarth said, is to get on the road and stay there. He has not been home since mid-August. He sleeps in his truck and has missed birthdays, volleyball games and date nights salsa dancing at a local club. He does not plan to return home until the holidays unless diesel prices fall sharply.

“I am just trying to hang on,” he said.

Diesel prices are averaging $6.39 a gallon nationally, up from $3.71 a year ago, according to AAA. The high cost of fuel is battering owner-operator truck drivers, who help deliver food, construction materials, medical supplies, electronics and other goods across the country.

Independent truckers, already dealing with stagnant freight rates, rising expenses, and wafer-thin profit margins, are doing all they can to stay afloat. Some have turned to crowdfunding to raise money for gas and maintenance. Others have simply parked their rigs as they hope for a reprieve.

“This is crushing to our industry,” said Lewie Pugh, executive vice president of the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association, which represents more than 135,000 members. “When fuel goes up a dollar a gallon at the pump, that’s another $400 per week that they have to spend. That’s a huge, huge hit to a small business trucker.”

Last week, Mr. Howarth said, he hauled a load of construction equipment from Rogers, Minn., to Johnstown, N.Y. With about 800 miles to go, he began the dreaded search for cheap diesel fuel, tapping on a mobile app to identify the best prices in real time. The final cost: $626 to top off for a load that grossed about $1,000. The profit was a fraction of the $5,300 he owes on his monthly truck payment and insurance.

Mr. Howarth often tries to match load drop-offs with nearby pickups to avoid empty miles and increase profits, but each jump in diesel price has felt like a gut punch, he said. He can make the numbers work with enough good-paying loads, but any more fuel spikes could wipe him out. For now, he is limiting jobs to the East Coast and Midwest, avoiding California, where the average cost of diesel is $8.38 a gallon.

“When I started, it cost me $500 to fill my tank, and now it’s $950 or $1,100-plus, depending on where I am in the country,” said Mr. Howarth, 36, who worked for a trucking company before starting his own business. “Right when things are starting to seem a little easier and go in the right direction, the fuel costs go through the roof.”

For many Americans, the rising price of regular gasoline is a grim reminder of the painfully expensive cost of living. But diesel prices reverberate beyond the gas tank to consumer goods trucked from ports and factories, agricultural products harvested by diesel-powered machinery, even the mail. Fuel supplies were disrupted not only by the war in Iran but by Ukraine’s attacks on Russian diesel refineries in response to Russia’s missile strikes on its cities.

Republicans, particularly those in close midterm races, are looking for ways to tamp down bubbling voter anger by calling for an end to the war and a ban on diesel exports. On Tuesday, Gov. Brian Kemp of Georgia, who would like another Republican, Rick Jackson, to succeed him when he retires this year, became the latest state leader to suspend gas taxes temporarily.

Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said President Trump met with refiners at the White House to try to find ways to expand refining capacity to bring prices down. She added, “As the U.S. continues to maintain full control of the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices will fall back to pre-conflict levels.”

Energy Secretary Chris Wright said this week on Fox News Channel that he intends to ask European countries to release strategic diesel reserves to draw down prices.

“There’s a very good chance we have hit peak prices,” he said. “We are almost surely going to see diesel prices decline.”

For truckers, a price drop cannot come fast enough. Mr. Pugh, who has been driving trucks for more than 25 years, said that about 90 percent of all trucking companies are small businesses and that many are forced to float costs until they get paid 30 to 90 days later. Most negotiate with a broker on the pay for each run, working “load to load.” They can’t raise their rates when fuel spikes in the same way their larger competitors can, he said.

The situation has set social media ablaze. Truckers have posted videos from gas stations and truck stops as fill-ups top $1,000. In one TikTok clip, an exasperated trucker standing next to his rig said the high cost effectively “takes food out of the mouths of your children.”

For about two years, Renardo Harmon has subcontracted with a small Alabama-based carrier to haul dry goods to stores such as Dollar General, Big Lots and Roses Discount Stores across the Southeast.

Mr. Harmon makes a flat rate of around $2.40 a mile and covers his own expenses, including diesel fuel, maintenance and insurance. It now costs him $900 to $1,000 to fill his tank, double the pre-Iran war price.

“These high diesel costs are trickling down to my house expenses, my rent, my groceries,” said Mr. Harmon, 40, of Atlanta. “If I am not making a profit, than I am not going to be able to afford my rent or make payments on my car.”

“At $3 to $4 a gallon, you can survive,” he continued. “But if the prices don’t drop, a lot of us might be forced to suspend operations until things get better,” he said, adding that he is not sure whether to blame “the government or the oil refineries.”

“What I know for sure, is that it doesn’t have to be this way,” he said. “We should be able to make a decent living.”

Kirsten Noyes and Alain Delaqueriere contributed research.
