ARTICLE

Extreme Heat in Los Angeles Area Expected to Last at Least a Week
Forecasters say a dangerous heat wave is descending across much of Southern California, which is likely to bring triple-digit temperatures.
By Livia Albeck-Ripka and Amy Graff
Published 2026-10-02 21:12 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/weather/extreme-heat-wave-california.html

The seasonal pools are closed. Many playground fountains have been turned off. Along Southern California’s beaches, some lifeguard towers are no longer staffed.

Summer is over.

But extreme heat is not. Forecasters say a dangerous heat wave is descending across much of Southern California, which is likely to bring triple-digit temperatures that will last at least a week.

Hot weather is not unusual in Southern California in October, but typically it lasts two or three days. The extended stretch of extreme heat makes this episode particularly dangerous, experts say.

October also tends to be one of the months when the risk of wildfires in Southern California is high because the vegetation has dried out after the summer and winds can grow stronger.

The wildfire risk will be elevated, particularly in inland valleys and mountains, but it is not expected to be so extreme as to prompt red-flag warnings.

Extreme heat warnings have been issued from Santa Barbara to San Diego, lasting through at least next Friday. Temperatures in downtown Los Angeles could reach 100 or higher on Saturday and Sunday, according to the National Weather Service. A few miles from downtown, the Dodgers are set to open a playoff series on Saturday in the middle of the day.

Temperatures will be even more extreme across the region’s inland valleys and deserts. Over the weekend, Death Valley National Park could reach 109 degrees, forecaster predict.

While the highest temperatures are likely to be recorded over the weekend, the weather next week is could feel equally stifling.

“We’re not going to see a pronounced peak in temperatures this weekend. It’s pretty much going to be hot through the entire week,” said Devin Black, a meteorologist with the Weather Service office in Oxnard, Calif.

Across the region, counties and cities were making preparations.

Officials were urging the public not to leave pets and children in vehicles. Crews were on alert for power outages. The Los Angeles County Fire Department has increased staffing and positioned units in some of the most high-risk places, said Jonathan Torres, a spokesman for the department.

County health officials also urged residents to stay hydrated and avoid going outdoors during the hottest hours. Those without air-conditioning, officials said, should take cool showers or baths, avoid using stoves and ovens, and seek shelter in a library, cooling center or mall.

Daniela Simunovic, the chief heat officer for the City of Los Angeles, said those at greatest risk were children, seniors and pregnant people, as well as people living in homes without air-conditioning or cooling. “This week is particularly dangerous,” she said.

Mr. Torres said high-risk heat conditions have become the norm.

“It used to be a season; now it’s year-round,” Mr. Torres said. “That’s just the reality that we have to live with here in Southern California.”

The expected heat wave is the first since the region suffered through scorching temperatures for two days in September, during which the temperature in downtown Los Angeles soared to 105, the highest recorded there so far this year.

Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Oxnard, warned that heat events lasting six or seven days — and including high temperatures at night — could overwhelm the body’s natural cooling system, since there is no time for recovery.

Above normal temperatures in the Pacific Ocean have fueled tropical storms that have sent big waves to the Southern California coast. The increased storm activity is in part driven by the weather pattern known as El Niño that is particularly powerful this year and expected to affect winter weather around the globe. But Ms. Schoenfeld said she and her colleagues are not aware of a direct correlation between the coming heat wave and El Niño.

The heat will be accompanied by the winds that blow dry, warm air from inland areas toward the coast, while simultaneously, the sea breeze that pushes cool air off the ocean toward the coast will weaken, she said.

“That wind pattern is critical to what our temperatures will end up being,” said Ms. Schoenfeld.

While Southern California was wrapped in hot, sticky air much of the summer, relative humidity levels during this event are not expected to be high. The offshore winds pulling in dry air will help prevent muggy weather, but a hurricane churning far offshore could send moisture to the region as early as Saturday.

“It could be a little muggy, but not like it was during a lot of the summer,” said Ms. Schoenfeld.

The hurricane could also cause high surf and rip currents. In a social media post, the Weather Service warned beachgoers seeking relief from the heat not to go into dangerous waters.

Lifeguards in Los Angeles County said last month that over the summer they rescued more than 10,000 people from the ocean.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/well/headaches-brain-sag-spinal-fluid-leak.html

In the early morning light of her home in Dover, Ohio, the 62-year-old woman carefully swung her legs over the side of the bed and stood. And there it was: A clamp tightened around the right side of her head. The pain was over her right ear, in her face and down the right side of her neck. She took a deep breath. Another day. Another headache.

She hadn’t been a headache person for most of her life. But that changed early in 2025 with these headaches that hit as soon as she got up in the morning. It was a pressure-like pain, always on the right side, and ibuprofen and acetaminophen barely touched it.

Given the severity of her pain, the nurse practitioner who was the woman’s primary care provider wondered if these were migraines. She prescribed a medication meant to stop this type of headache when taken as soon as the pain starts. But because it is unusual to start getting headaches at this age, and because the patient’s mother had suffered a ruptured brain aneurysm, she sent her for a head CT. It was a relief for the patient to hear that the CT was normal, but she needed to know the cause of her pain. She went to her eye doctor to find out if she needed a new glasses prescription. She did, but that didn’t help. Her boss installed a shade over her desk to cut the glare from the fluorescent light. She was grateful, but the headaches were unrelenting.

Her P.C.P., still wondering if this could be an aneurysm, referred her to a local neurosurgeon. Hearing her story, the physician assistant in the neurosurgery practice agreed that these probably were migraines and prescribed an additional medication, propranolol, to be taken daily. But the possibility of an aneurysm remained, so she also ordered an M.R.I. of her brain and a CT scan of the blood vessels in her brain. The woman had the two studies a couple of weeks later. There was no aneurysm. Her vessels were normal. Her brain, however, was not.

A Worrisome Explanation

When the patient saw the M.R.I. result, she was alarmed. She had, the report said, something called brain sag. She wasn’t sure what that was, but it sounded bad. She left a message for the P.A., and when she didn’t hear back, she got scared. She called her P.C.P. and was referred to another neurosurgeon, this time at the Cleveland Clinic.

The patient’s first thought when she saw Dr. Mohammed Abdulrazzak at the Cleveland Clinic branch in Canton, Ohio, was that he was too young to be a doctor, much less a neurosurgeon. He introduced himself, then sat in the chair across from hers. “I hear you have a headache,” he said. She felt a sense of real interest from him as she told her story. She explained how terrible her headaches were when she was upright, when she laughed or even spoke. When she sneezed, the pain was unbelievable. And recently the headaches seemed to be affecting her memory as well. She had to write things down to keep herself from forgetting. The migraine medications did help, but the only thing that made her headaches almost completely subside was lying down. When she said this, she thought she saw just a hint of excitement in the young doctor’s eyes.

Brain sag, Abdulrazzak explained, was usually caused by the loss of some of the spinal fluid that cushions and supports the brain. When standing, gravity pulls the already-depleted fluid farther downward, stretching the pain-sensitive membranes and structures around the brain. Lying down eases that stretch immediately. The woman’s story was classic for the diagnosis: a headache that responds to posture almost like a light switch, in a way that tension headaches and migraines rarely do.

Abdulrazzak pointed to the black and white curves of her brain on the M.R.I. Even when she was lying down, her cerebellum was so low that it was almost touching the skull near the foramen magnum, the hole through which the spinal column emerged. That’s why her brain appeared to be sagging. He asked the patient if she had had any recent surgery or trauma. She hadn’t. Abdulrazzak wasn’t surprised. Many of these leaks are spontaneous, the cause never discovered.

The hardest part of this disease was finding the leak. In the necessary test, called a myelogram, contrast is injected into the space around the spinal column and a CT scan captures where it leaks out.

The test was awful. The increased pressure caused by the injection of the contrast made her whole head ache. She waited anxiously for the results. No leak was seen. But Abdulrazzak was sure there was one. There was another study, he told her, only recently available, that would give them a better image. They could give her general anesthesia so she wouldn’t feel the pressure from the injected contrast. The woman considered this possibility then shook her head. The headaches were manageable with the medications, she said. She asked if she could just wait and see what happened. Abdulrazzak assured her she could, and told her to come back in a few months.

Another Test

She felt OK for awhile. But just over a year after the headaches started, the medications suddenly stopped working. Getting out of bed in the morning was almost torture, and some days she had to call in sick and spend the entire day in bed.

Her best friend was distressed to see the woman suffer so much. On weekends, the women and their husbands often went to listen to music in the local bars. But the last time they went out, the woman had to leave. The music, the crowd — it was all just too much for her. These days her friend couldn’t help noticing how tired she looked. She was pale. She had dark circles under her eyes. And she was so forgetful. The way she repeated herself reminded the friend of her own grandmother who had Alzheimer’s.

“You’ve got to go back to that doctor and see what he can do,” the friend exclaimed one evening when the woman was in the grips of a really bad headache.

Her friend went with her a few weeks later to see Abdulrazzak, who arranged the second test. In it, the patient lay on her right side. Once she was sedated, a catheter was inserted into the base of the sac containing the spinal cord, and contrast was injected. Then the table was tilted so that the contrast could flow upward, highlighting the entire spinal column. And there it was — the leak. A thin trickle of contrast filled one of the tiny veins leading away from the sac at the level of the 10th thoracic vertebra, just above the bottom of the rib cage.

Two weeks later, Abdulrazzak inserted a tiny catheter into the woman’s thigh. He slowly threaded it up the vein, carefully navigating toward the tiny vessel the spinal fluid was leaking into. He guided his way using a viewable X-ray called a fluoroscope to find the exact spot. Once he was at the site of the leak, he injected a material to completely seal off the vein.

When the patient woke up, Abdulrazzak told her that she would have a headache for a week or so. Her body had increased the amount of spinal fluid it made trying to compensate for the leak. Now that the leak was sealed, her body would have to reduce its spinal fluid output, and that would take a little time.

She went home the next day, and she did have a headache. But as promised, over the next couple of weeks, the pain gradually disappeared. Her memory started to improve. The real test, she knew, would come when she and her friend and their husbands went out. So, some six weeks after her procedure, the two couples struck out for one of their favorite places. She hadn’t had a headache for weeks, and worried the thunderous music would bring it all back. They found a seat as far from the speakers as they could get. Finally the band came out and picked up their instruments. The woman’s heart raced. But once the lead guitarist struck his first chord, quickly followed by bass, drums and keyboard, she sensed that her headaches were gone for good and life could finally return to normal.

SUMMARY

As China’s government pushes its citizens to embrace artificial intelligence, it is confronting a problem partly of its own making: overreliance on the technology. State media reports have featured stories that serve as cautionary tales: a farmer who lost 25 acres of seedlings after asking an A.I. for advice, children who have become so attached to chatbots that they want their parents to speak like them and A.I.-generated micro dramas with characters that look like carbon copies of one another. These cases and others have raised concerns in China that as it rushes to catch up with the United States in A.I., it is running into adverse side effects created by the new technology, which is accused of undermining human relationships and depriving people of their better judgment.

ARTICLE

China’s Push into A.I. Has Led to a Problem: Too Much Usage
As citizens embrace the technology for entertainment, relationships and even farming advice, the government is stepping up efforts to set limits.
By Yan Zhuang
Published 2026-10-02 04:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/world/asia/china-ai-overuse.html

As China’s government pushes its citizens to embrace artificial intelligence, it is confronting a problem partly of its own making: overreliance on the technology.

State media reports have featured stories that serve as cautionary tales: a farmer who lost 25 acres of seedlings after asking an A.I. for advice, children who have become so attached to chatbots that they want their parents to speak like them and A.I.-generated micro dramas with characters that look like carbon copies of one another.

These cases and others have raised concerns in China that as it rushes to catch up with the United States in A.I., it is running into adverse side effects created by the new technology, which is accused of undermining human relationships and depriving people of their better judgment. The government, seeking to direct how people use the technology, has responded by imposing new regulations and judicial guidelines on its use — and misuse.

The response reflects how the ruling Communist Party is trying to balance its ambitions to promote the widespread use of A.I. with a desire to avoid anything that might undermine social order, say analysts.

The party is “recognizing that the more they develop the technology, the more there’s going to be social challenges that they have to deal with,” said Scott Singer, a fellow and co-director of the China A.I. Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “Where the party is sensitive is any area where they feel like the technology is getting better in a way that fundamentally could disrupt social stability.”

Mr. Singer said the party is particularly sensitive to disruptions caused not only to human relationships but also the job market as A.I. threatens to replace workers.

Concerns about overuse are shared among China’s citizens, who say they see the spread of the technology as inevitable even as they question its benefits and tire of its ubiquity.

Xie Tong, a graphic designer in Beijing, uses A.I. in her own work at a consulting agency and can no longer imagine her life without it. But she despairs at encountering A.I. all around her — in the subway ads that she sees on her commute and in the work of contractors at her job who obviously relied on A.I.

“It’s like a marriage where you curse your partner but you can’t leave them,” she said.

Limits on Virtual Friends

For a time, China’s A.I. push created a boom in virtual companion apps, including ones offering romantic partners, personal tutors and A.I. avatars of family members.

In a country already struggling with a shrinking population and a historically low birthrate, the proliferation has led to concerns from Beijing about A.I. replacing human relationships. State media quoted experts saying people could soon find it hard to navigate real interactions. Reports cited a 2025 survey by the China Youth and Children Research Center of more than 8,500 minors that showed more than 20 percent “only wanted to chat with A.I. and did not want to talk with real people.”

That mirrored the concerns of some parents like Vivian Lyu, a stay-at-home mother in Hangzhou who two years ago introduced her 5-year-old daughter, Polly, to Doubao, an A.I. assistant created by ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok.

Soon, the child was chatting with the A.I. and a personalized companion on the app nearly every day. At first, Ms. Lyu thought the A.I. was good at keeping Polly entertained when the mother had to take care of household tasks. “When you feel like you don’t have a choice, you use Doubao,” she said.

Over time, though, Polly started asking for Doubao instead of seeking out activities that used to interest her, like playing with other children or drawing pictures. Ms. Lyu said she worried that the chatbot was warping her daughter’s understanding of how relationships worked, saying that Polly sometimes talked to Doubao in a “very self-centered, doing-whatever-she-wants kind of way.”

In July, the government imposed limits on A.I. companions that require platforms to step in if users exhibited unhealthy dependencies. Under the new rules, platforms must intervene if users show signs of self-harm.

The rules also banned virtual relationships between chatbots and minors, which forced ByteDance to shut down the feature on Doubao that allowed users to create companions.

Polly can no longer access her personalized A.I. companion, but she is still talking to Doubao’s A.I. chatbot, Ms. Lyu said. The mother considered banning her daughter from using chatbots but concluded that such a step could make it harder for Polly to adjust to the technology as she grows older. Instead, Ms. Lyu has limited Polly’s chatbot time to one hour a day.

“My hope is for her to understand from a young age that these electronic products, or all of these things related to A.I., are just tools,” Ms. Lyu said.

Real World Problems

Just as in many countries, China is struggling with so-called A.I. literacy — understanding how the technology works and its limits. In recent months, the media has documented a growing number of A.I. mishaps involving people who blindly believed in the technology.

There was the case of a hiker who became stranded atop a mountain in August after A.I.-generated instructions left him improperly equipped. In several separate cases earlier in the summer, people fell ill after eating poisonous mushrooms that were misidentified by A.I., including a 9-year-old boy who spent eight days in a hospital.

One of the most widely covered cases involved a farmer in the eastern province of Anhui who lost 25 acres of sesame seedlings in July after following a pesticide regimen drawn up by an A.I. assistant.

The 67-year-old farmer, whom the reports identified only by his last name, Wu, lost 150,000 yuan, or about $22,000, worth of crops after the A.I. recommended an herbicide that turned out to be unsuitable, the reports said.

The Communist Party’s mouthpiece, People’s Daily, argued in a commentary that A.I. in sectors like agriculture should use only information that comes from authoritative sources.

It also called for farmers to be trained in “critical thinking about A.I. suggestions, helping farmers transform from passive implementers of technology into active participants who can control the tools.”

A Backlash Against Cheap A.I. Fodder

A.I. has also become ubiquitous in micro dramas, the wildly popular short-form, soapy shows that are made for mobile viewing. In the first eight months of the year, more than 90 percent of the 430,000 micro dramas released in China were generated by A.I., the government said in late September.

These dramas can be churned out cheaply in minutes with no cameras, production crews or human performers. But they have come under fire for their low quality and for taking the jobs of humans.

An article in August in Beijing Youth Daily, the official publication of the Communist Youth League, complained that production companies were churning out A.I.-created micro dramas with boring, interchangeable characters.

Some influential voices have gone as far as to say they will boycott micro dramas generated entirely by A.I.

Hu Xijin, the former editor of the state-run Global Times, told his 25 million followers on the social media platform Weibo recently that he would not watch such dramas to avoid “filling up our recreational time with cheap A.I. fodder like pig feed.”

Siyi Zhao contributed research.

SUMMARY

On paper, the Democrats’ path to winning the Senate in November is daunting. Since Labor Day, Democrats have been tied or ahead in nearly every nonpartisan poll of not just two but five states that voted for Mr. Trump by between 11 and 16 points: Texas, Alaska, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas. The Times/Siena polls — and others over the last month — show Democrats building a consistent and potentially meaningful lead in both states.

ARTICLE

Democrats May Have Found the Recipe for Flipping Red-State Senate Seats
Five new Times/Siena polls continue a run of strong results for the party in states that President Trump won easily in 2024.
By Nate Cohn
Published 2026-10-03 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/03/upshot/polls-midterms-senate-times-siena.html

On paper, the Democrats’ path to winning the Senate in November is daunting. They need to flip at least two seats that President Trump won by 11 percentage points or more — no party has pulled off a similar feat since 2008.

But in polls over the last month, the party’s path to the Senate hasn’t seemed daunting at all. Since Labor Day, Democrats have been tied or ahead in nearly every nonpartisan poll of not just two but five states that voted for Mr. Trump by between 11 and 16 points: Texas, Alaska, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas.

Today’s latest New York Times/Siena polls continue the streak. They find Democrats ahead in Texas, Alaska and Ohio; tied in Kansas; and down by only one point in Iowa. If the polls were to be exactly right — they won’t be — Democrats would take the Senate with room to spare.

This is an extraordinary run of polls for Democrats, most of all in Texas and Alaska. The Times/Siena polls — and others over the last month — show Democrats building a consistent and potentially meaningful lead in both states. If Democrats won Texas and Alaska, held their own seats and added North Carolina, as expected, they would need to win only one more Republican-held state, whether in Maine, Ohio, Iowa or Kansas, or elsewhere.

Of course, leading polls in September is not the same thing as winning in November — especially in Republican-leaning states, where polls have often overestimated Democrats. And even if they’re not overestimating them this time, Republicans need only to win back reliably Republican voters over the next month to prevail. This is harder than it sounds in this political environment, but it would not be a surprise if they did so. Republicans will have the financial resources they need to make their case.

Nonetheless, just about everything has gone right for the Democrats so far. They enter the final month of the campaign in a better position than anyone would have imagined when the year began. While the story varies somewhat by state, Democrats are cooking with the same recipe across all five contests: At a time when Mr. Trump is very unpopular, Democrats have nominated popular, relatively moderate candidates against surprisingly unpopular Republicans.

Ingredient No. 1: Trump

By now, it’s hard to be surprised by bad poll results for Mr. Trump. Still, these results from such Republican-leaning states — which gave Mr. Trump an average of 56 percent of the vote in 2024 — are striking.

Across the five states, the president’s approval rating was just 40 percent, while 57 percent had an unfavorable view. That’s not much better than Mr. Trump’s ratings in recent national polls. The results also represent a significant decline in his support since our last polls in four of these states in June. Since then, his ratings have fallen by five points.

There are two basic possible explanations for how Mr. Trump’s numbers are this bad in these states. One is that his ratings have continued to slide everywhere, not just in these states, since our last Times/Siena poll, which wouldn’t necessarily be hard to explain with gas prices and mortgage rates rising.

Another possibility is that Mr. Trump is suffering disproportionate losses in these five Republican-leaning states. Demographics, alone, would not be a sufficient explanation. It would take something more, like greater exposure to high diesel prices in the Farm Belt. Or there could even be a break in Mr. Trump’s support among the traditional Republicans who never loved Mr. Trump’s conduct or his policies on issues like tariffs or immigration, but nonetheless consistently backed him in every general election.

Interestingly, all five of these states voted against Mr. Trump in the 2016 Republican presidential primary.

Ingredient No. 2: Candidate quality

In all five states, Democrats have something more going for them, even beyond Mr. Trump’s extraordinary unpopularity: a significant advantage in candidate quality.

Let’s take the simplest measure: favorability. In all five states, more voters view the Democrat favorably than unfavorably, while more voters view the Republican candidate unfavorably than favorably.

This is a real triumph for Democrats in such reliably Republican states. They’ve managed to find candidates who are both personally appealing and ideologically acceptable to red-state voters.

In all five states, voters say that the phrase “has good character” describes the Democratic candidate better than the Republican.

In four of the five states (in the fifth, Ohio, it’s essentially even), a greater share of voters say the Republican is “too far to the right” than say the Democrat is “too far to the left.”

In contrast, a majority of voters in all five states said the Democratic Party was “too far” to the left, and did not say the Republican Party was “too far” to the right. That’s to be expected in Republican-leaning states, and yet it didn’t translate to the candidates themselves.

Let’s look at some of the results by state.

Perfect storm in Texas

Of all the polls, none capture the Republican challenge better than Texas, where the Democrat James Talarico is leading the Republican Ken Paxton by six points.

If Democrats are cooking with the same recipe in all five of these states, Texas is the one where Republicans have contributed the finest ingredients. The president’s approval rating has fallen to just 38 percent among likely voters there — the same as in our last national poll — and Mr. Paxton is the least popular of all 10 Senate candidates tested in these polls. And all of this is occurring in a state where Hispanic voters, who are swinging hard toward the Democrats, represent a large share of the electorate.

While the G.O.P. is spending hundreds of millions of dollars to try to bring down Mr. Talarico, so far his candidacy appears essentially undamaged. His favorable ratings actually ticked up since the last Times/Siena poll in June. Only 40 percent say he’s “too far to the left,” barely changed from 39 percent in June — and less than the 47 percent who say Mr. Paxton is “too far to the right.”

If there’s a “glass half full” interpretation for Republicans, it’s that the poll found a very favorable electorate for Democrats. If the poll is right about who will show up to vote, then many Trump voters — especially Hispanic and young Trump voters — will stay home. At the same time, an influx of new Democratic-leaning voters would enter the electorate. Together, the electorate jolts to the left.

If the 2024 electorate showed up, the race would be a dead heat.

Alaska primaries and ranked choice

Can a seven-point lead for a Democrat in Alaska be unsurprising? If there ever were a case, this might be it.

Unlike most states, Alaska holds a top-four primary — all candidates from every party compete on the same ballot, and the top four candidates advance. In this year’s primary, the Democrat Mary Peltola finished eight points ahead of the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan — quite similar to the result of the poll.

One twist on the ballot — and in our poll — is the other Dan Sullivan. Yes, two people named Dan Sullivan are running for Senate in Alaska, and the other Dan Sullivan will indeed appear on the ballot in November.

This was an unexpected issue back in our June poll, when we didn’t specify which Dan Sullivan we were talking about — and may have gotten a handful of confused, serious or trolling responses. To avoid it this time, we asked voters about Dan Sullivan “the incumbent” (as he is described on the ballot).

A.I. in Ohio

As I wrote after our last national poll, artificial intelligence hasn’t quite emerged as a top-tier issue in electoral politics. For now, it’s a third-tier issue like climate change — something that activists care about and that might matter in a race under certain circumstances, but that doesn’t yet shape national electoral outcomes.

That story basically held in our state polls, with one exception: Ohio, where the Democrat Sherrod Brown led the Republican Jon Husted by three points.

In Ohio, 3 percent of voters said A.I. was the most important issue to their vote, compared with about 0.3 percent of voters in the other states. That may not sound like a big difference, but that puts A.I. alongside issues that regularly affect the outcome of national elections and the partisan leanings of a broader share of the electorate, like abortion or health care.

Ohio has been an epicenter of the backlash over data centers, and Mr. Brown was an early mover in trying to capitalize on the issue against the incumbent, Mr. Husted. As my colleague Shane Goldmacher reported in August, a memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that “more than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”

The Times/Siena poll found that voters preferred Mr. Brown on A.I. and data centers by 10 points — a bigger lead on A.I. than any candidate had in any of the polls. It was Mr. Brown’s biggest lead on any question.

Can Hamilton gain in Kansas?

Kansas? If you’re not the kind of person who follows the latest polls (and we have a great new page tracking the latest polls, if you would like to do so), you might be surprised that we’re polling Kansas at all. But it has been on the edge of the radar for a while, and over the last month a string of nonpartisan, Democratic and Republican polls have all shown an extremely close race. Our poll shows a tie.

How are Democrats so competitive in Kansas? There are a lot of factors, but what might get them over the top is the appeal of their candidate, Adam Hamilton. He is the senior pastor of the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, and he’s a first-time candidate who says he’s running against socialism and health care cuts.

Mr. Hamilton has the highest net favorability rating of any of the candidates tested in these polls, and he may have more room to grow. Overall, 28 percent of likely voters said they hadn’t heard of him. The danger for Republicans is obvious: If more voters learn that he’s no ordinary Democrat, Mr. Hamilton might gain more support.

Mr. Hamilton is actually performing worse than the Democratic Party on the generic congressional ballot among the voters who haven’t heard of him. Among the voters who do have an opinion of him, he’s running 12 points ahead of the generic ballot — which would be enough for him to win.

SUMMARY

The Trump administration’s talks with Russia about ending the war in Ukraine have expanded to include a multibillion-dollar oil deal that would benefit Middle Eastern business executives with ties to the two main U.S. negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The deal, which is contingent on approval from the U.S. government and the Kremlin, is for a sprawling set of oil fields, refineries and gas stations around the world owned by Lukoil, one of Russia’s biggest energy companies. President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia brought up the deal when he met with Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner at the Kremlin on Sept. 5, according to three people familiar with the meeting.

ARTICLE

U.S.-Russia Talks on Ukraine Now Involve an Oil Deal Tied to Trump Allies
President Vladimir V. Putin brought up a sale of Russian energy assets with President Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, pushing a deal that raises new questions about conflicts of interest.
By Anton Troianovski and Eric Lipton
Published 2026-10-03 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/03/us/politics/kushner-witkoff-russia-oil-deal.html

The Trump administration’s talks with Russia about ending the war in Ukraine have expanded to include a multibillion-dollar oil deal that would benefit Middle Eastern business executives with ties to the two main U.S. negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

The deal, which is contingent on approval from the U.S. government and the Kremlin, is for a sprawling set of oil fields, refineries and gas stations around the world owned by Lukoil, one of Russia’s biggest energy companies.

The leading group seeking the deal includes an American investor, Todd Boehly, who has donated $2 million to President Trump’s political causes; two Middle Eastern groups that have done business with Mr. Kushner or Mr. Witkoff’s family; and an arm of the U.S. government itself.

The monthslong negotiations, which were described by eight people familiar with them, shed new light on Mr. Trump’s latest approach to settling a four-year war that has killed hundreds of thousands. The people spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the negotiations.

There is no indication that Mr. Kushner or Mr. Witkoff themselves stand to profit. But the pending deal represents a striking intermingling of personal business ties with geopolitics, even for an administration that has regularly dismissed concerns about potential conflicts of interest.

President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia brought up the deal when he met with Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner at the Kremlin on Sept. 5, according to three people familiar with the meeting. Mr. Putin proposed it get done as a way of showing Russians that they can do business with the United States, according to one of the people.

The Americans responded that they would work on it, the person said, seeing it as a way to build good will with the Kremlin while also lowering global energy prices. But the deal is also a lucrative one for the buyers: U.S. approval for the sale would release the assets from American sanctions, instantly increasing their value.

In Moscow, the decision on the deal is widely seen as Mr. Putin’s to make, even though Lukoil is technically a private company. The upshot is that the giant transaction, involving assets as varied as oil fields in Cameroon, refineries in Europe and gas stations in New Jersey, comes down to Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump.

Mr. Trump has been promoting the promise of business deals with Russia since early last year, describing the country as a “tremendous opportunity.” The deal again brings Mr. Trump’s World Liberty Financial cryptocurrency company — co-founded by Mr. Witkoff — into focus. One of the investors in the Lukoil deal is a part owner of World Liberty.

Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner, who have traveled repeatedly to Russia for meetings with Mr. Putin, have argued that the potential to rebuild economic ties with the West could convince the Russian president to compromise in Ukraine. The administration has recently signaled it is open to deals with Russia even before the war ends, as a way of showing it is serious about resetting the United States’ relationship with Moscow.

The Lukoil sale, people familiar with the matter say, is one of those deals.

In a statement, a senior administration official confirmed that Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner played a direct role in helping negotiate the financial terms of the investment by the federal government in the deal to ensure that it included “a substantial upfront payment and profits interest for the United States.”

A spokeswoman for Mr. Witkoff said that he “takes no salary and travels the world on his own plane, at his own expense, working on behalf of President Trump to negotiate peace and bring hostages home to their families.” She added that Mr. Witkoff “has no conflict of interest and no financial stake in this matter.”

A Stalled Bid, and a New Contender

Numerous potential bidders expressed interest in at least part of Lukoil’s international holdings when the assets went on the market last fall, including U.S. energy giants like Chevron.

The Washington private equity firm Carlyle reached a tentative agreement in January to buy a large share of the assets, after making the pitch that bringing Lukoil’s international portfolio under U.S. ownership would further the Trump administration’s goal of “energy dominance.”

But in recent months, as U.S. approval for Carlyle’s bid stalled, a different group emerged as the leading bidder: one led by Mr. Boehly, a billionaire supporter of Mr. Trump’s, alongside well-connected figures in the Middle East and the U.S. government itself. The members of the partnership were reported last week by The Financial Times.

Mr. Boehly is a co-owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers and donated $1 million to MAGA Inc., the Trump-aligned political committee, in December 2025. He gave another $1 million through his investment firm, Eldridge Industries, to Mr. Trump’s inauguration.

The U.S. government is taking a stake in the deal through the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, an agency that invests in and lends to projects overseas. A D.F.C. official said in a statement that the potential Lukoil deal “would advance the Trump administration’s commitment to strengthen U.S. economic security, advance U.S. foreign policy and lower energy prices for everyday Americans.”

But it would not be an all-American purchase.

A major equity holder would be the Qatar-based conglomerate controlled by Moutaz Al-Khayyat and his brother Ramez Al-Khayyat, both of whom attended Mr. Trump’s inauguration in 2025 and have since formed a partnership with Mr. Kushner and his wife, Ivanka Trump, one of Mr. Trump’s daughters, to help finance a multibillion-dollar luxury hotel resort project in southern Albania.

Another major stakeholder would be an Abu Dhabi-based investment fund controlled by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the United Arab Emirates’s top national security adviser, who controls another fund that purchased a large stake in the Trump family’s cryptocurrency company, World Liberty, run in part by Mr. Witkoff’s son.

Steve Witkoff was a co-founder of World Liberty, and Mr. Trump’s sons are also involved in the company, which generated $799 million for Mr. Trump last year, in part because of an additional cryptocurrency purchase worth $2 billion that Sheikh Tahnoon’s affiliate made in 2025. Mr. Witkoff himself has sold off his stake in World Liberty, a person close to him said.

Sheikh Tahnoon also helps oversee an Abu Dhabi investment fund called Lunate, which is among the largest stakeholders in the private equity firm Mr. Kushner set up after he left the White House at the end of Mr. Trump’s first term. This means Sheikh Tahnoon is effectively a business partner of Mr. Kushner’s as well.

An ‘Alarming’ Set of Entanglements

Hui Chen, a former Justice Department prosecutor and a white collar crime and ethics adviser who served until the start of Mr. Trump’s first term, said the connections between Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner to players in the Lukoil deal illustrated why friends and family members of Mr. Trump’s should not be top foreign policy advisers.

“This is an alarming and very concerning set of entanglements,” said Ms. Chen, who has also worked as a corporate compliance lawyer. “And it means you have to question how the Trump administration is evaluating the different bidders involved here. Are the personal interests involved going to wrongly influence the outcome?”

Lukoil’s international division, which is based in Austria, hired its own Washington-based consultant who is close to Mr. Trump, Bryan Lanza, who served as a senior adviser to Mr. Trump’s 2024 election campaign and now works at Mercury Public Affairs. He is no longer working for Lukoil, a person familiar with the matter said.

The deal is not yet final, and would need to be approved by the Treasury Department, which oversees sanctions enforcement.

But in the case of Lukoil, people involved said, the key decisions are being made at the White House. Asked about its approach to the Lukoil decision, a Treasury Department spokeswoman said that the agency’s Office of Foreign Assets Control “implements foreign policy as determined by the White House.”

The Sept. 5 meeting with Mr. Putin was the first time that Lukoil came up in the Russian president’s conversations with Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner, one person familiar with the matter said.

But Kirill Dmitriev, Mr. Putin’s economic envoy, has been closely involved, people familiar with the sale process said. He traveled to New York and Washington for meetings last month, and told reporters that “dialogue” with the United States was “continuing across many areas, including energy.”

Lukoil’s refineries in the Netherlands, Bulgaria and Romania play an important role. They produce diesel and jet fuel, which have been in short supply since the start of the Iran war, which has driven up prices and given Mr. Trump an incentive to support a deal that could provide more access to energy.

Lukoil valued its international assets at $20 billion earlier this year, but the price and structure of the proposed deal are not clear.

An official with the D.F.C., the U.S. agency investing in the deal, described participation in the purchase as a way to strengthen the energy security of U.S. allies. The official also said the deal would produce significant profits for the American taxpayer and keep strategic infrastructure away from adversaries.

Scramble for Assets

The Trump administration imposed sanctions on Lukoil a year ago, describing the move as new pressure on Mr. Putin to “stop the killing.” It also created a lucrative opportunity: Lukoil was forced to sell off its sprawling portfolio of international holdings.

Investors around the world scrambled to bid on the assets, but the U.S. government held veto power because it controlled how to enforce its sanctions. Because of Russia’s autocratic system, Mr. Putin was seen as the final decision maker in Moscow .

The bidding frenzy accelerated last November, when the Treasury Department rejected an initial offer by Gunvor, a Swiss-based energy trading company with past ties to Russia, which had moved to buy Lukoil’s foreign assets. The Treasury Department said in a statement that “as long as Putin continues the senseless killings, the Kremlin’s puppet, Gunvor, will never get a license to operation and profit.”

Carlyle secured a “nonexclusive” agreement in January with Lukoil to sell its international assets. It was up to the Treasury Department to then sign off on the deal. As months passed with no final deal, other bidders intensified their efforts to step in.

Mr. Boehly has little experience in the oil and gas industry. He has made most of his money through investment firms such as Guggenheim Partners and Eldridge Industries, as well as sports team and entertainment industry investments, including Bruce Springsteen’s music catalog.

But over the last several years, the billionaire Khayyat brothers, who were born in Syria before moving to Qatar during the Syrian civil war, have begun to amass a collection of oil industry assets and planned projects in Syria, Libya and Iraq.

Even while the Lukoil negotiations were underway, the Khayyats were continuing to work with Mr. Kushner and Ivanka Trump over plans to build the luxury resort in Albania, an effort that included a meeting involving Ramez Al-Khayyat and Ms. Trump earlier this year in Albania, The Times reported.

The decision over Lukoil’s fate has taken so long that the Treasury Department has had to repeatedly issue extensions to its sanctions action, so that Lukoil gas stations in the United States and other businesses around the world could continue to engage with other financial partners. The most recent extension lasts until Oct. 29.

SUMMARY

In the go-big-or-go-home collective consciousness of Texas, no ambition is deemed too reckless, no daydream too wild. It is the idea, fantastical to many as it is irresistible to others, that the Democrats will win a statewide race in Texas for the first time in 32 years. So there are reasons for Texas Democrats to be optimistic.”

ARTICLE

In Texas, Talarico Inspires a Recurring Blue-Tinted Dream
After a dry spell of more than three decades, Democrats are daring (yet again) to believe they can win one or more top-of-the-ballot races in a vast and stubbornly red state.
By Robert Draper
Published 2026-10-03 09:45 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/03/us/politics/texas-talarico.html

In the go-big-or-go-home collective consciousness of Texas, no ambition is deemed too reckless, no daydream too wild. Save perhaps one.

It is the idea, fantastical to many as it is irresistible to others, that the Democrats will win a statewide race in Texas for the first time in 32 years.

According to the latest New York Times/Siena University poll of the race for U.S. Senate, James Talarico, a 37-year-old state legislator seen by national Democrats as one of the breakout stars of this cycle, is ahead of his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, the state’s scandal-plagued attorney general, by six points. The poll was conducted from Sept. 21 to Sept. 30. A survey from mid-September, the ReconMR/Siena Research Institute poll, also showed the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Gina Hinojosa, four points ahead of the three-term G.O.P. incumbent, Greg Abbott, the most dominant political figure in Texas.

Cue the fluttering heartbeats. Cue, as well, the eye-rolls.

Given how thoroughly Republicans have dominated the state, and how the hopes of Democrats have repeatedly crashed, some Texas pollsters remain skeptical.

“At some point, you do get conditioned by all that’s happened in the past,” said James Henson, the director of the University of Texas at Austin’s Texas Politics Project. “I mean, you look at the trends and you have to admit that something’s going on. But you still don’t want to believe your lying eyes, because you’ve been burned for so long.”

Mr. Henson was referring to the perennial spectacle of much-ballyhooed Texas Democratic aspirants face-planting against the Lone Star State’s red wall.

First came Tony Sanchez Jr., the swaggering and self-funding Laredo oilman whom Gov. Rick Perry dispatched in 2002 by an 18-point margin. Next was the state senator Wendy Davis, who attracted worldwide attention for her filibuster in the Texas Legislature against an anti-abortion measure but whom Mr. Abbott demolished by 20 points in 2014.

Finally, the El Paso congressman Beto O’Rourke came up 2.6 points short of defeating Senator Ted Cruz in 2018 but then suffered a 10-point loss to Mr. Abbott four years later.

Even with the awareness of such humiliations, Democrats find themselves maintaining that 2026 could, at long last, be the year. President Trump’s deep unpopularity and the prospect of a blue wave could, they insist, extend into the state he won by nearly 14 points in 2024. According to a September survey conducted by Texas Southern University, Mr. Trump is seven points underwater in Texas.

Mr. Talarico has run an energetic and well-financed campaign, while Mr. Paxton has staged far fewer public events and has had to rely on outside groups to fund an attack-ad blitzkrieg against his Democratic opponent. Mr. Abbott, meanwhile, has outspent Ms. Hinojosa by a 10-to-one ratio, yet has been unable to build an insurmountable lead.

“People have vastly underestimated Gina,” said Ms. Davis, now a political consultant and a senior adviser to Planned Parenthood Texas Votes, an advocacy organization. “Dollar for dollar, she’s running the best statewide campaign we’ve ever seen.”

Such optimism stands in defiance of the political axiom that Texas is where idealistic Democrats go to be mugged by reality. The party’s demise there is not a product of ill fortune, Mr. Henson said. “Governor Abbott has built an impressive election machine that has benefited state-level Republicans again and again for a decade and a half,” he said. “And the Democratic machinery here is almost nonexistent.”

A ‘Hollowing-Out’

I have written about the politics of my native state at regular intervals for more than three decades. After watching the Democrats’ century-long rule in Texas come to a decisive end with Gov. Ann Richards’s loss to George W. Bush in 1994, I saw the party descend into atrophy in which failure begot more failure.

“The 30-year drought has done a lot of things,” said Luke Warford, the chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party and the founder of the Agave Democratic Infrastructure Fund. “It’s kept donors on the sidelines, which makes a lot of potentially good candidates not run because there’s no belief they can win. And it also makes a lot of really talented staff leave to find better-paying work in true battleground states.”

The Democratic Party has no counterpart to Mr. Abbott, and hasn’t since 1993, when Senator Lloyd Bentsen moved to Washington to join President Bill Clinton’s cabinet. Its weaknesses are even more glaring farther down the hierarchy.

In recent elections, as many as one-third of state races have gone uncontested by Democrats. One-fifth of the party’s county chairs and two-thirds of its precinct chairs have been left unfilled. Until last year, the state party had a negative operating budget. As the veteran Democratic consultant Matt Angle observed, “There’s been a hollowing-out of the party.”

Still, those of us who recall the satisfied sense of invincibility among Texas Democrats after roughly a century of one-party rule have detected similar signs of overconfidence among the state’s ruling party. The party’s rightward tilt, increasingly forceful with each legislative session, reached its apotheosis in March, with Mr. Paxton’s primary victory over the more moderate Republican four-term incumbent, Senator John Cornyn.

Mr. Paxton, a close ally of Mr. Trump, was impeached by the Republican-controlled State House (and later acquitted by the State Senate) in 2023 over allegations that included bribery. He was also accused by his wife of adultery. Mr. Trump endorsed him anyway, all but guaranteeing his landslide primary triumph over Mr. Cornyn but in the process testing the allegiance of center-right Texans.

In similar fashion, the Texas G.O.P. is in danger of losing many Latino voters who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 after years of siding with Democrats. “We adopted a lazy way of campaigning that bit us on the ass, and we’ve learned from that,” Mr. O’Rourke said. “Now it’s the Republicans who’ve gotten really lazy and complacent and comfortable.”

Signs of Republican Overreach

Simply spending one week driving through the vastness of Texas, as I did in September, is all it takes to appreciate an underdog party’s uphill battle.

The state’s 32 million residents are spread across 20 media markets, many of them distinct ecosystems, from the urban colossi of Houston and the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex to the oil patch of the Texas Panhandle to the Latino-dominated borderlands of the Rio Grande Valley.

“When national donors are deciding where to invest, they look at a place like Iowa, where $5 million can fully fund a race,” said Katherine Fischer, the director of the Texas Majority PAC, which was established by the liberal philanthropist Soros family. “That’s why Texas is always at the bottom of their list. It’s just so damned big.”

Reaching so many markets presents a daunting challenge for an upstart candidate like Ms. Hinojosa, a state representative from the border city of Brownsville. “There’s still 20 percent of the electorate that doesn’t know who I am,” she said in an interview in mid-September. To date, Ms. Hinojosa’s campaign has said that it has raised about $20 million.

For his part, Mr. Talarico spent about $30 million earlier this year to introduce himself statewide as a man of Christian faith and a member of the Texas House with a record of supporting bipartisan legislation.

Since that time, however, Mr. Paxton and his associates have invested more than $100 million in an effort to redefine his opponent as “radical” and “weird,” with ads that quote from remarks Mr. Talarico made several years ago (and later renounced) suggesting that “God is nonbinary” and that there are six biological sexes. Mr. Paxton and his allies have at times questioned Mr. Talarico’s manhood and even his Christianity, an effort to jolt the sensibilities of a state prone to mythologizing godly and masculine archetypes.

“How they’re negatively defining Talarico is kind of a bank-shot way of saying that he’s not a true Texas conservative,” Mr. Henson said.

Whether money can overwhelm conditions on the ground is the riddle looming over the Texas races. In the border city of Laredo, which Mr. Trump won in 2024 — the first time a Republican had done so in over a century — signs of buyer’s remorse are evident. Arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Laredo were higher in July than in any other American city. Mr. Trump’s erratic trade policies have further created instability at the city’s port of entry.

While acknowledging the economic concerns that many border residents share, Adrian Zapata, a business executive in the health industry who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, said in an interview that the negative ads against Mr. Talarico were resonating with some of his family members. “They see Talarico as an ultraliberal,” he said. “They’re done with the ‘they/them.’ They’re going to vote for Paxton just because of that.”

As for Mr. Zapata, “I’m not ready to vote for Talarico,” he said. “But I don’t like Paxton. He’s never done anything for South Texas, and his personal and business dealings have hurt him a lot with folks down here.”

There is a similarly muddled electoral picture in the cattle country of deep West Texas adjacent to Big Bend National Park. Mr. Trump and Mr. Abbott have aggressively championed a border wall and artificial intelligence data centers, both of which threaten to disrupt the region’s pastoral ethos.

A coalition of more than 200 landowners has sued the federal government over the border wall, while other residents have circulated a petition to protest the construction of a new data center near Fort Stockton. George Johnson, a cattle feed operator in Alpine, waved off such concerns, saying: “Folks worrying about data centers were also worried when the internet got started. It’s Talarico who scares me to death, him and all that socialist talk.”

Others in this largely conservative region harbor the view that Republicans have failed to make good on their promises. Thaddeus Cleveland, the Republican sheriff of Terrell County, said that both he and his county had voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, but added, “Everything he campaigned on, we’re seeing the opposite of, like going to war.” Sheriff Cleveland predicted that the negative campaign ads by the Republicans would not factor as significantly into the votes of his neighbors as “the price of groceries and gas, which are compounded here because we’re so far from everywhere else.”

But it is in purple Tarrant County, dominated by Fort Worth, where the party could pay the price for having potentially overestimated its mandate from the voters. Conservative leaders have cut funds for nonprofits that aid at-risk children, subjected school library books to right-wing litmus tests and eliminated free bus rides to polling stations in poor neighborhoods.

“The far-right leaders here have implemented Project 2025 on a county level,” said Alisa Simmons, a Democrat and county commissioner who is running to unseat the conservative county judge, Tim O’Hare.

In an early sign this year that area Republicans may be out of step with Tarrant County’s constituents, a Democratic aviation machinist and union leader, Taylor Rehmet, defeated Leigh Wambsganss, a well-funded Republican Christian activist who led the conservative takeover of several metroplex school boards. He won by 14 points in a January special election for a State Senate seat covering a region that Mr. Trump won by 17 points in 2024.

A ‘Gradualist’ Theory

Which party prevails in Texas is a complicated riddle. Historically a low-turnout state — it ranked second to last in the 2024 election, ahead of only Arkansas — Texas held a primary in March that saw nearly one in four voters showing up to the polls, a modern record for midterm participation, with Democrats slightly outpacing Republicans.

A few factors could conspire to thwart a blue wave in Texas. As of 2020, straight-ticket voting is no longer possible in the state, which could impact the mostly Democratic urban counties where that practice has frequently been used by voters in past elections. Texas is one of only eight states that lack universal online registration, while voting by mail is also highly restricted.

In January, Mr. Abbott turned over the state’s list of approximately 18.7 million registered voters to the Trump administration, and 1.2 million of them have subsequently been put on the “suspense list” because their addresses have not been verified. The recent shuttering of nearly one-third of Tarrant County’s polling sites by its Republican-controlled county commission is particularly worrisome for Democrats.

“The reason we’ve lost these statewide races in the past is because we’ve never gotten enough out of Tarrant County to overcome the margins in rural Texas,” Ms. Davis said of the turnout. “If we don’t get it to 53 or 54 percent this November, it’s game over. James and Gina can’t win.”

But the state’s Republicans have reasons of their own to be fretful. Partly because of the recruitment efforts of the Texas Majority PAC and Blueprint Texas, a down-ballot candidate support organization co-founded by Ms. Davis earlier this year, the Democrats are fielding a full slate in all 150 state races for the first time in a half-century. Though many of these aspirants face long odds, their presence on the ballot could energize the Democrats in predominantly conservative regions who have not bothered to turn out in the past.

“If we win on Nov. 3, most of those names running down-ballot in really tough areas like East Texas and the Hill Country and the Panhandle will be responsible,” Mr. O’Rourke said.

Mr. Henson added that while he remained skeptical about Democratic enthusiasm being sufficient to carry the day for Mr. Talarico, he also doubted that a last-minute avalanche of negative ads would prove decisive for Mr. Paxton. “At a certain point, there’s diminishing impact once you get past an absurd level of spending,” he said.

Rather than project a winner in November, Mr. Henson said he felt more comfortable embracing a “gradualist” theory, one in which Texas does not become blue overnight, but instead competitive.

“Even if Talarico loses by a Beto-like margin,” he said, “the next cycle is a presidential election, where Trump likely won’t be popular and Democratic turnout will be higher. So there are reasons for Texas Democrats to be optimistic.”

Trump administration officials are celebrating how the Boehly-backed deal would help U.S. energy security, as the package includes everything from oil production sites to refineries and gas stations.

ARTICLE

Trump, Putin, Ukraine and an Oil Deal: 5 Takeaways
A proposal to bolster relations with the Kremlin through the purchase of Russian energy assets is striking even for an administration that regularly mixes personal business interests with foreign policy.
By Eric Lipton and Anton Troianovski
Published 2026-10-03 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/03/us/politics/trump-putin-ukraine-oil-deal-5-takeaways.html

It is one of the most alluring opportunities in global energy.

The foreign assets of Lukoil, the Russian energy giant, are being sold off at fire sale prices because U.S. sanctions have made them nearly worthless for investors in Russia. Gas stations in the United States, refineries in Eastern Europe and oil fields around the world are up for grabs.

Now, the process of selling off those assets has become intertwined with White House efforts to negotiate an end to Russia’s war in Ukraine. And some of the key figures poised to benefit from the Lukoil sale have ties to President Trump’s family and his associates — including the administration’s envoys to Russia. The revelation raises new questions about conflicts of interest in an administration that has regularly mixed personal interests with national interests.

Here are five takeaways from The New York Times’s investigation of the proposed transaction.

Completing the deal is a factor in Ukraine peace talks.

The Trump administration has long argued that discussing business deals with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia could help convince him to mend ties with the West and end his war on Ukraine. The administration signaled recently that some deals could move forward before the war ends. But the specifics have been murky until now.

When Mr. Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, met with Mr. Putin at the Kremlin last month, the Russian president asked them to get the Lukoil deal done. The Americans said they would work on it, reasoning that doing so could build good will with the Kremlin while also lowering global energy prices.

The deal’s leader is a big political donor to Mr. Trump.

The leader of the investor group is Todd Boehly, a billionaire asset manager and co-owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers, among other holdings. He is also a major donor to Mr. Trump’s political causes. He contributed $1 million to Mr. Trump’s affiliated MAGA Inc. political committee last December, just as negotiations on the Lukoil deal were heating up.

Family ties to the investors are widespread.

Mr. Trump; his three sons; Mr. Kushner; Ivanka Trump, one of the president’s daughters; and the Witkoff family all have financial ties to partners in the deal, which requires sign off from the Trump administration and the Kremlin. The Trump family and the president’s advisers do not have a direct financial stake in the transaction. But their business partners would benefit financially if the multibillion-dollar deal is completed.

The investors who have teamed up with Mr. Boehly include one of the richest investment funds in the Middle East, International Holding Company, which is overseen by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the Abu Dhabi royal family.

Sheikh Tahnoon separately runs outfits that own nearly half of World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency company co-founded by Mr. Witkoff and still run by Zach Witkoff, one of Steve Witkoff’s sons. Donald Trump Jr. and Barron Trump, two of the president’s sons, also are stakeholders and co-founders of the company, and so they too are effectively business partners with Sheikh Tahnoon.

Sheikh Tahnoon, one of the most powerful players in Abu Dhabi and the United Arab Emirates, controls companies that oversee Lunate, an investment fund that took a major stake in the private equity firm Affinity Partners, which was set up by Mr. Kushner after he left the White House at the end of Mr. Trump’s first term.

Another investor in Mr. Boehly’s group is a pair of Syrian-born Qatari billionaires, Moutaz Al-Khayyat and his brother Ramez Al-Khayyat, who have partnered with Mr. Kushner and Ms. Trump to build a multibillion-dollar resort complex planned for the Mediterranean coast of Albania.

Large chunks of the profits would go overseas.

Trump administration officials are celebrating how the Boehly-backed deal would help U.S. energy security, as the package includes everything from oil production sites to refineries and gas stations. The U.S. government would also take a direct stake in the new enterprise via the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, an agency that helps finance projects overseas. But given the makeup of the investment group, a large share of the resulting company — and the profits it creates — would be foreign owned, according to participants in the negotiations.

Another prominent bidder would lose out.

Approving the Boehly deal now being negotiated with the help of the White House would mean rejecting a competing offer from Carlyle, a Washington-based global investment management firm that already has investments in refineries in Europe. Carlyle’s bid, by comparison, would mean an all-American owner. But Carlyle does not have similar financial ties to Mr. Trump’s family and political advisers.

SUMMARY

A month before the midterm elections, Democrats have opened leads or battled their way to ties or near-ties in five reliably Republican states where they are trying to flip Senate seats to win control of the chamber, according to new New York Times/Siena University polls. Democrats lead among likely voters in the Senate races in Texas and Alaska, two states that consistently vote Republican, the polls found. ARTICLE

Senate Races in Republican States Tilt Toward Democrats, Polls Find
Democrats are performing strongly in five reliably Republican states where they are trying to flip Senate seats to win control of the chamber, new New York Times/Siena polls found.
By Patricia Mazzei, Ruth Igielnik and Sophia June
Published 2026-10-03 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/03/us/senate-polls-texas-kansas-ohio-alaska-iowa.html

A month before the midterm elections, Democrats have opened leads or battled their way to ties or near-ties in five reliably Republican states where they are trying to flip Senate seats to win control of the chamber, according to new New York Times/Siena University polls.

Democrats lead among likely voters in the Senate races in Texas and Alaska, two states that consistently vote Republican, the polls found. They have an edge in Ohio, which has been tilting rightward for years. Republicans have a slim edge in Iowa, and Democrats are neck-and-neck with Republicans in Kansas, which has not voted for a Democratic senator since 1932.

President Trump’s deep unpopularity, disapproval of the Iran war and frustration over high gas prices and the cost of living are reshaping the electoral landscape, the polls found.

Taken together, the new polls suggest that the Democrats have multiple paths to retake the Senate majority, despite a challenging map that had favored Republicans going into the midterms. To win Senate control, Democrats need to flip four Republican-held seats while holding on to their current seats in three battleground states, a difficult task.

But there are signs that it is increasingly possible. On Friday, a top Republican super PAC pulled its money out of the Senate race in North Carolina, signaling that the party is not optimistic about being able to defend its seat there. The super PAC, called the Senate Leadership Fund, plans to redirect resources to Kansas, where Republicans have growing concerns about holding their seat.

The polling suggests Democrats are increasingly competitive in these Republican states.

[Follow all of the latest polls heading into November’s elections.]

In Texas, James Talarico, a Democratic state representative, has opened up a six-percentage-point lead in the race against Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued attorney general and Republican nominee who has been strongly supported by Mr. Trump.

Austin Vaughn, 30, an independent voter who works for a nonprofit and lives in the Houston area, said he voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 but plans to support Mr. Talarico this fall.

“He’s the one actually listening and hearing that those are problems,” said Mr. Vaughn, referring to rising costs. “And the Republicans on the other side are gaslighting everyone and saying they aren’t real problems.”

In Alaska, former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat, is ahead of Senator Dan S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, by seven percentage points. The polling aligns with the results of the state’s nonpartisan primary in August, when Ms. Peltola and Mr. Sullivan appeared on the same ballot, and she won by eight points. A majority of voters there said that they viewed Ms. Peltola favorably; the poll was conducted after allegations of poor treatment toward her staff came to light.

In Ohio, former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, holds a narrow three-point edge in his comeback bid against Senator Jon Husted, the Republican incumbent, with voters saying they prefer the well-known Mr. Brown over Mr. Husted on nearly every issue in the poll. Mr. Brown has an 11-point advantage over Mr. Husted on the question of who would better handle the increasingly potent political issue of data centers, the poll found.

And in Iowa and Kansas, two Midwestern states that have been hit hard by the economic effects of Mr. Trump’s policies, the races are neck-and-neck. In Iowa, Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee, has a one-point edge over State Representative Josh Turek, the Democrat. In Kansas, the Rev. Adam Hamilton, the Democratic nominee, and Senator Roger Marshall are locked in a dead heat.

The polls suggest Democrats are performing well with independent voters, who often decide elections. Across the five states, Democrats hold a 24-point advantage with the group. On issue after issue, independent voters say they trust Democrats over Republicans — including a 30-point advantage on which party does what’s best for ordinary people in their state.

In all but one of the states, Democratic candidates are seen as less ideological than their Republican counterparts. In Ohio, voters were about equally concerned that the candidates were too ideological; 37 percent said they thought Mr. Brown was too far to the left, and 36 percent said Mr. Husted was too far to the right.

It is a striking transformation in five states Mr. Trump won every time he was on the ballot. In Ohio, which he carried with 55 percent of the vote in 2024, only 38 percent now approve of Mr. Trump’s job performance, down from 44 percent in June.

Soaring gas prices, which were driven above $4 a gallon by the Iran war, have continued to hurt the president’s popularity, particularly in the Midwest. About half of Republicans in Iowa and Ohio said that they disapproved of Mr. Trump’s handling of gas prices. Across all five states, Democrats are now more trusted than Republicans to handle the cost of living — reversing the advantage Mr. Trump had on the issue in those states just two years ago.

“You used to be able to get a house — a pretty good house — for under $200,000,” said Bethany Deines, a 58-year-old Democrat in Hamilton, Ohio, who supports Mr. Brown for Senate. Homes in her area now go for more than double that, she added: “I mean, it’s just not manageable for everyday people to be able to really even afford quality housing.”

Perhaps nowhere is Democrats’ advantage more remarkable than in Texas, where Mr. Talarico has been boosted by a growing share of voters — now 60 percent — who say that he has the right kind of moral values, up from 51 percent in June.

Many establishment Republicans, including Senator John Cornyn, whom Mr. Paxton defeated in a primary, warned this year that Mr. Paxton was a flawed candidate who could put what had been seen as a safe Senate seat at risk.

The poll suggests that may have proved true, with a majority of Texas voters saying Mr. Paxton does not have good character. And 45 percent say his past scandals, including his impeachment over corruption charges and a messy divorce from his wife, make them question supporting him — or mean they will not support him at all.

But Mr. Paxton will have a big financial advantage heading into November. Republican groups recently began spending large amounts of money to prop him up, reserving about $190 million in ads supporting him for the final two months of the race.

About half of voters across the five states — 49 percent — say they want a candidate who can provide a check on the president, according to the polls. Just 27 percent say they would prefer candidates who support Mr. Trump.

Nowhere is that more apparent than Iowa, where 53 percent of likely voters, including nearly 20 percent of Mr. Trump’s own supporters, say they want a candidate who can provide a check on the president.

Brayden Blocker, an 18-year-old Republican and college student in Iowa City, said Congress should be “less extreme.”

“With the new Congress coming in, I would say that I think it should just be more moderate members that aren’t necessarily, like, just what Trump wants to do,” he said. “It’s what their constituents want to do instead.”

The divide in voter concern about parties being too ideological is particularly stark in Kansas, where voters are more likely by a 10-point margin to say that the Republican is too far to the right than to say that Mr. Hamilton, the Democrat, is too far to the left.

Senator Marshall, the state’s Republican incumbent, is an obstetrician-gynecologist who filed lawsuits against hundreds of patients over outstanding bills, leading to the arrest of at least 81 patients, a New York Times investigation found. That has become an issue in the campaign.

Half of voters also say they worry that he will support Mr. Trump too much.

“You couldn’t pay me enough money to back Donald Trump or anybody that backs him,” said Alexis Price, 42, a travel adviser in Kansas City who said she does not align with either party. “I think what the Republican Party and a lot of the Republican nominees are doing is disgraceful and disgusting. And I have to vote to my conscience over any sort of party affiliation.”

Across the five polled states, Democrats hold an advantage on nearly every issue, including on the cost of living, which is the single most important issue to voters, along with the economy. Even Republicans’ edge on immigration is slipping. Republicans held just a three-point advantage on the issue across the five states.

Among the strongest measures for Democrats is that voters say that they trust them more to do what’s best for ordinary voters. In Alaska, Ms. Peltola has a eight-point advantage on that question.

Ms. Peltola is viewed very favorably by a majority of Alaskans, including 15 percent of Republicans, and has managed to grow her lead in a state that nonetheless favors Republicans continuing to hold control of the Senate.

“I see her out in the community,” said Jessica Romer, a 38-year-old Democrat in Anchorage. “And I just really like that she’s interacting with people, like getting to know them and what their needs and wants are.”
