SUMMARY

Russia has a new target on its rapidly growing list of Ukrainian infrastructure to bomb: bridges. Over the past three days, Russia has attacked bridges in the capital, Kyiv, six times. The bridges are the latest target in a sweeping Russian strike campaign against Ukrainian infrastructure that is far from the front lines.

ARTICLE

Russia Turns to Striking Kyiv’s Bridges, Threatening a Vital Lifeline
The bridges, used by many commuters in the Ukrainian capital, are the latest target in a broad Russian bombing campaign against infrastructure.
By Constant Méheut
Published 2026-10-03 11:59 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/03/world/europe/russia-ukraine-bridges-kyiv.html

Russia has a new target on its rapidly growing list of Ukrainian infrastructure to bomb: bridges.

Over the past three days, Russia has attacked bridges in the capital, Kyiv, six times. Three drones hit one in the city’s south on Thursday, and the same bridge was struck twice on Friday. On Saturday morning, another attack hit a bridge in the north.

The structures still stand, but the damage and the threat of more attacks have prompted the local authorities to restrict or stop traffic on five of the capital’s six road bridges. That has severely disrupted daily life in Ukraine’s largest city, which, like much of the country, is bisected by the broad Dnipro River.

Many in Kyiv commute between the mostly residential eastern bank, home to roughly a million people, and the western bank, where most government offices and businesses are located.

The bridges are the latest target in a sweeping Russian strike campaign against Ukrainian infrastructure that is far from the front lines. That campaign has expanded in recent weeks to include warehouses, trains, data centers, medical depots and steel factories and comes on top of an intense assault on Ukraine’s power grid that Russia plans to escalate this winter.

The goal, Ukrainian officials and military experts say, is to devastate Ukraine’s economy — and the country’s ability to sustain the war effort — while breaking the population’s will to fight by making everyday life increasingly difficult.

Ukraine has withstood other such campaigns since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. But a critical shortage of air defenses coupled with Moscow’s growing arsenal of weapons now leaves the country more vulnerable than ever to such attacks.

“The enemy is destroying Kyiv,” the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko said in a social media post on Friday. “It is no longer possible to pretend that we can live as we did in peacetime!”

Mr. Klitschko’s message echoed a feeling that has grown across the capital in recent weeks: The relative safety Kyiv enjoyed through most of the war — demonstrated by crowded cafes and nail salons — is over.

Drones now buzz over the city all day, setting off near-constant air raid alerts. People caught outside during an attack can be seen checking phone apps that track the drones’ flight paths. On Monday, a drone hit a university in the city center and set the building ablaze, shocking residents of a neighborhood that had been spared Russian attacks for most of the war.

The assault on Kyiv’s bridges could disrupt life even more. Officials temporarily shut the northern bridge after Saturday’s attack, closed the southern bridge to cars and the metro, and limited traffic on three other bridges.

The first attack on the southern bridge, on Thursday, happened as a metro train was crossing the bridge. No one was injured, but service across the bridge was suspended. On Friday evening, residents crossing the bridge on foot watched as another drone struck it, according to a video posted on social media.

Destroying the bridges would be difficult. They are large concrete structures that would need to be hit multiple times to be taken down. Ukraine’s own attacks on Russian bridges have yielded mixed results. The Kerch Bridge, which connects the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula to Russia, closed temporarily several times after attacks but was never knocked out.

Still, attacks could weaken the bridges’ supporting structures and prompt the authorities to close them indefinitely rather than risk a collapse.

The result would be a logistical nightmare for Kyiv and the whole country. Bridges in the capital carry all kinds of food and equipment across the Dnipro River, which runs north to south through Ukraine and splits the country in two. There would be few alternatives if they closed.

One road bridge crosses the river north of Kyiv. To the south, the nearest is about 90 miles away, a roughly 2.5-hour drive. More bridges lie farther downriver, but using them would mean a long detour, and their proximity to the southern front leaves them even more exposed to Russian attacks.

In the early days of the war, Ukrainian officials considered blowing up Kyiv’s bridges to halt Russian troops closing in on the eastern bank. They held off as counterattacks eventually succeeded in routing the Russian forces advancing from the east.

Dzvinka Pinchuk contributed reporting.

SUMMARY

Sign up for our Watching newsletter to get recommendations on the best films and TV shows to stream and watch, delivered to your inbox. As Netflix pours more of its resources into original content, Amazon Prime Video is picking up the slack, adding new movies for its subscribers each month. (Scorsese’s “The Age of Innocence” is also streaming on Amazon.)

ARTICLE

The Best Movies on Amazon Prime Video Right Now
New films, and classics, just keep coming, but you don’t have to drill down to find the finest selections to stream. We’ll do the heavy lifting. You press play.
By Jason T. Bailey
Published 2020-09-10 05:52 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/article/best-movies-amazon-prime.html

Sign up for our Watching newsletter to get recommendations on the best films and TV shows to stream and watch, delivered to your inbox.

As Netflix pours more of its resources into original content, Amazon Prime Video is picking up the slack, adding new movies for its subscribers each month. Its catalog has grown so impressive, in fact, that it’s a bit overwhelming — and at the same time, movies that are included with a Prime subscription regularly change status, becoming available only for rental or purchase. It’s a lot to sift through, so we’ve plucked out 100 of the absolute best movies included with a Prime subscription right now, to be updated as new information is made available.

Here are our lists of the best TV shows and movies on Netflix, and the best of both on Hulu and Disney+.

‘Frankenstein’ (1931)

Horror cinema was changed forever in the year 1931, when Universal — a scrappy studio known primarily for B-movies and programmers — went all in on monster movies. Tod Browning’s adaptation of Bram Stoker’s “Dracula” (also on Prime) set the template for every vampire movie to follow (doubly so for Bela Lugosi’s title turn), and James Whale’s take on Mary Shelley’s mad scientist novel, released nine months after, further solidified the template for Universal horror: moody, slyly funny, carefully crafted and sneakily poignant, thanks in no small part to Boris Karloff’s wounded work as the monster. Our critic called it “a stirring grand-guignol type of picture.” (Universal’s similarly beloved “The Invisible Man” is also streaming on Amazon.) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Damsels in Distress’ (2012)

Once upon a time, the “Barbie” mastermind Greta Gerwig was known not as the director behind a billion-dollar blockbuster, but as one of the most charismatic actresses on the indie film scene. Her talents are nicely showcased in this sharp-witted, frequently quotable comedy of manners and satire of campus life. The writer and director is Whit Stillman, who helped define smart, talky ’90s indies with his triple play of “Metropolitan,” “Barcelona” and “The Last Days of Disco”; this, his first feature in 13 years, was a welcome return to form. Gerwig is at her complicated best as Violet, who helps her friends (Megalyn Echikunwoke, Carrie MacLemore and Lio Tipton, all memorable) navigate the unfortunate men of the fictional Seven Oaks College; Adam Brody is likably squirrelly as the campus cad. (If you like female-forward comedy-dramas, stream “The Edge of Seventeen” or “Valley Girl.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘The Sheep Detectives’ (2026)

As our critic Alissa Wilkinson noted, a certain kind of movie has all but gone extinct: “family-friendly, PG-rated movies” that were “intended for the whole family to watch.” This gentle, charming mystery-comedy is a fine demonstration of what we’ve lost. The director Kyle Balda and the screenwriter Craig Mazin (adapting the 2005 novel “Three Bags Full” by Leonie Swann) tell the story of George (Hugh Jackman), a kind shepherd who unexpectedly turns up dead. But every night at bedtime, he read murder mysteries to his flock (voiced by a boisterous supporting cast, led by Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Bryan Cranston), who then help the seemingly clueless local constable (Nicholas Braun) solve his murder. As a premise, it sounds inane — “Babe” meets “Knives Out” — and perhaps it is. But the entire enterprise is undertaken with such good humor and quiet grace that it somehow plays. You’ll laugh, you’ll cry, you’ll believe that sheep can solve crimes. (For more fun yet melancholy family entertainment, stream “The Wild Robot.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Project Hail Mary’ (2026)

When Drew Goddard last adapted a novel by Andy Weir, the resultant film, “The Martian” was an earnest crowd-pleaser, with much of the drama rooted in the human need for company and companionship. This film, based on Weir’s 2021 novel of the same name, retains some of that quality, but its tone and style is shifted considerably by the directors Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, whose brainy irreverence made “21 Jump Street” and “The Lego Movie” into unlikely successes. Ryan Gosling stars as a middle-school teacher who is brought in to consult on an international effort to save the sun from losing its energy; over his loud objections, he becomes a last-minute addition to a crew of astronauts. Gosling’s charisma and self-aware wit have rarely been put to better use, while Sandra Hüller proves an unlikely but effective comic foil. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ (2019)

All of Quentin Tarantino’s films are, in their own way, valentines to the movies — steeped in the tropes and traditions of the films of his youth, and the ways that they influenced his perceptions of human behavior and the world around him. But this hangout movie and western riff is his most direct love letter, and specifically to the cinema of the late-1960s in which it’s set, spending a few days in the life of Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio), a TV cowboy whose career is on the skids; his stuntman and right-hand Cliff Booth (an Oscar-winning Brad Pitt); and his neighbor Sharon Tate (Margot Robbie). A.O. Scott praised its “ambling, shaggy-dog structure and the easygoing rhythm of its scenes.” (Tarantino’s “Reservoir Dogs” and “Pulp Fiction” are also on Prime.) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘One Battle After Another’ (2025)

Paul Thomas Anderson’s Oscar winner (nominated for 13, winner of six) and most acclaimed picture to date was in the works for decades, first getting into the filmmaker’s head in the form of the 1990 Pynchon novel “Vineland.” Over the years, that story evolved into Anderson’s tale of Bob Ferguson (Leonardo DiCaprio, pitch perfect), a burned-out formula revolutionary whose years of paranoia are finally borne out when a twisted military man (Sean Penn) organizes the kidnapping of Bob’s daughter, Willa (Chase Infiniti). The resultant “carnivalesque epic about good and evil, violence and power, inalienable rights and the fight against injustice” is the culmination of Anderson’s screen work to date, fusing the loosey-goosey friskiness of his early features with the more disciplined aesthetics and towering performances of his middle period. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

x

‘Eephus’ (2024)

On paper, a group of middle-aged men getting together to play amateur baseball may not sound like riveting cinema. But these characters are developed with such singularity and sensitivity, and played with such next-door-neighbor familiarity, that their seemingly slight hopes and dreams attain end-of-the-world gravitas. They meet at the baseball diamond in the small town of Douglas, Mass., for their weekly games, but they won’t anymore; “Eephus” dramatizes the final innings they’ll play before their Soldier’s Field is bulldozed to make way for a new public school. There are no last-minute efforts to save the field, nor is there a big game whose outcome will change anyone’s life in any particular way. Instead, this is a movie about the act of playing and watching baseball, which involves a lot of hanging out, talking trash, eating garbage food and occasionally hitting a ball. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Support the Girls’ (2018)

The writer and director Andrew Bujalski (“Funny Ha Ha,” “Computer Chess”) creates what looks like a sunny workplace comedy. But he’s up to something much slyer, a smart examination of class and gender politics in one of their most pointed playgrounds: a Hooters-style sports bar and grill, where customers leer at scantily clad waitresses while the manager, Lisa (Regina Hall), tries to keep temperatures cool (and maintain her own sanity). It’s a wise, winning comedy, with a particularly sparkling supporting turn by Haley Lu Richardson, a “White Lotus” favorite. (Hall also shines in “Girls Trip.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Shiva Baby’ (2021)

Rachel Sennott found her breakthrough role as a messy young woman who finds all of the potential land mines in her life exploding simultaneously at the shiva of a family friend in this nerve-racking comedy from the writer and director Emma Seligman. The single location and collapsed time frame give it the efficiency of a well-constructed stage play, but “Shiva Baby” is as tense as any thriller, with the strained small talk, copious side-eyes and unapologetic gossip augmented by nervous camerawork, jarring sound effects and a dissonant musical score. It’s rare for a film to balance such wildly divergent tones simultaneously — to interweave big laughs with gut-wrenching discomfort — but Seligman pulls it off. (For more smart comedy, stream “Modern Romance.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Death Becomes Her’ (1992)

A commercial disappointment upon its original release, this blend of science fiction and social satire subsequently found enough of a cult audience to spawn a Broadway musical. The film stars Meryl Streep and Goldie Hawn as old friends turned romantic rivals, whose shared quest for perpetual youth leads them to a magic potion from the mysterious Lisle von Rhuman, played by the convincingly youthful Isabella Rossellini. Turns out, immortality has its drawbacks. This was one of Streep’s first major comic roles, and she throws herself into the pratfalls and verbal jousts with abandon. Hawn, meanwhile, reconfirms why she is one of the funniest actors of her time. But the real surprise is Bruce Willis, who as the object of their affections eschews his customary smirk and swagger to turn his nebbishy doctor into an inspired comic creation. (If you love wild comedies, stream “Used Cars” and “Matinee.)” Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Collateral’ (2004)

What could have been a formulaic action flick is transformed into an unpredictable, introspective two-hander, thanks to the moody direction of Michael Mann and the thrilling performances of its leads. Go-to good guy Tom Cruise is frighteningly convincing as a businesslike contract killer, the kind of villain who never raises his voice and always gets the job done; Jamie Foxx is sympathetic as the cabdriver who becomes a combination of chauffeur and hostage. The best moments in “Collateral” are the quiet ones, in which these two characters contemplate their stations in life, and their limited options for changing them. “Mann makes thrillers the way that John Ford made westerns,” our critic wrote, “using genre as a way into meaning rather than as an escape.” (Mann’s “The Last of the Mohicans” is also on Prime.) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Atomic Blonde’ (2017)

Charlize Theron starred in this mash-up of a Bond-style spy thriller and a contemporary bone-smashing action movie, directed by the “John Wick” co-creator David Leitch. He carries over that franchise’s “lavishly violent, inventively choreographed fights,” including one corker using kitchen utensils and other household items (giddily if incongruently scored to George Michael’s “Father Figure”), another finding our heroine taking on an army of challengers in one seemingly unbroken take. It’s an ideal role for Theron, who channels all of her sensuality, toughness and physical grace into the role; John Goodman, Toby Jones, Eddie Marsan and James McAvoy appear in memorable supporting roles. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Rain Man’ (1988)

Dustin Hoffman won his second Oscar for his meticulously wrought performance as Raymond Babbitt, an autistic savant who meets his brother Charlie (Tom Cruise) after the death of their father. But “Rain Man” is not a heartfelt, tear-jerking family drama; it’s “a becomingly modest, decently thought-out, sometimes funny film” in which Charlie, a small-time hustler, has to drag his brother on a cross-country road trip to fight what he feels is an unfair inheritance. In retrospect, though Hoffman collected all the awards and accolades, this is Cruise’s film — he’s the character who changes between the beginning and the end — and it’s a marvelous performance, expertly revealing and exploring the psychological cracks in the gleaming golden-boy persona he spent the 1980s perfecting. (If you like ’80s tear-jerkers, you can’t go wrong with “Beaches.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Blue Valentine’ (2010)

As the married couple Cindy and Dean, Michelle Williams and Ryan Gosling are “exemplars of New Method sincerity,” according to our critic, and “able to be fully and achingly present every moment on screen together.” Their director, Derek Cianfrance, tells this story in pieces as they come together and fall apart, in timelines separated by years of hard, unsatisfying living (but shot with only a month between them, an astonishing feat of physical and psychological acting). Aching and heartfelt, the film is an often upsetting yet undeniably powerful account of how not all love stories end in “happily ever after.” Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Blow Out’ (1981)

The director Brian De Palma took an “everything but the kitchen sink” approach to the conspiracy thrillers of the 1970s with his “flashy, eclectic” and ultimately tragic 1981 masterpiece, which cheerfully cribs elements of Chappaquiddick, Watergate and the Kennedy assassinations to create the hybrid story of a movie sound man (John Travolta, excellent) who accidentally tape-records what may have been a politically motivated murder. Nancy Allen gracefully transcends the clichés of her role as a prostitute, while John Lithgow is as scary as he’s ever been — which is no small statement. (DePalma’s “Carrie” and “Carlito’s Way” are also on Prime.) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Dirty Rotten Scoundrels’ (1988)

The 1964 comedy “Bedtime Story” wasn’t exactly a career highlight for Marlon Brando or David Niven, so it probably shouldn’t come as a surprise that this remake from the director Frank Oz has replaced it in the popular consciousness. “Scoundrels” takes the clever premise of the original — warring con artists team up and then compete for the affections and pocketbook of a scene-stealing mark (Glenne Headly) — and gives it several delicious twists, making full use of the comic gifts of Headly, Steve Martin and Michael Caine. An “enchanted featherweight folly,” it makes the case for better remakes: Rather than tampering with the classics, why not fix good ideas that were improperly executed? (For more laugh-out-loud comedy, stream “Borat” or “Fletch.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘The Blackcoat’s Daughter’ (2017)

Osgood Perkins (“Longlegs”) wrote and directed this snowy and chilling jigsaw puzzle of a movie, in which two seemingly unrelated stories of young women teetering on the edge of madness merge in unexpected (and satisfying) ways. Kiernan Shipka is a revelation as a boarding school freshman seemingly abandoned during winter break by her parents and driven to the brink by her feelings of rejection and fear. Emma Roberts is appropriately enigmatic as a capricious hitchhiker, en route to the school for reasons that become increasingly (and troublingly) clear. Read the review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Cape Fear’ (1991)

Martin Scorsese took on his first remake with this iteration of the 1962 potboiler from the director J. Lee Thompson, with Robert De Niro and Nick Nolte in the roles that had been played by Robert Mitchum and Gregory Peck. But Scorsese had no interest in a conventional thriller, so he juiced up this version with his trademark moral ambiguity, transforming Peck’s square-jawed good guy into a flawed adulterer who earns De Niro’s ire by purposefully failing in his duty as defense attorney. Throw in a scenery-chewing performance by De Niro and an astonishingly assured portrayal by a young Juliette Lewis as Nolte’s daughter and you’ve got a fascinating (and violent) fusion of Thompson’s suspense and Scorsese’s sensibility. Our critic deemed it “an essential work by one of our masters.” (Scorsese’s “The Age of Innocence” is also streaming on Amazon.) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘The Queen of Versailles’ (2012)

Perhaps the most trenchant (and entertaining) commentary on the 2008 financial crisis, this biting documentary concerns David and Jackie Siegel, an obscenely rich Florida couple who are in the process of building a comically outsized mansion when the real estate bubble bursts. The director Lauren Greenfield may very well trigger gasps and laughter about the couple’s insane consumption and their subsequent attempts to curb it. But she isn’t content to take cheap shots. She sees her subjects as both perpetrators and victims of a system of conspicuous capitalism, in which too much is somehow never enough. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Chef’ (2014)

Jon Favreau began his career with intimate, indie comedy-dramas, yet he ended up at the helm of giant productions like “Iron Man” and “The Mandalorian.” This was something of a return to his roots, with Favreau writing, directing and starring as a chef who abandons his high-profile restaurant gig to get back to basics in a food truck. The sense of art imitating life is a bit much, but this low-key effort boasts plenty of charm, a handful of laughs and enjoyable appearances by Favreau’s famous friends. (For more indie comedy-drama, stream “Trees Lounge.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Bridesmaids’ (2011)

Kristen Wiig stars in and writes (with her frequent collaborator Annie Mumolo) this comedy smash from the director Paul Feig. Wiig is Annie, an aimless baker whose lifelong pal Lillian (Maya Rudolph) is getting hitched and asks Annie to serve as maid of honor. This duty sets off an uproarious series of broad comic set pieces and thoughtful introspection; both the comedy and drama are played to the hilt by an ensemble that includes Rose Byrne, Jon Hamm, Wendi McLendon-Covey, Ellie Kemper, Chris O’Dowd and an Oscar-nominated Melissa McCarthy. (For more wild comedy, stream “Joy Ride” or “Overboard.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Something Wild’ (1986)

This thrillingly unpredictable romantic comedy and crime movie mash-up from the director Jonathan Demme (“The Silence of the Lambs”) begins as a boy-meets-girl movie with a slightly psychosexual edge, seeming to tell the story of how a wild girl (Melanie Griffith) and a straight guy (Jeff Daniels) meet in the middle. Then Ray (a sensational Ray Liotta) turns up and hijacks the entire movie, turning it into something much darker and more dangerous. Throughout, Demme keeps the focus on his colorful characters and sharp dialogue. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘The Silence of the Lambs’ (1991)

Few fictional characters have embedded themselves in the pop culture consciousness as firmly as Dr. Hannibal Lecter, the brilliant monster brought to bone-chilling life by an Oscar-winning Anthony Hopkins in Jonathan Demme’s 1991 adaptation of the Thomas Harris best seller. The film also won awards for Best Picture, Best Director, Best Screenplay, and Best Actress — a quintuple play only matched two other times in film history — all deserving, none perhaps more so than Jodie Foster, whose indelible portrayal of the rookie F.B.I. investigator Clarice Starling sharply combines small-town naïveté with quick-witted strength. Our critic called it “pop film making of a high order.” (Fans of smart horror will also enjoy “Let the Right One In.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘The Thing’ (1982)

The director John Carpenter loved the 1951 sci-fi-horror thriller “The Thing From Another World” — so much so that he had the characters in his 1978 breakthrough hit, “Halloween,” watch it on television. Four years later, he went a step further by directing this terrifying update of that snowy creature feature, which gets a considerable boost from the more realistic language, themes and gore afforded by the times, as well as the jaw-dropping advances in makeup and effects. But both versions work for the same reason: the skill with which they place their characters in the claustrophobic grip of an isolated location, and then squeeze. (Carpenter’s “They Live” is also on Prime.) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘The Long Goodbye’ (1973)

Robert Altman adapted Raymond Chandler’s late-period Philip Marlowe novel as only he could: idiosyncratically, by updating the hard-boiled story’s setting to the feel-good California of the 1970s and casting one of the era’s most of-his-time actors, Elliot Gould, in the role made famous by Humphrey Bogart. Purists resisted, and some critics scratched their heads. But Gould is brilliant, Altman’s direction is brash and confident, and this “tough, funny, hugely entertaining movie” homes in on the character’s essential, outsider nature, while ingeniously rethinking the conventions of the genre. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Raging Bull’ (1980)

Robert De Niro won his second Academy Award for his fiercely physical and psychologically punishing performance in this searing adaptation of the autobiography of the middleweight champion Jake LaMotta. The stylish boxing sequences are visceral and overwhelming, shot and cut to approximate the disorientation and violence of the sport. But the most disturbing sequences are those of LaMotta in his home, terrorizing his wife, Vickie (Cathy Moriarty, in an electrifying debut) and terrifying his brother and manager, Joey (Joe Pesci, also remarkable). It’s a relentlessly downbeat piece of work, but the force of De Niro’s performance and the energy of Martin Scorsese’s direction are hard to overstate, or to forget. Our critic called it Scorsese’s “most ambitious film as well as his finest.” Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘The Taking of Pelham One Two Three’ (1974)

One of the greatest of all “gritty Gotham” tales — our critic called it “a movie that really catches the mood of New York and New Yorkers” — this darkly funny, white-knuckle thriller from the director Joseph Sargent concerns four armed men who take a subway car hostage, demanding a million-dollar ransom for the lives of the passengers aboard. Robert Shaw is coolly ruthless as the leader of the gang while Walter Matthau is at his hangdog best as the cynical transit cop hot on their trail. (For more old-school action, stream “The Train” and “The Great Escape.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Inherit the Wind’ (1960)

Our critic deemed Stanley Kramer’s adaptation of Jerome Lawrence and Robert E. Lee’s stage play (based on the notorious Scopes “monkey trial”) to be “triumphant,” its climax “one of the most brilliant and engrossing displays of acting ever witnessed on the screen.” The actors Fredric March and Spencer Tracy are in career-best form as the Bible-pounding orator and the agnostic defense attorney on opposite theological and philosophical sides of the evolution debate. Kramer cranks up the carnival atmosphere, to great effect, and pulls a rare (and entertaining) nonmusical supporting turn from Gene Kelly as an H.L. Mencken-esque newspaper reporter. (For more classic drama, stream “Bicycle Thieves” and “Wuthering Heights.”) Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

‘Memento’ (2000)

Christopher Nolan made his first big splash with this, his second feature film, a stylish film noir riff that tells its familiar story in an exuberantly inventive way: In order to mirror the disorientation of its protagonist, Leonard (Guy Pearce), who has lost his ability to create new memories, Nolan tells the story by ordering its scenes in reverse chronology. As Leonard pursues an investigation of his wife’s murder, revelations fold back on themselves and betrayals become clear to the audience before they’re known to him. Yet even without that narrative flourish, “Memento” would be a scorching piece of work, loaded with sharp performances, moody cinematography and a noir-inspired sense of doom. Read our review. Watch it on Amazon.

SUMMARY

We are living in an era of protein hype. A doughnut with 10 grams of protein is still a doughnut. Peak protein may not last forever.

ARTICLE

Have We Reached Peak PROTEIN?
Protein is everywhere — in chips, candy, cookies, even water. Does that make these products healthy?
By Margot Sanger-Katz and Larry Buchanan
Published 2026-09-28 09:05 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/09/28/upshot/protein.html

In our age of protein, there are now protein candies and cookies:

There’s protein coffee and protein water:

And protein chips and crackers:

New food start-ups have proliferated:

While legacy brands have revamped their most famous offerings:

We are living in an era of protein hype. The macronutrient has become a focus of trendy weight-loss advice. It’s an obsession of weight lifters and longevity biohackers. Doctors have been advising higher protein consumption for patients taking GLP-1 weight loss drugs. And the government’s new dietary guidelines, released last year, boosted the levels of recommended protein by more than 50 percent. The guidelines tell Americans to “prioritize protein foods at every meal.”

The food industry, naturally, has caught on to this nutritional trend. Yogurt and cheese are now being positioned as high-protein foods, which they always have been. Prepackaged salami snacks are called “protein packs.”

But protein is also finding its way into foods that haven’t traditionally contained much of it. You can find protein tortilla chips, granolas, baby food, pudding — even ranch dressing.

Over one week, reporters and editors at The Upshot were asked to snap photos of protein marketing in foods they came across in their daily lives. The folder of images grew rapidly. The protein foods are in bodegas, gas stations, grocery stores, warehouse clubs, coffee shops and chain restaurants.

The trend has puzzled many nutritionists, including experts involved in developing the new protein-enhanced nutritional guidelines.

“A snack food is an indulgent food, and people need to understand it that way,” said Donald Layman, an emeritus professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign who helped inform the protein chapter for the guidelines. He said protein-packed chips and cupcakes are “a bad choice.” A doughnut with 10 grams of protein is still a doughnut.

The guidelines advise Americans to eat less processed food and to focus on foods that are naturally high in protein, including dairy, meat, nuts and beans. Protein added to processed snack foods is not the same thing, he said.

“I refer to it as fairy dust,” Professor Layman said. “Fairy dusting over products that don’t need to have protein in them is useless.”

(We neglected to ask him about his views on several protein-infused vodkas, including one that claims it is “crafted for the wellness-minded and fitness-forward.”)

Protein bars, powders and shakes have been around for a while; they long ago broke out from bodybuilding to the mainstream. They now occupy an expanding share of real estate in grocery stores and gas station convenience stores — in many cases, entire aisles.

But there are now also protein versions of everything else, with a range of claims. Sources of protein and good sources of protein. High PROTEIN, PROTEIN-packed, and sometimes just “PRO.” It is almost always in all caps, and often in the product’s name.

And there are snack categories that appear to exist primarily in the protein universe, like sticks and balls.

Even white-label supermarket brands now offer protein foods.

“If you're not evolving and the consumer is, you’re dead in the water,” said Bonnie Herzog, an equity analyst at Goldman Sachs, who tracks the food and beverage industry. Ms. Herzog, a vegan, said her social media feed was filled with advice to eat more protein and tips on how to do it.

NIQ, which collects detailed data on retail food sales, counts 37,232 products in stores carrying front-of-package protein claims.

It has measured around $90 billion in consumer spending on these products over the last year, including more than $2 billion on protein pizzas and $35 million on protein toaster pastries. (Yes, Protein Pop-Tarts exist.)

“You’ve got the claims sneaking into categories that don’t make a lot of sense,” said Chris Costagli, a vice president at NIQ, who monitors the food and beverage industries. “All of a sudden, you’ve got people that are buying the product just because they see the word.”

Whey, the milk-based protein that is the key ingredient in most protein powders, bars and even ice creams, was once considered a waste product of cheese production. It is now in such demand that prices have doubled in the last five years, according to Ever.Ag, an agricultural risk management firm that closely tracks prices in the dairy industry.

“There were a lot of questions over the last few months of are we at the jump-the-shark moment with some of these new products,” said Kathleen Wolfley, the company’s vice president for insights.

But, she said, “we continue to see further innovation in this marketplace.” She also noted that the protein bonanza had been great news for struggling cheesemakers.

Nearly 90 percent of Americans already get enough protein, according to a recent analysis from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. (If you’re curious how much you should be getting, here’s a calculator.) But consumers still seem hungry for more.

Sales of protein-packed breakfast cereals and granola have increased by 15 percent over the last year, according to NIQ. They are often paired with ultrafiltered high-protein milks. (It is those filtered milks that are used to make the protein foams at your local coffee shop.)

Tortilla chips with protein are also selling at a steady clip, driving PepsiCo’s new launch of Protein Doritos, located on a supermarket endcap near you:

Do protein Doritos taste good? Matt Rosenman, a graphic designer who makes social media content examining food marketing and health, said he had tried nearly all the protein snacks, including tortilla chips that were close to inedible. His verdict on protein Doritos was more positive: “Slightly worse version of Doritos, but they are pretty close.”

In videos, Mr. Rosenman shows some of the common tricks food companies use to make junk foods look like responsible choices. Neutral colors and pictures of farms and mountains signify healthy products. Unregulated words like “plant-based” and “natural” help give foods a virtuous halo. But as the protein arms race has intensified, these subtle techniques have faded. Font size has come to dominate protein claims.

With ubiquitous giant bubbles, companies emphasize protein content, sometimes even when products don’t offer much of it. The Food and Drug Administration, which regulates health claims on foods, has relatively lax rules about how brands use the word “protein” on the front of their packages. While there are rules about claiming a product has “high protein” or is a “good source,” vaguer claims in product names and giant bubbles are almost always unregulated.

“It works, and it works for me,” Mr. Rosenman said. “I saw the giant word ‘protein’ and it stopped me in my tracks.”

Doritos itself is a useful case study. The brightly packaged chips have been around since the 1960s, with reformulations for nearly every major diet trend. The original Doritos emphasized that they were tasty with dips. But nutrition claims started showing up in the 1970s, with the information they contained “no preservatives!”

Since then, there have been versions marketed as cholesterol free, less oil,

Low calorie, low carbohydrate,

“Light” and “naked of dyes.”

Of course, you can protein-max by cooking your own food. There are endless TikToks and Instagram Reels about how to consume more than 150 grams of protein a day, often by sneaking chicken breasts and cottage cheese into just about every meal. (Cottage cheese fatigue has become such an issue that there is now a subcategory of videos on how to make high-protein meals without it.)

But junk food is more fun.

Dariush Mozaffarian, a cardiologist who directs the Food Is Medicine Institute at Tufts University, compared protein chips and protein brownies to SnackWell’s Cookies of yore — products that are no healthier than the highly processed foods they replaced, but sheathed in a patina of virtue.

“It’s a bizarre trend, and not supported by the science,” he said.

As Doritos teaches, nutritional fads come and go. Peak protein may not last forever. (Several industry experts casually mentioned that fiber may be the next big thing.) Around 70 years ago, food scientists at what was then the Kellogg Company teamed with researchers at the Harvard School of Public Health to develop a new cereal, called Special K. Its main selling point? PROTEIN!

SUMMARY

Across millions of math sessions by a group that ranged from fifth graders to college students, the researchers compared performance from before 2022, when ChatGPT first came out, with the work that followed its arrival. Researchers found that after 2022, the time students spent mulling over online test questions dropped precipitously on the questions readily handled by chatbots, while their performance improved. But the students who had used A.I. more like a tutor, to explain complex concepts or clarify ideas, not only retained high test scores in the second round, but their essays were higher quality as well.

ARTICLE

Will A.I. Make Your Brain Lazy? Here’s What the New Research Actually Shows.
We’re starting to learn more about how the technology can change us.
By Juliana Castro Varón and Dylan Freedman
Published 2026-09-29 20:34 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/09/29/magazine/ai-chatbots-brain-development-study.html

Machine Learnings

Artificial intelligence is changing the world, and the humans in it, in ways we don’t yet understand. People are increasingly worried that if we rely on chatbots for thinking, our brains will become slower and less engaged. Is A.I. making us stupider? Scientists, too, want to know.

A team of researchers from the University of California, Irvine, and the education company McGraw Hill examined a decade of data from a popular online learning tool by McGraw Hill, starting in 2015. Across millions of math sessions by a group that ranged from fifth graders to college students, the researchers compared performance from before 2022, when ChatGPT first came out, with the work that followed its arrival.

To analyze the results, they split the questions into two types. First: text-based problems that students could easily copy into a chatbot.

And next: visual, interactive or multistep questions that were harder for a chatbot.

Researchers found that after 2022, the time students spent mulling over online test questions dropped precipitously on the questions readily handled by chatbots, while their performance improved.

But when the students were given proctored tests away from their computers, their results were worse than they had been before A.I.

Sina Rismanchian, a Ph.D. candidate at U.C. Irvine and one of the lead authors of the preliminary study, noted that A.I. lets students offload the process required to solve a mathematical problem.

Another multi-institutional study, prepared for the forthcoming Conference on Language Modeling and cited by Rismanchian and his co-authors, shows that when people (in this experiment, adults) become accustomed to skipping the productive struggle of logical and analytical tasks and having the process automated, they are more likely to give up on hard questions that they could otherwise figure out.

A.I. tools condition people to expect immediate responses and deny them the experience of working through challenges, the authors say, which is crucial for skill development and one of the strongest predictors of long-term learning.

“Part of how A.I. is making us dumber,” says Dr. Adam Green, a cognitive neuroscientist at Georgetown University, is “undercutting the development of learning how to think in younger people that now have an alternative.”

Green compares the brain’s tendency to conserve effort to calorie retention.

“Whatever you could do that exerted the least calories but didn’t kill you was the best thing to do evolutionarily,” he says.

But all is not lost. Studies suggest that — for the brain — there are better ways to use A.I.

In July, professors at Middlebury College released a preprint study in which more than 200 undergraduates were asked to write an essay and take a proctored multiple-choice test.

One group of students had access to A.I. to research a topic and write the essay. The other group didn’t. The researchers found that the A.I.-enabled group wrote longer and slightly higher-quality essays. Their test scores were also higher.

A week later, the participants returned for a similar test, but now both groups worked unassisted. The authors broke down the students’ second-round performance based on how A.I. was used in the first round.

The students who relied on A.I. to draft their entire essays in the first round floundered. Their test scores decreased.

But the students who had used A.I. more like a tutor, to explain complex concepts or clarify ideas, not only retained high test scores in the second round, but their essays were higher quality as well.

Experimental evidence suggests that using A.I. not as a full shortcut, but as a means to exercise what they were supposed to learn, allowed them to outperform the remaining participants in the A.I. group and those who hadn’t used A.I. at all.

In other words, these studies so far agree: Artificial intelligence is affecting how people, especially the young, learn and remember. Whether we will be dumber as a result might depend on how — not if — we use A.I.

ai-super-pac-money-midterm-elections.html

SUMMARY

Artificial intelligence companies racing to shape how the federal government might regulate their industry amid rising safety and economic concerns are spending heavily to influence which candidates make it to Congress. A New York Times analysis of federal campaign finance data shows that the political groups aligned with the two leading A.I. developers, OpenAI and Anthropic, have quietly but decisively intervened in key 2026 races, spending on campaign advertising and outreach to voters to the tune of $55.7 million. The Times analysis of federal advertising and campaign outreach expenditures made by the four major super PACs during this cycle showed that they have spent far more money in support of Democrats — $28 million to back 21 Democrats and nearly $19 million to boost 30 Republicans — and that the candidates they backed almost always won.

ARTICLE

A.I. Groups Are Spending Millions to Influence the Midterms
See how groups aligned with Anthropic and OpenAI have funneled major money into the fight for control of Congress.
By Catie Edmondson, Matt Zdun and Daniel Wood
Published 2026-09-29 04:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/09/29/us/politics/ai-super-pac-money-midterm-elections.html

Artificial intelligence companies racing to shape how the federal government might regulate their industry amid rising safety and economic concerns are spending heavily to influence which candidates make it to Congress.

A New York Times analysis of federal campaign finance data shows that the political groups aligned with the two leading A.I. developers, OpenAI and Anthropic, have quietly but decisively intervened in key 2026 races, spending on campaign advertising and outreach to voters to the tune of $55.7 million.

So far, the spending has been concentrated almost entirely in the primaries. The two groups have spent $52.6 million on safe seats — those that are unlikely to change party hands but that often feature intense intraparty contests. The big A.I. players have also spent more heavily for Democrats than Republicans. They have boosted candidates who align with their agendas, helped defeat those they see as hostile to it and ingratiated themselves with front-runners who are likely to be in positions of power in the next Congress to make decisions critical to their bottom lines.

But with voters quickly souring on their industry — including demanding that lawmakers do more to regulate A.I. and halt or mitigate the proliferation of data centers — they have taken pains to obscure their involvement. With few exceptions, they have intervened without ever explicitly mentioning A.I. or data centers in the TV and digital ads they have purchased.

(The Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

The Times reviewed 95 unique ads bought by four A.I. super PACs heavily funded by the two biggest players — the OpenAI-aligned Leading the Future and the Anthropic-aligned Public First Action — each of which funnels its money through separate Republican and Democratic groups. None of the ads mentioned data centers. Only seven mentioned A.I. or an A.I. company directly.

An ad for Representative Barry Moore, Republican of Alabama, featured the phrase “CHAMPION AMERICAN INNOVATION” as he shook hands with firefighters in a garage — one of several A.I.-backed advertisements that used that phrase over images of workplaces that appeared to have nothing to do with artificial intelligence.

Another was in support of former Representative Jesse Jackson Jr., a Democrat running for an open House seat in Illinois. It was paid for by Think Big, which is aligned with OpenAI, and praised him as committed to reducing gun violence and supporting law enforcement.

And in some instances, both the Republican and Democratic groups funded by the same big A.I. player created advertisements advocating opposing sides of an issue. For example, these two spots for House candidates in Texas, one Democrat and one Republican, praise opposite positions on immigration. Both are funded by the Anthropic-aligned super PACs.

“It’s so cynical,” said Nate Blouin, a state senator in Utah who lost a Democratic primary to an opponent who had been backed by more than $1 million in A.I.-funded ads. “They’re coming into races in safe seats that they know that they’re going to be decided in the primaries, and they are spending millions of dollars on things that are unrelated to the core issue that they are pushing for.”

It is a strategy that has also been deployed this cycle by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, another major interest group whose brand has become a liability in recent years and has spent in the midterms to the tune of tens of millions of dollars while rarely mentioning its top issue.

The companies behind the spending have somewhat different policy agendas. Anthropic generally supports stricter regulation on A.I. development, while OpenAI, tends to push for fewer guardrails to allow for the acceleration of A.I. development. But they both share the same goal: promoting A.I. and electing policymakers who hold a favorable view of it.

In a statement, Anthony Rivera-Rodriguez, a spokesman for Public First Action, vehemently denied that the Anthropic-aligned group had a parallel agenda to the political group affiliated with OpenAI.

“We reject any suggestion that we have anything in common with Leading the Future, a group that exists to gut every serious attempt to regulate artificial intelligence,” he said. His organization, he added, “was founded to be the counterweight to Big Tech’s political machine,” and stands “with the people willing to fight for real rules on this technology and protect kids, workers and families from A.I. harms.”

Jesse Hunt, a spokesman for Leading the Future, said the group was “focused on building a bench of champions who understand the need for a national A.I. framework that keeps America at the forefront of innovation while putting responsible safeguards in place to protect workers, families and communities.”

The Times analysis of federal advertising and campaign outreach expenditures made by the four major super PACs during this cycle showed that they have spent far more money in support of Democrats — $28 million to back 21 Democrats and nearly $19 million to boost 30 Republicans — and that the candidates they backed almost always won.

Rewarding the A.I.-Friendly

Late last year, Representative Valerie P. Foushee, a Democrat who represents most of North Carolina’s research triangle, was staring down a formidable primary challenge.

Then, two days before Nida Allam, a younger, more progressive candidate who had challenged her in the past, announced that she was running again against Ms. Foushee, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader, named the congresswoman as co-chairwoman of the party’s new Commission on A.I. and the Innovation Economy.

Two months later, the Anthropic-aligned Jobs and Democracy PAC spent $1.6 million in support of Ms. Foushee. She won narrowly, defeating Ms. Allam by less than 1 percentage point.

“These committees and task forces — they’re basically a flag or indicator to the lobbyist industry that these are people who will have decision-making power over your industry and so you need to go spend money on their campaigns,” Ms. Allam said in a recent interview. “No one is spending that amount of money unless they’re getting something in return.”

In a statement, Ms. Foushee denied that the money had bought any favorable treatment for A.I., saying that her work on the issue “has centered on establishing guardrails, holding corporations accountable, and protecting our children, communities and jobs.”

She pointed to legislation she joined after her primary win that would tax large A.I. companies to establish a federal jobs program and direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology “to ensure proper watermarking, digital fingerprinting and metadata is required for audio and visual content generated by artificial intelligence.”

That record, Ms. Foushee said, “clearly demonstrates that I am here to put A.I. regulations in place that prioritize people over corporations and billionaires.”

Still, unlike many Democrats who have aggressively criticized the industry, Ms. Foushee, a member of the House Science, Space and Technology Committee who also sits on a bipartisan A.I. task force, had already signaled an embrace of the technology. In 2024, she led legislation that aimed to increase diversity in A.I. research and education.

(She was not the only Democrat on the party’s A.I. task force to benefit from the industry’s largess. Public First bought ads in support of Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey that advocate implementing A.I. safeguards, including one that praises him as someone who “can make sure A.I. serves us — not the other way around.”)

In Washington State, American Mission waded into the G.O.P. primary to replace Representative Dan Newhouse, who is retiring at the end of this Congress, to back Amanda McKinney. Ms. McKinney, a Yakima County commissioner, won President Trump’s endorsement this cycle, but was running against a former racecar driver who had won Mr. Trump’s endorsement in 2024 when he challenged Mr. Newhouse.

“She believes the United States must lead in artificial intelligence and advanced technologies, not surrender leadership to China or other adversaries,” her campaign website says. “Amanda opposes heavy-handed regulation that stifles innovation or drives jobs overseas.”

American Mission spent about $780,000 to support Ms. McKinney. She advanced from her primary with 35 percent of the vote.

Punishing the Skeptics

With other seats, in Utah, Illinois and New York, the PACs moved to undercut candidates who had established themselves as foes of A.I.

The most prominent example was in the primary to succeed Representative Jerrold Nadler, Democrat of New York. The race was inundated by outside spending after Alex Bores, an assemblyman, sponsored legislation seeking to regulate advanced artificial intelligence models. That set off a multimillion-dollar influx from rival A.I. interests, with Think Big, aligned with OpenAI, attacking Mr. Bores and Jobs and Democracy, aligned with Anthropic, defending him. He narrowly lost the race.

Along with Ms. Foushee’s contest in North Carolina and a primary in the district of Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz, the former chairwoman of the Democratic National Committee, the race drew the most money from the A.I. PACs this cycle.

In Utah, Think Big intervened to boost Ben McAdams, a former Democratic congressman.

It was not expected to be a highly competitive primary, and was made even less so after Punchbowl News unearthed a series of old posts in which his opponent, Mr. Blouin, joked about sexual assault and made offensive comments about women and Mormons. Mr. McAdams made no mention of A.I. on his campaign website, though he wrote an opinion essay arguing that schools “should begin treating A.I. fluency as a basic form of literacy.” He said he opposed the construction of a 40,000-acre A.I. data-center campus proposed in the district.

But Mr. Blouin, the state senator, described himself as a “leading skeptic of the push for unchecked growth of data centers,” and grew increasingly vocal about A.I. and data-center regulation as the race went on.

Think Big spent about $1.1 million on television and digital ads and text-message blasts supporting Mr. McAdams. Asked for comment, Mr. McAdams reiterated a previous statement he had made during a June debate, in which he said that “every member of Congress needs to be proactive in providing oversight of A.I. in order to protect jobs, our kids, the environment and the fabric of our communities.”

“That will require federal guardrails to make sure this technology happens carefully and transparently, with appropriate regulation, strong oversight, human accountability, and safeguards for data privacy and civil rights,” he said. “A.I. could potentially cure cancer, but it could also destroy our kids. I believe thoughtful policy can unleash the good and stop the bad.”

And in a pair of crowded Democratic primaries in the Chicago area and parts of central Illinois, Think Big spent a combined $2.6 million in support of two centrist former members of Congress — Melissa Bean and Mr. Jackson — who were both running against more progressive opponents.

Mr. Jackson was lagging in fund-raising behind both Robert Peters, a state senator, and Donna Miller, a Cook County commissioner. In the two months before the primary, his campaign raised just $72,000, compared with Ms. Miller’s $670,000 and Mr. Peters’s $224,000.

That is when Mr. Jackson leaned into talking about A.I. He cited it in an opinion column touting the benefits of the technology for family caregivers, discussed it at a local candidate forum and even used it in an ad in which A.I. simulated the voice of former Representative Bobby Rush, whose vocal cords had been damaged by cancer, offering his endorsement of Mr. Jackson.

The progressive candidate in that race, Mr. Peters, had supported a law banning A.I. mental health therapy, and legislation creating legal safeguards for artists whose work was copied or reproduced using A.I.

As Think Big began pouring money in support of Mr. Jackson into the race, Fairshake, a pro-cryptocurrency group, began running advertisements against Mr. Peters, who was backed by Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and other progressives, accusing him of being beholden to corporate interests.

“For me,” Mr. Peters said, “it was like a punishment on my legislative record.”

In the end, neither man won the primary. The victor, Ms. Miller, was not backed by either of the major A.I. players. But they may have seen her as an ally, anyway.

The A.I. section of the “Priorities” section of Ms. Miller’s campaign website is roughly seven times as long as all other issue sections, including health care and jobs.

“I’ll support responsible innovation in technology, digital assets and business development that benefits working people and local communities,” she wrote.

Backing the Front-Runners

The A.I. groups spent in support of clear front-runners in primaries all across the country, including favorites of party leaders, many of them Republican. Representative Kevin Hern of Oklahoma, who was widely expected to win the nomination to replace Markwayne Mullin in the Senate, was backed by nearly $1.3 million spent by American Mission and Defending Our Values before his victory in June.

Defending Our Values also supported Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Representative Monica De La Cruz of Texas, who both received speaking slots at the midterms convention in Dallas. Mr. De La Cruz is favored to win his election; the nonpartisan Cook Political Report recently rated Ms. De La Cruz’s race as a “tossup.”

American Mission spent about $375,000 to support Senator Lindsey Graham for his primary campaign in South Carolina, though it was never expected to be particularly competitive. After he died, the super PAC spent nearly $1.2 million supporting his sister, Darline, in the primary and general contests.

A Vanishing Money Trail

With five weeks left until the midterms, the A.I. groups have yet to wade into many general election contests.

American Mission has doled out roughly $500,000 each on behalf of three Republican candidates for Senate who are running in less competitive races: Representative Julia Letlow in Louisiana, and Senators Darline Graham of South Carolina and Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi. Think Big, the Democratic super PAC, has spent nearly $300,000 to support three House candidates — Representatives Greg Stanton of Arizona, Emilia Sykes of Ohio and Steven Horsford of Nevada — as well as roughly $50,000 to support Representative Joseph D. Morelle in New York.

The amounts could grow. But political operatives closely following their spending believe that the groups will have to shift their strategy amid the furious outpouring of anti-A.I. sentiment, and will instead move money through other means. That could include donating directly to the major political PACs associated with House Democrats or Republicans, or establishing smaller, more obscure groups to move the money through, as AIPAC has done.

Usamah Andrabi, the communications director for Justice Democrats, the ultraprogressive organization that backed many candidates whom A.I. groups spent against, said the industry’s influence was already becoming as difficult to track as that of AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups.

“There was a time where I could tell you every Israel lobby super PAC, and I cannot tell you that anymore because there’s so many pop-up PACs, there’s so many shell PACs, there’s so many pass-throughs,” Mr. Andrabi said. “And I think the same thing is happening with the A.I. lobby.”

Live Updates: Plane to Israel Narrowly Averts Disaster After Pilot Stabbing
Passengers said that they entered the cockpit and subdued the attacker, who Israeli officials said was one of the pilots. The motive for the attack was not clear.
By David M. Halbfinger, Aaron Boxerman, Natan Odenheimer, Max Bearak, Josh Holder, Ismaeel Naar, Johnatan Reiss, Adam Rasgon, Natan Odenheimer and Isabel Kershner, Adam Rasgon, Adam Rasgon and Natan Odenheimer, Isabel Kershner, Karla Adam, Zane Irwin and Leo Sands

Latest

Here’s the latest.

One pilot stabbed another at the controls of an Emirati flight to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, causing it to suddenly plunge thousands of feet until passengers and the crew won a fight to regain control of the plane.

Passengers described a terrifying fall during the attack, which ended when some of them stepped into the melee and managed to subdue the aggressive pilot. Overhead bins swung open, parents clung to their children, and videos from inside the plane showed at least one wounded man and others on board covered in blood.

Crew members and passengers made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, the Israeli prime minister said, and all of the passengers arrived safely in Israel by Wednesday night, after a replacement aircraft was sent to retrieve them by FlyDubai, the airline operating the original flight. As they disembarked, they shared harrowing stories of what happened on board.

A dentist, Shota Musayev, said he was one of the first to reach the cockpit after the attack, finding the injured pilot thrown to the ground there. He said he treated him in midair, including for severe wounds to his head and cuts on his fingers.

Those in the cabin recalled fear racing through them. “In my head, I said, ‘I’m so screwed, I’m so screwed. I don’t deserve to die like this,’” said Peleg Itali, 16, a high school student who was on the plane.

And Asaf Rajuan, one of the passengers who raced to the cockpit, said he and five others “acted on instinct” to restrain the attacker as they realized the plane was out of control.

The plane nose-dived for what felt like 10 to 15 seconds, he said, adding that the passengers’ only hope of rescuing the plane was to work together. Without his fellow passengers, he said, “we’d never have survived.”

One of two other pilots who had been sitting in the row in front of him managed to stabilize the plane, he said, and the pair later landed the aircraft in Saudi Arabia.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video statement that one pilot had stabbed the other and “apparently attempted to crash the plane with its passengers on board,” nearly all of them Israelis.

He called the pilot who was stabbed, whom he identified as Capt. Smit Machchhar, a hero who saved the lives of 174 people.

“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic midair disaster,” he said.

Much about the episode, including the cause of the struggle in the cockpit, remains unclear. The Israeli authorities were investigating whether it was an attempted attack on Israelis or a suicide attempt, among other possible explanations, according to several Israeli officials, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity in accordance with government protocol.

The aircraft sent distress signals and abruptly reversed course near the Saudi-Jordanian border before making an emergency landing at an airport in Tabuk at about 9:45 a.m. local time. Israeli officials said the plane was carrying 160 to 180 passengers.

The pilot and co-pilot were hospitalized in Saudi Arabia after sustaining injuries, according to a statement from officials at the Tabuk airport. Three Israeli security sources, speaking on the condition of anonymity to comply with government protocol, said the pilot who they believed had carried out the aggression was a citizen of Oman. The Omani foreign ministry declined to immediately comment.

Here’s what else we’re covering:

Passengers describe panic and heroics after the cockpit stabbing.

Passengers on a morning flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv recounted scenes of panic and terror on Wednesday as their aircraft suddenly plunged thousands of feet while screams for help came from behind the cockpit door.

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said one of the pilots had stabbed the other, Capt. Smit Machchhar, an Indian citizen, and then had tried to crash the plane. The identity of the pilot who attacked Captain Machchhar has not yet been released.

What began as a routine flight became terrifying when the violent altercation broke out inside the cockpit. Passengers, most of them Israelis, described a desperate scramble inside the cabin, as travelers realized the plane was out of control.

A few rushed into the cockpit and tackled the pilot who had stabbed his colleague before two off-duty pilots, who had been traveling in the main cabin, helped land the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia.

Meital Zoller, who was traveling with her husband and child, said they realized something was wrong when “the plane went up and down.” Then they heard screams, and the plane began diving.

“Within a few minutes, our plane completely lost control, and we felt that this was it — we were about to crash,” one passenger, Miriam Ohayon, told Israel’s I24 News, a television channel. “We heard screams on the plane, and when they opened the cockpit, there was a lot of blood.”

Asaf Rajuan, one of the Israeli passengers who helped subdue the attacker, told reporters that he and five other passengers “acted on instinct” after realizing that the plane was in a steep nosedive. They burst into the cockpit and wrestled with the pilot who had attacked his colleague.

“We neutralized him very quickly,” he said, adding that crew members helped restrain him.

Dr. Shota Musev, a dentist who said he was one of the first to reach the cockpit after the attack, said that he and another passenger tied the attacker’s hands together with headphone cables.

Dr. Musev said he treated the injured pilot for severe wounds to his head and cuts on his fingers. He said the attacker’s body was bloody as well, but it was not immediately clear if the blood was his or someone else’s.

Hila Gaier, who was also on the flight, said that when the plane dived many passengers couldn’t move because of the forces acting on their bodies. “You were sucked downward,” she told Kan, Israel’s public broadcaster. She said she was flying with her partner and two daughters. “I embraced them, told them I loved them, and we tried to practice breathing exercises,” she said.

Flight-tracking data from Flightradar24 showed Flight 1073 descended more than 17,000 feet in less than two minutes. “The plane kept stabilizing and then dropping again for several long seconds,” one passenger, Almog Itali, told Channel 12. The plane landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, and the pilots were taken to a hospital.

Adam Polovincik, 40, who was on the flight with his family, described it as an “extreme experience,” even as he tried to remain calm for his children.

Speaking by phone from Saudi Arabia, which has no formal diplomatic relations with Israel, Mr. Polovincik said the circumstances in the Saudi airport were surreal.

“They brought us food and drink, served us coffee,” Mr. Polovincik said. “Yes, there are a lot of soldiers here and government officials, but the atmosphere is very relaxed, pleasant and respectful.”

The passengers were later flown on a replacement plane to Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv, where they were greeted with Israeli flags. Many said they were still reeling from the ordeal. Peleg Itali, a high school student, described his thoughts as he felt the plane start to plummet.

“In my head, I said, ‘I’m so screwed, I’m so screwed. I don’t deserve to die like this,’” he said.

What to know about the clash between pilots on the FlyDubai flight.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said a pilot tried to seize control of a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, stabbing the other pilot. Passengers and crew members charged the cockpit and subdued the assailant, with crew members making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

According to Mr. Netanyahu, one of the pilots attacked the other midair in a possible attempt to crash the plane, FlyDubai Flight 1073. He said a passenger and member of the crew broke into the cockpit to “neutralize” the pilot-assailant, while another crew member stabilized the plane. The flight suddenly plunged thousands of feet and made an emergency landing at an airport in Tabuk, in northwestern Saudi Arabia.

Israeli officials said the plane was carrying between 160 and 180 passengers. FlyDubai said the passengers were all safe and accounted for. The flight’s pilot and co-pilot were treated in a hospital for injuries, according to the airport in Tabuk. The Saudi authorities arrested the suspected assailant, Mr. Netanyahu said.

Much of what happened aboard the flight remained unclear, including the cause of the sudden altitude loss and any possible motive.

What have passengers said?

What have the aviation authorities said?

Israel and Saudi Arabia don’t have formal ties, but Israelis have occasionally landed there.

The flight to Israel that was diverted Wednesday morning after a clash in the cockpit landed safely in Saudi Arabia, a country that Israeli citizens rarely set foot in.

The two nations don’t have formal diplomatic, trade or tourism ties, though attempts to forge them have been central to U.S. regional diplomacy in recent years.

Still, their proximity has taken Israelis to Saudi Arabia under exceptional circumstances.

The 1944 Convention on International Civil Aviation, known as the Chicago Convention, laid the foundation for how global civil aviation is governed. It states that all parties to the agreement, which include Israel and Saudi Arabia, should assist aircraft in distress in their territory.

After Wednesday’s emergency landing at the Tabuk airport, a civil-military facility in northwestern Saudi Arabia, the Saudi authorities said that they would provide “necessary care” to passengers. Their statement did not mention the flight’s connection to Israel. The FlyDubai aircraft had been flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv.

In the past few years, at least two other passenger flights en route to Tel Aviv have made emergency landings in Saudi Arabia.

In September 2025, a flight from Dubai landed in the kingdom because of a medical emergency on board, according to a statement by the Israeli Foreign Ministry carried by Israeli news media. The plane then continued on to its destination, according to the statement, which did not say which airline operated the flight or where it landed in Saudi Arabia.

In 2023, an Air Seychelles flight from the Seychelles, an island nation in the Indian Ocean, landed in Jeddah because of a technical malfunction, according to the government-funded Seychelles News Agency. The airport said at the time that roughly 130 passengers were staying at an airport hotel.

In a statement at the time, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel thanked the Saudi authorities for their “good neighborliness” and “warm attitude” toward the Israeli passengers.

FlyDubai operates up to 10 daily flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv.

FlyDubai became the first airline offering commercial flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv in 2020 after Israel and the United Arab Emirates signed an agreement to normalize relations.

The new route meant that Israeli passengers could catch connecting flights in the Persian Gulf, rather than having to go via Europe, significantly cutting down on travel time.

FlyDubai operated the first scheduled commercial flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv in November 2020, after Israel and the Emirates signed the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords, strengthening economic, political and security relations.

A low-cost carrier, FlyDubai initially offered two daily flights from Dubai International Airport to Tel Aviv and now operates up to 10. One of those flights made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after what passengers described as a midair altercation between the pilots, which the Israeli authorities were still investigating.

The airline, which began flying in 2009, is wholly owned by Dubai through the Investment Corporation of Dubai, the government’s main investment arm, which also owns Emirates Airlines.

All of the flights between Dubai and Israel travel through Saudi airspace. On Aug. 31, 2020, an El Al jet carrying American and Israeli officials flew to Abu Dhabi along nearly the whole length of Saudi Arabia, the first time Riyadh had allowed an Israeli passenger plane to cross its skies. Two days later, Saudi Arabia said flights from any country to and from the Emirates could fly over its territory, without naming Israel. Saudi Arabia does not have diplomatic relations with Israel.

Most FlyDubai flights fly out of Dubai International Airport’s Terminal 2. Passengers bound for Tel Aviv check in from the much larger Terminal 3, which has heightened security, and can add roughly an hour to the process.

Etihad Airways, Abu Dhabi’s main carrier, added a sixth daily flight to Tel Aviv this summer, making the route its busiest weekly route worldwide.

A passenger describes the chaos of the FlyDubai flight and fears that it would crash.

A passenger on the FlyDubai flight where a clash in the cockpit set off fears of a hijacking Wednesday morning described chaos on board and said that she and others on the plane had thought that it might crash.

The passenger, Miriam Ohayon, spoke to an Israeli television station in one of the first detailed witness accounts to emerge from the plane.

Passengers felt the jet lose control, Ms. Ohayon told Israel’s Channel 24, but some of them intervened to take control. The plane, Flight 1073, which was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv, landed safely in Saudi Arabia.

“We heard screams on the plane, and when they opened the cockpit, there was a lot of blood,” she said.

Ms. Ohayon’s mother, Yasmin Ohayon, told The New York Times that a woman sitting next to her daughter was among the first to realize something was wrong. The woman saw people fighting inside the cockpit as she was returning from the bathroom and alerted other passengers, Yasmin Ohayon said at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv, where families were gathering to wait for the passengers.

“Within a few minutes, our plane completely lost control, and we felt that this was it — we were about to crash,” the younger Ms. Ohayon said, adding that she began reciting a Jewish prayer often said in times of distress.

“I’ve already lost my brother; I can’t do this to my mother,” she said she thought. Her brother, Evyatar Ohayon-Abuksis, a soldier, was killed in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel.

She said that passengers had subdued the attacker and that a nurse and doctor on board provided initial medical care to the pilot.

Asked how the passengers had stopped the attacker, Ms. Ohayon said, “I believe with their bare hands inside the cockpit.”

SUMMARY

The death row inmate Christa Pike was in critical condition and receiving medical care, her lawyers said Thursday, a day after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her. The failed execution on Wednesday night was the state’s second bungled death penalty attempt this year, and Mr. Lee on Thursday said he was suspending executions — including Ms. Pike’s — to allow an independent review. Christa Pike’s botched execution is the second this year in which Tennessee has failed to execute an inmate using lethal injection drugs.

ARTICLE

Live Updates: Tennessee Inmate in Critical Condition After ‘Torturous’ Botched Execution, Lawyer Says
The inmate, Christa Pike, is “alive right now” after surviving an attempt to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyer said. He called on Gov. Bill Lee to reduce her sentence to life in prison.
By Billy Witz, Emily Cochrane, Jacey Fortin, Maia Spoto, Nicholas Bogel-Burroughs, Benjamin Mueller, Shaila Dewan, Rick Rojas and Yan Zhuang
